Our spiritual forefathers had much to say on the many issues facing the American Mennonite church in their time, and we can still learn from the collected writings of these church leaders and brethren. We will look first at the hermeneutics of the early American Mennonite church, endeavoring to draw examples from which we, as 21st-century Christians, can learn.

First, the correct interpretation of Scripture was a matter of great importance to these earlier Christians. They had only recently emigrated away from a largely hostile area, where they had been constantly tested to the point of death on matters of faith and now faced a different set of challenges when confronted with peace and religious freedom. We will look at how they navigated these challenges by studying several of their doctrines and practices.

The Doctrine of Nonresistance

One matter that was well interpreted and applied by many of the early Mennonite writers is the principle and doctrine of the nonresistant Christian. Although many of their Anabaptist descendants of today still hold, to varying degrees, this doctrine, it is oftentimes not done with the clarity and solemnity of their forefathers. The early American Mennonites understood nonresistance as a foundational aspect of the Christian life, as it should be, and taught extensively on the practical application and appearance of nonresistance in the life of a believer. Their primary motivation for living peaceably and without malice toward one’s fellow man was the given example of Jesus. Christ typified the acceptable response to violence and ill-will: gentleness, meekness, as befitted one who is called a Lamb.

The Emphasis of Biblical Foundations

There was also a firm focus amongst early Mennonite writers against building doctrine on the writings of men. This emphasis comes through strongly in their works, as they quote Scripture extensively. They made their point by bringing in an example of Christ or by way of an applicable Scripture verse, rather than building on the sandy soil of a man’s opinions. One of the areas in which they did so was the matter of salvation.

Importance of Practical Salvation

We can learn much from the early Mennonites about the practical working out of salvation. First, salvation is portrayed as both an inward and an outward change. The inward is affected first through the working of the Holy Spirit in the willful sinner’s life. It is an important distinction that the sinner is willful. This position was contrary to most of the greater established churches of the time. If a sinner must be willful, then it implies that all men can willfully accept salvation, an idea that is fundamental in nature, if not always verbalized, to the church of today.

In the early Mennonites’ time, predestination as taught by Calvinism seems to have necessitated this emphasis on man’s ability to choose freely, which is still true today. There is also another flavoring of the “unwillingly saved” interpretation, and that comes from the aftereffects of the charismatic movement and the effect it has had on Mennonite and Amish circles. This “unwilling salvation” is not a matter of predestination, but rather is described as almost a coercive calling by the Spirit. It has been observed in several salvation testimonies where the testifiers recalled how they were completely comfortable in their lives of sin and debauchery when suddenly they would be struck down in the manner of Saul and could not help themselves but follow after God and give their lives to Him. There are numerous pitfalls with this dramatic understanding of conversion, namely that it absolves responsibility from the one converted for his decision to convert. This leads to a lack of counting the cost of Christianity, which is a death of oneself, a death of pride, and a death of favor with man. If the believer hops headfirst into Christianity, not reckoning that he must give up all these self-pleasing traits, how will he be able to grow spiritually if he cannot let go of his former vices? While this form of conversion may be genuine at the beginning, it does not often progress beyond the milk of the Word to the meat of which a mature Christian must partake. This maturing of a Christian is emphasized in writings ranging from those of Menno Simons up to Abraham Goshalk. It is also important for the sake of the church that the believer be firmly committed and engaged in the steady growth of his faith.

The Seriousness of a Pure Church

The idea of church to the early American Mennonite seems to have been a more serious thought, less individualistic than our current state. It is the pitiable state of nominal Christianity that the church has become a social organization with room for all sin and depravity.

It behooves us to consider closely the character of the church that Christ established and to note as well the character of the true churches, unspotted by apostasy and laxness. This character is, like Christ himself, simple and yet incredibly full of meaning and spiritual vitality.

The first aspect of the church to recognize is its pure state as the bride of Christ. Here again, we should consider the character of Christ. Did He ever give Himself space for sin? Do we find Him occasionally indulging in a brief enjoyment of a “guilty pleasure”? The understanding reader will agree that Christ was pure in His entirety, and so how else should the bride be with which He is to be intimately and eternally joined? To aid our minds in answering such a question, let us consider the earthly symbol of this heavenly union: that of a man and a woman joined together for life. This earthly union is recognized even by non-Christians as something set aside purely for the two individuals involved, a relationship and a sharing of each other that is not and never to be partaken of by anyone outside of the intimate union. This paints clearly for our earth-bound minds the mind of Christ, insomuch as that marriage is a symbol of Christ and His bride. The bride and Christ are for each other and give themselves to nothing and no one other.

Now that we can see the purity of the church, let us examine its practical working out amongst fallen man. If it is to be pure, then how are we to be a part of it? Here enters the need for a clear understanding of regeneration, a doctrine held in high regard by these Mennonite forefathers. They taught that the Spirit affects the spiritual washing and cleansing that will be made apparent in a changed state of thought and action in the believer. This change is still at variance with our fallen nature, but through continued surrender and a deep humility, the Spirit will fill the believer until the nature of sin becomes the dominated instead of the dominant. It is important to realize, however, that this victory over sin is brought into effect by the believer yielding his will and allowing the Spirit complete control.

Thus, a pure church is a surrendered, Spirit-filled group of believers who recognize in true humility that their power is not in any way linked to their own merit. The absence of pride, achieved only by the constant aid of the Spirit, gives further room for purification of the willing believer. In this way, we can see the Christian life in shoe leather.

The Teachings of Practical Christianity

The practicality of the early American Mennonite’s faith was continually on display. In his book, “Pride and Humility,” John M. Brenneman maintains that the outward appearance of a person is directly related to his inward heart, a view which extends as well to the actions of the individual. It is necessary to build on the beliefs of willful salvation, regeneration, and a pure church previously examined to frame the mindset of a Mennonite’s interactions in daily living.

To these serious-minded Christians, there was no difference in importance between the religious belief expressed on Sundays and the mundane actions of the rest of the week. This is evidenced by their general abstinence from political matters and other elements of a worldly nature that would infringe upon the beliefs they held. This put them in direct opposition to many of the churches of their day, where thrived two schools of thought: either that one’s earthly duties in a political manner were carried out completely separate from one’s faith, or that the accomplishment of these civic duties were incorporated in the will of God and so permissible for the Christian to engage in freely.

To the early American Mennonite, these types of stances betrayed the very meaning of his Christianity: he was a new person, alive only in the power of Christ that flowed through him. This influenced and directed every aspect of his life, from his business dealings, which were carried out in a way so as not to take advantage of any party involved, to his dress and manner of deportment, which was to be based on humility and plainness, to his method of conversing with his fellow man, which was to show a genuine concern for the spiritual well-being and eternal destiny.

Conclusion

The sum of all these colonial Mennonite beliefs was the doctrine of how to grow into a mature, humble, repentant, but spiritually powerful servant of God. He denied the allures of the world around him in favor of an eternal reward promised upon the purity of his faith and willing renunciation of the sin in which he had formerly lived. This example, lived out by believers like us, should inspire us to further press into the Kingdom of God, working out our faith in humility and repentance.

我们的属灵祖先在其时代对美国门诺教会所面临的诸多问题有许多论述，我们仍然可以从这些教会领袖与弟兄们的文集里学习。我们首先要看的是早期美国门诺教会的诠释学，努力从中提取一些范例，供我们这些21世纪的基督徒学习。

首先，经文的正确解释对这些早期基督徒来说是极其重要的事。他们不久前才从一个大体上敌对的地区移居而来，在那里他们曾因信仰之事屡受考验，甚至至死，如今在面临和平与宗教自由时又遇到另一套挑战。我们将通过研究他们的若干教义和实践，来观察他们如何驾驭这些挑战。

The Doctrine of Nonresistance

许多早期门诺作家对非抵抗基督徒的原则与教义有清晰的解释与应用。尽管许多今日的门诺派和再洗礼宗的后裔在不同程度上仍持守此教义，但常常缺少他们先辈那样的明晰与庄重。早期美国门诺教会把非抵抗理解为基督徒生命的根基性方面，正如它应当被理解的那样，并广泛教导非抵抗在信徒生命中实际的应用与彰显。他们以耶稣所赐的榜样为他们和平相处、无恶意待人的主要动机。基督示范了对暴力与恶意可接受的回应：温柔、谦和，正如称为羔羊者所当有的态度。

The Emphasis of Biblical Foundations

早期门诺作家们也坚决反对将教义建立在人的著述之上。这一重视在他们的作品中表露无遗，他们广泛引用圣经。他们通过引入一个基督的例子或相关的经文来阐明观点，而不是建立在人的意见这类沙土之上。他们在这样做的领域之一就是关于救恩的论述。

Importance of Practical Salvation

我们可以从早期门诺派那里学到许多关于救恩实际运行的事。首先，救恩被描绘为内在与外在的改变兼具。内在的改变首先由圣灵在有意的罪人生命中运行而成。强调“罪人是有意的”是一个重要的区分。这个立场与当时大多数既有教会相抵触。如果罪人必须是有意的，那么这意味着人人都能有意接受救恩；这一观点在本质上对今日教会仍是基本的，尽管并不总是口头表述出来。

在早期门诺派的时代，加尔文主义所教的预定论似乎促成了对人能够自由选择这一强调，这在今天仍然存在。还有另一种“非自愿得救”的诠释，其渊源是灵恩运动的余波及其对门诺和阿米什圈子的影响。这种“非自愿得救”并非预定论的结果，而是被描述为圣灵近乎强制性的呼召。在若干得救见证中有人回忆说，他们在淫乱与放荡的生活中非常安逸，忽然像扫罗那样被击倒，无法自制，只能跟随上帝并把生命交给祂。对这种戏剧性悔改理解存在诸多陷阱，主要在于它将悔改者对转变决定的责任免除。这导致不计代价地进入基督徒生活的倾向，而基督徒生活的代价是自我的死、骄傲的死以及与世人的人情往来之丧失。如果信徒不考虑必须放弃所有这些自我取悦的特性就头也不回地投入基督徒生活，那么当他无法放下旧恶习时，怎能在灵命上成长？尽管这种形式的悔改在起初可能是真诚的，但常常不会从“道的奶”长进到成熟基督徒必须享用的“道的肉”。从门诺·西蒙斯到亚伯拉罕·高沙尔克（Abraham Goshalk）等人的著作均强调基督徒的成熟。为了教会的缘故，信徒坚定地致力并参与信心的稳步成长亦十分重要。

The Seriousness of a Pure Church

对早期美国门诺教会而言，教会观似乎更为严肃，不像我们当前的状态那样个人主义。名义上的基督教处境令人惋惜：教会已成为一个包容一切罪恶与堕落的社交组织。

我们当仔细思考基督所建立教会的品格，并留意那些无沾染异端与懈怠的真实教会的品格。这种品格像基督自己一样，简单却极富意义与属灵活力。

首先要认识教会的一个方面是其作为基督新妇的洁净状态。在这里，我们应当再次考虑基督的品格。祂是否曾为自己留下容纳罪的余地？我们是否看到祂偶尔纵容一时的“罪恶享受”？有悟性的读者会同意，基督在其整体上是圣洁的，那么祂将与之永远亲密联合的新妇理应如何呢？为帮助我们地上的思维回答此问，且让我们考虑这一天上联合的地上象征：即男女为终生结连的婚姻。这一地上联合甚至为非基督徒所承认为专属于两位当事人的纯洁关系，是一种彼此分享、且绝不为婚外之人所共有的关系。这清楚地为我们的属地心思描绘出基督的心意，因为婚姻是基督与祂新妇的象征。新妇与基督彼此属于对方，不将自己给予任何他者。

既然我们能看见教会的纯洁，让我们检视其在堕落人中实际的实现。若要纯洁，我们当如何成为其中的一分子？此处便进入了重生的清晰理解，这是这些门诺先辈高度尊重的教义。他们教导，圣灵施行属灵的洗涤与洁净，这在信徒思想与行为的改变中将显明。这种改变仍然与我们堕落的本性相抵触，但通过持续的降服与深刻的谦卑，圣灵将充满信徒，直到罪的本性不再是支配者而成为被支配者。须认识的重要一点是，胜过罪的这项功效是由信徒交出意志并允许圣灵完全掌权而成就的。

因此，纯洁的教会是一个降服、被圣灵充满的信徒群体，他们以真实的谦卑承认自己的能力绝不与自身的功绩相连。骄傲的缺席——只能靠圣灵不断的帮助才能达成——为愿意被洁净的信徒提供更大的空间。如此，我们可以在切实生活中看见基督徒生命。

The Teachings of Practical Christianity

早期美国门诺信仰的实用性持续显露。在约翰·M·布伦纳曼（John M. Brenneman）的著作《骄傲与谦卑》中，他坚持认为一个人的外在显现直接关联其内心，这一观点同样适用于个人的行为。要构建门诺人在日常生活交往中的心态，必须以先前审视的有意得救、重生与纯洁教会的信念为根基。

对这些严肃的基督徒来说，周日所表达的宗教信念与其余一周平凡行为之间并无轻重之分。这一点可由他们通常远离政治事务及其他世俗元素以免侵扰他们所持之信念中看出。这使他们与当时许多教会发生直接对立，那时存在两种思想流派：要么认为人在属世的政治责任与信仰完全分开执行，要么认为这些公民责任包含在神的旨意内，因此基督徒可以自由参与。

对早期美国门诺人而言，这类立场背叛了其基督徒身分的真正意义：他是一个新人，仅在流经他里面的基督能力中而活。这影响并指引他生命的每个方面，从其经商方式——以不占任何一方便宜的方式进行——到其服饰与举止——以谦卑与朴素为基准——再到他与人交谈的方法——应当表现出对他人属灵福祉与永恒命运的真切关怀。

Conclusion

所有这些殖民地门诺信念的总和是关于如何成长为一位成熟、谦卑、悔改但属灵有能力的上帝仆人的教义。他否认周围世界的诱惑，转而追求在信心纯洁与甘愿舍弃他过去生活中的罪上的应许永远赏赐。这样的榜样，由像我们这样的信徒在生活中实践，应当激励我们更加迫切进入上帝的国度，在谦卑与悔改中操练我们的信心。

This hymn became precious to my family and me several years ago as we awaited the birth of our fourth genetically challenged baby. We knew she couldn't stay with us very long. She passed away at just three days old. After researching this hymn, I was amazed to find out that the man whose story had inspired this hymn had lost eight out of his nine children.

The story of this man is a notable one. His 61 years on earth were marked by grief and loss, persecution and imprisonment. Yet, his dedication to Christ was outstanding, and his fire for God and zeal for preaching the gospel never waned until his last day.

Samuel Rutherford, son of a prosperous farmer, was born in the year 1600. His life began in the small village of Nisbet, Scotland. As we glimpse into his life, we notice the hand of God at work in Samuel’s early years. At only three years old, he was playing with his friends when he fell into the town well. His sister and friends ran to get help. When they returned, they found a very wet Samuel sitting on the grass beside the well. They asked him how he got out, and his reply was, "A bonny white man came and drew me out of the well." His family believed that God sent an angel to rescue him that day.

From what we know about Samuel Rutherford, he had two brothers and one sister. He was sent to school when he was young, and he became a very diligent scholar. He learned Latin and Greek so well that he eventually became a professor. He married Eupham Hamilton around 1624, soon after he began teaching at Edinburgh University. At this time, Samuel was yet unconverted and cared only for pursuing his academic goals.

In 1626, at the age of 26, Samuel came to a clear and saving faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. He said, "O but Christ hath a saving eye. When He first looked on me I was saved. It cost Him but a look to make hell quit to me." From that moment he was filled with a passion to preach and to speak about his Saviour. This change of life caused such a stir in the university that Rutherford ended up resigning his professorship.

In 1627, Samuel took his wife and two young children to Galloway, Scotland, where he began pastoring the small church of Anwoth. As he commenced his calling there he said, "I have received the commission from the royal and princely Master, my Lord Jesus, to preach Christ to the people." His passion was for the conversion of the people, and it is said that he seemed to be always praying, always preaching, always visiting the sick, always teaching and instructing, always writing or studying. The zeal with which he preached and his concern for the welfare of his congregation had a great effect on them. Not only them, but folks came from the surrounding towns and villages to hear his preaching. A friend once reported, "Many times I thought he would have flown out of the pulpit when he came to speak of Jesus Christ."

Samuel was not estranged from grief and sorrow. In 1631, only four short years after he began his work as a pastor, his wife passed away. His two children also became ill and left this world. In 1636, after nine years of preaching, he was banished to Aberdeen, where he was forbidden to preach the gospel. This was a very difficult time for him as he greatly missed his wife and children as well as his congregation, the Church at Anwoth. This time in his life is indeed one reason he is so well remembered, for he began writing letters back to his church people and friends. Out of the 365 letters he wrote, 220 of them were written during these 22 months of banishment.

The government eventually changed hands, which gave more liberty to the non-conformist Covenanters. Thereupon Rutherford quickly returned to his beloved flock at Anwoth. About a year later, in the fall of 1639, he again reluctantly left Anwoth but this time to fulfill an appointment to become Professor of Divinity at St Mary's College in St. Andrews. This change was difficult for him, as he again greatly missed his congregation. He writes, "My removal from my flock is so heavy to me, that it maketh my life a burden to me, I had never such a longing for death. The Lord help and hold up this sad clay."

After five months in his new position and having been alone for nearly ten years, the 40-year-old Samuel married Jean McMath. Together they had seven children. Sadly, six of them died in infancy and early childhood. Only a daughter named Agnes survived to adulthood.

Rutherford continued to be an influential leader in the non-conformist movement in Scotland for the next 20 years until 1660. With the death of Cromwell, the rule of the commonwealth came to an end, and Charles II was restored to power. Once again, the wrath of the monarchy fell on Samuel. He was summoned to appear before the judge and charged with high treason against the government for preaching the truth. He was put in prison to await execution. However, before the king could put him to death, Samuel became quite sick. He said, "I have a summons already from a superior Judge, and I behoove to answer my first summons and when your day arrives I shall be where few Kings and great folks come."

Late in the afternoon of the last day of his life in answer to the question, "What think ye now of Christ?" answered thusly, "Oh, that all my brethren in the land may know what a Master I have served, and what peace I have this day! I shall sleep in Christ, and when I awake, I shall be satisfied with His likeness. This night shall close the door, and put my anchor within the veil, and I shall go away in a sleep by five of the clock in the morning. Glory! glory to my Creator and my Redeemer forever! I Shall live and adore Him. Oh, for arms to embrace Him! Oh, for a well-tuned harp! Glory! glory dwelleth in Immanuel's land!" These words were heard by his wife, daughter and friends, and he was indeed with his Lord by five in the morning.

Nearly two centuries later, Annie Ross Cousin, a Scottish poet and hymn writer and the wife of a minister, was inspired by the life and writings of Samuel Rutherford. She summarized his life in a biographical hymn,"The Sands of Time are Sinking". This hymn was first published in 1857 in the Christian Treasury. Out of the nineteen original verses, only four are used in our hymn books. (in bold copy)

The sands of time are sinking,
The dawn of heaven breaks,
The summer morn I’ve sighed for,
The fair, sweet morn awakes:
Dark, dark hath been the midnight,
But dayspring is at hand,
And glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

2. Oh! well it is forever,
Oh! well forevermore
My nest hung in no forest
Of all this death-doomed shore!
Yea, let the vain world vanish,
As from the ship the stand,
While glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

3. There the Red Rose of Sharon
Unfolds its heart-most bloom.
And fills the air of Heaven
With ravishing perfume;
Oh, to behold its blossom,
While by its fragrance fann’d
Where glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

4. The King there in His beauty,
Without a veil is seen:
It were a well-spent journey
Though seven deaths lay between:
The Lamb with His fair army,
Doth on Mount Zion stand;
And glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

5. Oh! Christ He is the fountain,
The deep sweet well of Love!
The streams on earth I’ve tasted,
More deep I’ll drink above;
There, to an ocean fullness,
His mercy doth expand,
And glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

6. E’en Anwoth was not heaven—
E’en preaching was not Christ;
And in my sea-beat prison
My Lord and I held tryst:
And aye my murkiest storm-cloud
Was by a rainbow spann’d,
Caught from the glory dwelling
In Immanuel’s land.

7. But that He built a heaven
Of His surpassing love,
A little New Jerus’lem,
Like to the one above,—
“Lord, take me o’er the water,”
Had been my loud demand,
“Take me to love’s own country,
Unto Immanuel’s land.”

8. But flowers need night’s cool darkness,
The moonlight and the dew;
So Christ, from one who loved it,
His shining oft withdrew;
And then, for cause of absence,
My troubled soul I scann’d—
But glory, shadeless, shineth
In Immanuel’s land.

9. The little birds of Anwoth,
used to count them blest,—
Now, beside happier alters,
go to built my nest:
O’er these there broods no silence,
No graves around them stand,
For glory, deathless, dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

10. Fair Anwoth by the Solway,
To me thou still art dear!
E’en from the verge of Heaven
I drop for thee a tear.
Oh! if one soul from Anwoth
Meet me at God’s right hand,
My Heaven will be two Heavens,
In Immanuel’s land!

11. I’ve wrestled on towards Heaven,
‘Ganst storm, and wind, and tide;—
Now, like a weary traveler,
That leaneth on his guide,
Amid the shades of evening,
While sinks life’s ling’ring sand,
I hail the glory dawning
From Immanuel’s land.

12. Deep waters cross’d life’s pathway,
The hedge of thorns was sharp;
Now these lie all behind me,—
Oh, for a well-tuned harp!
Oh, to join Hallelujah
With yon triumphant band,
Who sing where glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land!

13. With mercy and with judgment
My web of time He wove,
And aye the dews of sorrow
Were lustered with His love!
I’ll bless the hand that guided,
I’ll bless the heart that plann’d,
When throned where glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

14. Soon shall the cup of glory
Wash down earth’s bitterest woes,
Soon shall the desert brier
Break into Eden’s rose:
The curse shall change to blessing–
The name on earth that’s bann’d,
Be graven on the white stone
In Immanuel’s land.

15. Oh! I am my Beloved’s,
And my Beloved’s mine!
He brings a poor vile sinner
Into His “house of wine:”
I stand upon His merit,
I know no other stand,
Not e’en where glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

16. I shall sleep sound in Jesus,
Fill’d with His likeness rise,
To live and to adore Him,
To see Him with these eyes:
‘Tween me and resurrection
But Paradise doth stand;
Then—then for glory dwelling
In Immanuel’s land!

17. The bride eyes not her garment,
But her dear Bridegroom’s face;
I will not gaze at glory,
But on my King of Grace—
Not at the crown He giveth,
But on His pierced hand:
The Lamb is all the glory
Of Immanuel’s land.

18. I have borne scorn and hatred,
I have borne wrong and shame,
Earth’s proud ones have reproach’d me,
For Christ’s thrice blessed name:
Where God His seal set fairest
They’ve stamp’d their foulest brand;
But judgment shines like noonday
In Immanuel’s land.

19. They’ve summoned me before them,
But there I may not come,—
My Lord says, “Come up hither,”
My Lord says, “Welcome home!
My King now at His white throne,
My presence doth command,
Where glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

The fine complementary tune for this text was composed in the early 1800s by a French musician, Chretien D`Urhan. It is well fitted to the words of the hymn—its solemn tempo matches the solemnity of the words. The rising melodic line of the last phrase perfectly matches the anticipated joy expressed by the refrain—"And glory, glory dwelleth in Immanuel's land."

As we conclude this hymn history, let us continue to marvel at the providence of God in the lives of those who have gone before us. May we follow Christ with all our hearts and be vessels ready for the Master's use! One last quote by Samuel Rutherford to take with us. "They lose nothing who gain Christ."

Sungguh menakjubkan bagi saya melihat bagaimana Allah memakai umat-Nya sepanjang sejarah untuk membawa kemuliaan bagi nama-Nya. Ia memakai hal-hal yang lemah untuk membingungkan orang-orang bijak; hal-hal rendah untuk meniadakan hikmat orang-orang cerdik di dunia. Himne ini menjadi berharga bagi keluarga saya dan saya beberapa tahun yang lalu ketika kami menantikan kelahiran anak keempat kami yang memiliki gangguan genetik. Kami tahu ia tidak bisa tinggal bersama kami dalam waktu yang lama. Ia meninggal pada umur baru tiga hari. Setelah meneliti himne ini, saya terkejut mengetahui bahwa pria yang kisahnya mengilhami himne ini telah kehilangan delapan dari sembilan anaknya.

Kisah pria ini sungguh mengesankan. 61 tahunnya di dunia ditandai oleh dukacita dan kehilangan, penganiayaan dan pemenjaraan. Namun, pengabdiannya kepada Kristus luar biasa, dan semangatnya untuk Tuhan serta gairahnya memberitakan Injil tak pernah pudar sampai hari terakhirnya.

Samuel Rutherford, putra seorang petani yang makmur, dilahirkan pada tahun 1600. Hidupnya bermula di desa kecil Nisbet, Skotlandia. Saat kita menengok kehidupannya, kita melihat tangan Allah bekerja pada tahun-tahun awal Samuel. Pada umur hanya tiga tahun, dia sedang bermain dengan teman-temannya ketika ia jatuh ke dalam sumur kota. Saudari dan teman-temannya lari meminta tolong. Ketika mereka kembali, mereka menemukan Samuel yang sangat basah duduk di atas rumput di sebelah sumur. Mereka bertanya bagaimana ia bisa keluar, dan jawabnya, "Seorang pria putih yang cantik datang dan menarikku keluar dari sumur." Keluarganya percaya bahwa Allah mengutus seorang malaikat untuk menyelamatkannya hari itu.

Dari apa yang kita ketahui tentang Samuel Rutherford, ia memiliki dua saudara laki-laki dan satu saudara perempuan. Ia dikirim bersekolah ketika masih muda, dan ia menjadi seorang pelajar yang sangat tekun. Ia belajar bahasa Latin dan Yunani begitu baik sehingga akhirnya menjadi seorang profesor. Ia menikahi Eupham Hamilton sekitar tahun 1624, tak lama setelah ia mulai mengajar di Universitas Edinburgh. Pada masa itu, Samuel belum bertobat dan hanya peduli mengejar tujuan akademisnya.

Pada tahun 1626, pada usia 26 tahun, Samuel datang kepada iman yang jelas dan menyelamatkan kepada Tuhan Yesus Kristus. Ia berkata, "Oh tetapi Kristus mempunyai mata yang menyelamatkan. Ketika Dia pertama kali menatapku aku diselamatkan. Hanya perlu satu tatapan dari-Nya untuk membuat neraka melepaskan aku." Sejak saat itu ia dipenuhi hasrat untuk berkhotbah dan berbicara tentang Juruselamatnya. Perubahan hidup ini menimbulkan kehebohan di universitas sehingga Rutherford akhirnya mengundurkan diri dari jabatan profesor.

Pada tahun 1627, Samuel membawa istrinya dan dua anak kecil ke Galloway, Skotlandia, tempat ia mulai melayani sebagai pendeta jemaat kecil Anwoth. Saat ia memulai panggilannya di sana ia berkata, "Aku telah menerima komisi dari Sang Tuan yang kerajaan dan bangsawan, Tuhanku Yesus, untuk memberitakan Kristus kepada orang-orang." Hasratnya adalah untuk pertobatan orang-orang, dan dikatakan bahwa ia tampak selalu berdoa, selalu berkhotbah, selalu mengunjungi orang sakit, selalu mengajar dan menasihati, selalu menulis atau belajar. Semangat yang ia miliki dalam berkhotbah dan perhatiannya terhadap kesejahteraan jemaatnya memberi pengaruh besar bagi mereka. Bukan hanya mereka, tetapi orang-orang datang dari kota dan desa sekitar untuk mendengar khotbahnya. Seorang teman pernah melaporkan, "Banyak kali aku berpikir ia akan melayang keluar dari mimbar ketika ia mulai berbicara tentang Yesus Kristus."

Samuel tidak asing dengan dukacita dan kesedihan. Pada tahun 1631, hanya empat tahun setelah ia memulai tugasnya sebagai pendeta, istrinya meninggal. Dua anaknya juga jatuh sakit dan meninggalkan dunia ini. Pada tahun 1636, setelah sembilan tahun berkhotbah, ia diusir ke Aberdeen, di mana ia dilarang berkhotbah tentang Injil. Ini adalah masa yang sangat sulit baginya karena ia sangat merindukan istrinya dan anak-anaknya serta jemaatnya, Gereja di Anwoth. Masa ini dalam hidupnya memang salah satu alasan mengapa ia dikenang begitu baik, karena ia mulai menulis surat kembali kepada jemaat dan teman-temannya. Dari 365 surat yang ia tulis, 220 di antaranya ditulis selama 22 bulan pembuangannya ini.

Pemerintahan akhirnya berganti tangan, yang memberi lebih banyak kebebasan kepada para Covenanter non-konformis. Maka Rutherford segera kembali kepada kawanan terkasihnya di Anwoth. Sekitar setahun kemudian, pada musim gugur 1639, ia sekali lagi dengan enggan meninggalkan Anwoth tetapi kali ini untuk memenuhi penunjukan menjadi Profesor Teologi di St Mary's College di St. Andrews. Perubahan ini sulit baginya, karena sekali lagi ia sangat merindukan jemaatnya. Ia menulis, "Pindahku dari kawanan adalah begitu berat bagiku, sehingga membuat hidupku menjadi beban bagiku, aku belum pernah mempunyai kerinduan sebesar untuk mati. Tuhan tolong dan tahanlah tanah yang sedih ini."

Setelah lima bulan di posisi barunya dan setelah hampir sepuluh tahun sendirian, Samuel yang berusia 40 tahun menikahi Jean McMath. Bersama mereka memiliki tujuh anak. Sayangnya, enam di antaranya meninggal pada bayi dan masa kanak-kanak awal. Hanya seorang putri bernama Agnes yang hidup sampai dewasa.

Rutherford terus menjadi pemimpin berpengaruh dalam gerakan non-konformis di Skotlandia selama 20 tahun berikutnya sampai tahun 1660. Dengan wafatnya Cromwell, pemerintahan republik berakhir, dan Charles II dipulihkan berkuasa. Sekali lagi, murka monarki jatuh pada Samuel. Ia dipanggil untuk tampil di hadapan hakim dan didakwa pengkhianatan tinggi terhadap pemerintahan karena berkhotbah tentang kebenaran. Ia dimasukkan ke penjara untuk menunggu eksekusi. Namun, sebelum raja sempat mematikannya, Samuel menjadi sangat sakit. Ia berkata, "Aku sudah menerima panggilan dari Hakim yang lebih tinggi, dan aku harus menjawab panggilan pertamaku dan ketika hari kalian tiba aku akan berada di tempat di mana sedikit Raja dan orang besar datang."

Menjelang sore hari pada hari terakhir hidupnya sebagai jawaban atas pertanyaan, "Apa yang kamu pikirkan sekarang tentang Kristus?" ia menjawab demikian, "Oh, kiranya semua saudara-saudaraku di tanah ini tahu siapa Tuan yang telah kupakai, dan damai apa yang kumiliki hari ini! Aku akan tidur dalam Kristus, dan ketika aku bangun, aku akan dipuaskan dengan rupa-Nya. Malam ini akan menutup pintu, dan menaruh jangkarku di dalam tabir, dan aku akan pergi dalam tidur pada pukul lima pagi. Kemuliaan! kemuliaan bagi Penciptaku dan Penebusku selamanya! Aku akan hidup dan menyembah Dia. Oh, untuk lengan yang mampu memeluk-Nya! Oh, untuk kecapi yang selaras! Kemuliaan! kemuliaan berdiam di negeri Immanuel!" Kata-kata ini didengar oleh istri, putri dan teman-temannya, dan ia memang bersama Tuhannya pada pukul lima pagi.

Hampir dua abad kemudian, Annie Ross Cousin, seorang penyair Skotlandia dan penulis himne serta istri seorang pendeta, terinspirasi oleh kehidupan dan tulisan-tulisan Samuel Rutherford. Ia meringkas hidupnya dalam sebuah himne biografis, "The Sands of Time are Sinking". Himne ini pertama kali diterbitkan pada tahun 1857 di Christian Treasury. Dari sembilan belas bait asli, hanya empat yang digunakan dalam buku himne kita. (dalam salinan tebal)

The sands of time are sinking,
The dawn of heaven breaks,
The summer morn I’ve sighed for,
The fair, sweet morn awakes:
Dark, dark hath been the midnight,
But dayspring is at hand,
And glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

2. Oh! well it is forever,
Oh! well forevermore
My nest hung in no forest
Of all this death-doomed shore!
Yea, let the vain world vanish,
As from the ship the stand,
While glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

3. There the Red Rose of Sharon
Unfolds its heart-most bloom.
And fills the air of Heaven
With ravishing perfume;
Oh, to behold its blossom,
While by its fragrance fann’d
Where glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

4. The King there in His beauty,
Without a veil is seen:
It were a well-spent journey
Though seven deaths lay between:
The Lamb with His fair army,
Doth on Mount Zion stand;
And glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

5. Oh! Christ He is the fountain,
The deep sweet well of Love!
The streams on earth I’ve tasted,
More deep I’ll drink above;
There, to an ocean fullness,
His mercy doth expand,
And glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

6. E’en Anwoth was not heaven—
E’en preaching was not Christ;
And in my sea-beat prison
My Lord and I held tryst:
And aye my murkiest storm-cloud
Was by a rainbow spann’d,
Caught from the glory dwelling
In Immanuel’s land.

7. But that He built a heaven
Of His surpassing love,
A little New Jerus’lem,
Like to the one above,—
“Lord, take me o’er the water,”
Had been my loud demand,
“Take me to love’s own country,
Unto Immanuel’s land.”

8. But flowers need night’s cool darkness,
The moonlight and the dew;
So Christ, from one who loved it,
His shining oft withdrew;
And then, for cause of absence,
My troubled soul I scann’d—
But glory, shadeless, shineth
In Immanuel’s land.

9. The little birds of Anwoth,
used to count them blest,—
Now, beside happier alters,
go to built my nest:
O’er these there broods no silence,
No graves around them stand,
For glory, deathless, dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

10. Fair Anwoth by the Solway,
To me thou still art dear!
E’en from the verge of Heaven
I drop for thee a tear.
Oh! if one soul from Anwoth
Meet me at God’s right hand,
My Heaven will be two Heavens,
In Immanuel’s land!

11. I’ve wrestled on towards Heaven,
‘Ganst storm, and wind, and tide;—
Now, like a weary traveler,
That leaneth on his guide,
Amid the shades of evening,
While sinks life’s ling’ring sand,
I hail the glory dawning
From Immanuel’s land.

12. Deep waters cross’d life’s pathway,
The hedge of thorns was sharp;
Now these lie all behind me,—
Oh, for a well-tuned harp!
Oh, to join Hallelujah
With yon triumphant band,
Who sing where glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land!

13. With mercy and with judgment
My web of time He wove,
And aye the dews of sorrow
Were lustered with His love!
I’ll bless the hand that guided,
I’ll bless the heart that plann’d,
When throned where glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

14. Soon shall the cup of glory
Wash down earth’s bitterest woes,
Soon shall the desert brier
Break into Eden’s rose:
The curse shall change to blessing–
The name on earth that’s bann’d,
Be graven on the white stone
In Immanuel’s land.

15. Oh! I am my Beloved’s,
And my Beloved’s mine!
He brings a poor vile sinner
Into His “house of wine:”
I stand upon His merit,
I know no other stand,
Not e’en where glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

16. I shall sleep sound in Jesus,
Fill’d with His likeness rise,
To live and to adore Him,
To see Him with these eyes:
‘Tween me and resurrection
But Paradise doth stand;
Then—then for glory dwelling
In Immanuel’s land!

17. The bride eyes not her garment,
But her dear Bridegroom’s face;
I will not gaze at glory,
But on my King of Grace—
Not at the crown He giveth,
But on His pierced hand:
The Lamb is all the glory
Of Immanuel’s land.

18. I have borne scorn and hatred,
I have borne wrong and shame,
Earth’s proud ones have reproach’d me,
For Christ’s thrice blessed name:
Where God His seal set fairest
They’ve stamp’d their foulest brand;
But judgment shines like noonday
In Immanuel’s land.

19. They’ve summoned me before them,
But there I may not come,—
My Lord says, “Come up hither,”
My Lord says, “Welcome home!
My King now at His white throne,
My presence doth command,
Where glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

Melodi pelengkap yang halus untuk teks ini disusun pada awal tahun 1800-an oleh seorang musisi Prancis, Chretien D`Urhan. Melodi itu sangat cocok dengan kata-kata himne—tempo yang khidmat sesuai dengan kesakralan kata-katanya. Garis melodi yang naik pada frasa terakhir sangat cocok dengan sukacita yang dinantikan yang diungkapkan oleh bait pengulangan—"And glory, glory dwelleth in Immanuel's land."

Saat kita menyudahi sejarah himne ini, marilah kita terus takjub atas penyelenggaraan Allah dalam kehidupan mereka yang telah mendahului kita. Semoga kita mengikuti Kristus dengan segenap hati dan menjadi bejana yang siap dipakai Sang Tuan! Satu kutipan terakhir oleh Samuel Rutherford untuk kita bawa. "They lose nothing who gain Christ."

The glory of the spring, how sweet!
The newborn life, how glad!
What joy the happy earth to greet
In new, bright raiment clad!

Divine Redeemer, Thee I bless;
I greet Thy going forth;
I love Thee in the loveliness
Of Thy renewed earth.

But O these wonders of Thy grace,
These nobler works of Thine,
These marvels sweeter far to trace,
These new births more divine:

This new-born glow of faith so strong,
This bloom of love so fair,
This new-born ecstasy of song,
And fragrancy of prayer!

Creator Spirit, work in me
These wonders sweet of Thine;
Divine Redeemer, graciously
Renew this heart of mine.

Still, let new life and strength upspring,
Still, let new joy be given;
And grant the glad new song to ring
Through the new earth and Heaven.

Vårens herlighet, så søt!
Det nyfødte liv, så glad!
Hvilken fryd å møte jordens møte
I nytt, lyst draktelag!

Gjenløser Gud, jeg priser Deg;
Jeg hilser Din utgangs ferd;
Jeg elsker Deg i skjønnheten
Av Din fornyede jord.

Men å, disse under av Din nåde,
Disse edlere gjerninger av Deg,
Disse under søtere å spore,
Disse nyfødte mer guddommelige fødsler:

Dette nyfødte mot til tro så sterk,
Denne kjærlighets blomstring så skjønn,
Denne nyfødte salighet i sang,
Og bønnens velduft!

Skaperens Ånd, arbeid i meg
Disse dine søte undere;
Gjenløser Gud, nådig forny
Dette mitt hjerte.

La dog nytt liv og styrke spire,
La dog ny glede bli gitt;
Og la den glade nye sangen klinge
Gjennom den nye jord og Himmelen.

A wonderful thing about being a Christian is anticipating the day when we feast our eyes on the magnificent beauty of our God. Quite likely, we have all created mental pictures of what we think God might look like, although we know that our wildest imaginations will be exceeded. “Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty: they shall behold the land that is very far off” (Isaiah 33:17). The Bible is full of descriptive word pictures attempting to give us a brief glimpse into the realms of the heavenly. The landscape on the hills of glory, the wonderful creatures that dwell there, and most of all, the Supreme Being on the throne, all defy our human attempt to grasp and understand the beauty and glory of our God.

At times we admire beauty in a song, a work of art, a story, or even another person, but David describes the delight of gazing at the beauty of God. “One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to inquire in his temple” (Psalm 27:4). God is beautiful because His excellence is attractive— His character is flawless. David experienced the pleasure that comes from knowing and experiencing God in all His fullness. How does God express His Beauty?

Through the Gospel

“In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them. For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake. For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:4-6). In the awfulness of the Passion of Christ, we find a profound and sober beauty— the beauty of a sacrifice made by a sinless Savior for undeserving humanity. Sometimes the most stirring kind of beauty is found in things we cannot fully comprehend.

There is beauty in weeping of Mary and the disciples around the cross that held the lifeless body of their beloved Master. But when dawn broke on resurrection morning, despair turned into hope and grief into joy.

We see a beautiful scene at the Mount of Olives forty days later as the same disciples wistfully gazed into the sky, watching as their risen Lord disappeared into the heavens. With great joy, they returned to Jerusalem, with the promise of His return burning in their hearts, to wait for the coming of the Holy Spirit.

Today we expectantly wait for the Son of God to appear from heaven with power and great glory to complete the work of salvation. Then will we look upon Him in all His splendor and beauty. “For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

How should we, as God's image-bearers, reflect His beauty through the Gospel? God is an uncreated eternal being, and man was created in His image to reflect His glory and beauty. However, this beauty has been marred by sin and is no longer a worthy representation of God's character. But, there is redemption! Very little surpasses the beauty of a life that was once bruised and broken by sin but is now restored, redeemed, and made whole by the Gospel. “To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He might be glorified” (Isaiah 61:3). Atheists challenge the existence of God, scientists argue against Biblical creation, scholars question the inerrancy of scripture, but nobody can dispute the testimony of a redeemed life.

Through Creation

“The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament showeth His handy work” (Psalm 19:1). All beauty in the created world comes from God. A beautiful sunset, a lovely rose, a towering redwood, a majestic mountain peak, all testify of the beauty of God illustrated in creation. As road signs along the highway guide us to our destination, likewise, creation directs mankind to God himself. “For the invisible things of Him from the creation of the world are clearly seen . . .” (Romans 1:20). These gifts of creation are given to give us a brief glimpse of the One who created them.

How should we, as part of God's creation, reflect His creative beauty? Although we cannot make something out of nothing, God has designed us to be creative, using the resources of His creation and our intellectual abilities to make life practical. The fulfilling sense of accomplishment derived from a job well done has its origin in creation, where God regarded His work and declared it to be good. In our attempt to live non-extravagant lives we sometimes fail to take joy in the beautiful things in life. It is right and good and in harmony with how we were created to find pleasure in things of beauty. Ungodly men have used this gift of creativity many times for evil means. So much the more, let us glorify God by using His creation in ways that reflect His character.

A warning for all who love nature and creation (natural and man-made): let us be careful to not elevate earthly beauty above the Creator, which leads to idolatry. Sunsets fade, redwoods tumble, roses wilt, the human body turns to dust again, but God remains. Life and all of its beauty begins and ends with God.

Through Music and Sound

“And I heard a voice from heaven, as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of a great thunder: and I heard the voice of harpers harping with their harps” (Revelation 14:2) According to the book of Revelation, God's throne is surrounded by sound: thundering and lightning; praises flowing from the angels, the four beasts and twenty elders, and the great multitude which no man can number; and the new song by the one hundred and forty four thousand.

God created the beauty of sound to glorify Himself in ways that mere words cannot. The intricacy of His creativity is powerfully displayed in the way various sound frequencies come together to create a beautiful and heavenly harmony. It is honoring to God for mankind to take pleasure in the beauty of sounds He has created for His glory. The person who loves God will be drawn to Him whenever He is serenaded by pleasing sounds: the people of God singing the songs of Zion, the prayers of the saints, the wind whispering through the treetops, the songbird praising its Maker, the rumble of thunder, or the simple patter of rain on the roof.

How should we, as instruments of sound, reflect God's beauty through sound? We should always seek to listen to and resemble the sounds and harmonies of heaven. Although we will never be able to completely accomplish this on earth, it should be a lifelong endeavor. The questions have been asked,” Should we always be trying to improve our music making?” and “when have we reached ‘good enough’?” We will never be able to attain heavenly perfection, so the question should rather be asked, “Are we giving God the best we have?” Some people have more singing capabilities than others, but the question remains. “Are we giving our best or are we satisfied with an inferior sacrifice?” Let us be producers of God-honoring sounds that bring joy to the heart of the Creator!

Through the Church:

The Bible speaks extensively about the beauty of God's people. “Zion,” “The Temple,” “The Mountain of God,” “Jerusalem,” and“The Church” are synonymous expressions woven throughout scripture referring to the habitation of God's people on the earth. It is God's desire that His beauty would be reflected in the lives of His people. “Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, in the mountain of His holiness. Beautiful for situation, the joy of the whole earth, is Mount Zion, on the sides of the north, the city of the great King” (Psalm 48:1-2).

Nothing is dearer to the heart of God than His church. When the children of Israel journeyed through the wilderness, they built the tabernacle as a place for God to dwell among them. When Solomon dedicated the temple as God's dwelling place, God was very pleased and 2 Chronicles 7:1 says the glory of the Lord filled the temple. The temple was considered the House of the Lord–Jesus himself referred to it numerous times as God's house and was very passionate that it should be kept holy.

Today, neither the tabernacle nor the temple hosts the presence of God but rather His divine passion is concentrated on the church of Jesus Christ. Here are the people who truly love Him and are willing to lay down their lives for Him. Here are the people who are willing to give up their rights as individuals and surrender themselves to a greater cause. Here is where many a saint has given His very life's blood for the Gospel. And here is where one day our Savior will return as He has promised, and will transport His bride, the church, to her eternal habitation. “And I John saw the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a great voice out of heaven saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be His people, and God Himself shall be with them, and be their God” (Revelation 21:2-3).

How should we, as God's people, reflect His beauty in the church? By dwelling together in unity and harmony with love for all men, especially the household of God. The church should be a place where the world can get a glimpse of what goes on in heaven. It should be a place where Christ is always elevated as the victorious conqueror of sin, death, and hell.

Sadly, many people have become disoriented with the church's failures and have walked away from the true apostolic faith. In spite of our disappointments, let us “lift up the hands which hang down and the feeble knees” (Hebrews 12:12) and let us press on. We will never have a higher calling, and never a more noble warfare to wage.

Lastly, how should we reflect His beauty in our lives? By delighting in Him. “Delight thyself also in the LORD; and He shall give thee the desires of thine heart” (Psalm 37:4). The greatest fulfillment in life comes from finding pleasure in bringing joy to the heart of God by delighting in what He delights in and loving what He loves. Let us never lose the wonder of the beauty of our Salvation!

Een prachtig aspect van christen zijn is het vooruitzien naar de dag waarop we onze ogen zullen laven aan de geweldige schoonheid van onze God. Waarschijnlijk heeft iedereen wel mentale voorstellingen gemaakt van hoe God eruit zou kunnen zien, hoewel we weten dat zelfs onze wildste verbeelding te kort zal schieten. “Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty: they shall behold the land that is very far off” (Isaiah 33:17). De Bijbel staat vol met beschrijvende woordbeelden die ons een korte blik willen geven in de hemelse gebieden. Het landschap op de heuvels van heerlijkheid, de wonderlijke schepselen die daar wonen, en bovenal het Opperwezen op de troon, tarten allemaal onze menselijke poging om de schoonheid en glorie van onze God te bevatten en te begrijpen.

Soms bewonderen we schoonheid in een lied, een kunstwerk, een verhaal, of zelfs een ander mens, maar David beschrijft de vreugde van het aanschouwen van de schoonheid van God. “One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to inquire in his temple” (Psalm 27:4). God is mooi omdat Zijn voortreffelijkheid aantrekkingkracht heeft— Zijn karakter is onberispelijk. David ervoer het genoegen dat voortkomt uit het kennen en ervaren van God in Zijn volheid. Hoe drukt God Zijn Schoonheid uit?

Through the Gospel

“In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them. For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake. For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:4-6). In de afschuwelijkheid van de Passie van Christus vinden we een diepe en ernstige schoonheid— de schoonheid van een offer gebracht door een zondeloze Redder voor onverdiende mensheid. Soms wordt de meest ontroerende soort schoonheid gevonden in dingen die we niet volledig kunnen bevatten.

Er is schoonheid in het wenen van Maria en de discipelen rondom het kruis dat het levenloze lichaam van hun geliefde Meester droeg. Maar toen de dageraad van de opstandingsmorgen aanbrak, veranderde wanhoop in hoop en verdriet in vreugde.

We zien een prachtig tafereel op de Olijfberg veertig dagen later terwijl dezelfde discipelen weemoedig in de lucht staarden, kijkend hoe hun opgewekte Heer in de hemelen verdween. Met grote blijdschap keerden zij terug naar Jeruzalem, met de belofte van Zijn terugkeer brandend in hun hart, om te wachten op de komst van de Heilige Geest.

Vandaag wachten we vol verwachting dat de Zoon van God uit de hemel zal verschijnen met kracht en grote heerlijkheid om het werk van de zaligheid te voltooien. Dan zullen we Hem aanschouwen in al Zijn pracht en schoonheid. “For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

Hoe zouden wij, als Gods beelddragers, Zijn schoonheid door het Evangelie moeten weerspiegelen? God is een ongeschapen eeuwig Wezen, en de mens is naar Zijn beeld geschapen om Zijn heerlijkheid en schoonheid te weerspiegelen. Deze schoonheid is echter door de zonde beschadigd en is niet langer een waardige weergave van Gods karakter. Maar er is verlossing! Weinig overstijgt de schoonheid van een leven dat ooit gekwetst en gebroken was door zonde maar nu hersteld, verlost en geheeld is door het Evangelie. “To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He might be glorified” (Isaiah 61:3). Atheïsten betwisten het bestaan van God, wetenschappers debatteren tegen Bijbelse schepping, geleerden betwijfelen de onfeilbaarheid van de Schrift, maar niemand kan het getuigenis van een verlost leven weerleggen.

Through Creation

“The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament showeth His handy work” (Psalm 19:1). Alle schoonheid in de geschapen wereld komt van God. Een prachtige zonsondergang, een mooie roos, een indrukwekkende sequoia, een majestueuze bergtop, allen getuigen van de schoonheid van God geïllustreerd in de schepping. Zoals wegwijzers langs de snelweg ons naar onze bestemming leiden, zo wijst de schepping de mensheid naar God zelf. “For the invisible things of Him from the creation of the world are clearly seen . . .” (Romans 1:20). Deze geschenken van de schepping zijn gegeven om ons een korte blik te gunnen op Degene die ze geschapen heeft.

Hoe zouden wij, als onderdeel van Gods schepping, Zijn scheppende schoonheid moeten weerspiegelen? Hoewel we niet iets uit niets kunnen maken, heeft God ons ontworpen om creatief te zijn, gebruikmakend van de middelen van Zijn schepping en onze intellectuele vermogens om het leven praktisch te maken. Het vervullende gevoel van voldoening dat voortkomt uit goed werk heeft zijn oorsprong in de schepping, waar God Zijn werk bekeek en het goed noemde. In onze poging om niet-uitbundige levens te leiden falen we soms in het genieten van de mooie dingen in het leven. Het is juist en goed en in overeenstemming met hoe we geschapen zijn om vreugde te vinden in dingen van schoonheid. Ondogmatische mensen hebben dit geschenk van creativiteit vaak voor kwade doeleinden gebruikt. Des te meer, laten we God verheerlijken door Zijn schepping te gebruiken op manieren die Zijn karakter weerspiegelen.

Een waarschuwing voor allen die van de natuur en schepping (natuurlijk en door de mens gemaakt) houden: laten we oppassen dat we aardse schoonheid niet boven de Schepper verheffen, wat tot afgoderij leidt. Zonsondergangen vervagen, sequoia's vallen om, rozen verwelken, het menselijke lichaam keert weer tot stof, maar God blijft. Het leven en al zijn schoonheid begint en eindigt bij God.

Through Music and Sound

“And I heard a voice from heaven, as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of a great thunder: and I heard the voice of harpers harping with their harps” (Revelation 14:2) Volgens het boek Openbaring is Gods troon omgeven door geluid: donderslagen en bliksem; lof die opwelt van de engelen, de vier levende wezens en de twintig ouderlingen, en de grote menigte die niemand kan tellen; en het nieuwe lied van de honderdvierenveertigduizend.

God schiep de schoonheid van geluid om Zichzelf te verheerlijken op manieren die loutere woorden niet kunnen. De ingewikkeldheid van Zijn creativiteit wordt krachtig getoond in de wijze waarop verschillende geluidsfrequenties samenkomen om een mooie en hemelse harmonie te vormen. Het is eervol voor God wanneer de mens geniet van de schoonheid van geluiden die Hij geschapen heeft tot Zijn heerlijkheid. Degene die God liefheeft zal tot Hem worden aangetrokken wanneer Hij wordt omgeven door aangename klanken: het volk van God dat de liederen van Sion zingt, de gebeden van de heiligen, de wind die fluistert door de boomtoppen, de zangvogel die zijn Schepper prijst, het gedonder van onweer, of het eenvoudige getik van regen op het dak.

Hoe zouden wij, als instrumenten van geluid, Gods schoonheid door geluid moeten weerspiegelen? We zouden altijd moeten streven naar het luisteren naar en lijken op de geluiden en harmonieën van de hemel. Hoewel we dit op aarde nooit volledig kunnen bereiken, zou het een levenslange inspanning moeten zijn. De vragen zijn gesteld: “Should we always be trying to improve our music making?” en “when have we reached ‘good enough’?” We zullen nooit de hemelse perfectie bereiken, dus de vraag zou eerder moeten zijn: “Are we giving God the best we have?” Sommige mensen hebben meer zangcapaciteiten dan anderen, maar de vraag blijft. “Are we giving our best or are we satisfied with an inferior sacrifice?” Laten we producenten zijn van God-verheerlijkende klanken die vreugde brengen in het hart van de Schepper!

Through the Church:

De Bijbel spreekt uitvoerig over de schoonheid van Gods mensen. “Zion,” “The Temple,” “The Mountain of God,” “Jerusalem,” and“The Church” zijn synonieme uitdrukkingen die door de Schrift verweven zijn en verwijzen naar het verblijf van Gods volk op aarde. Het is Gods verlangen dat Zijn schoonheid weerspiegeld zou worden in het leven van Zijn volk. “Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God, in the mountain of His holiness. Beautiful for situation, the joy of the whole earth, is Mount Zion, on the sides of the north, the city of the great King” (Psalm 48:1-2).

Niets is dierbaarder voor het hart van God dan Zijn kerk. Toen de kinderen van Israël door de woestijn trokken, bouwden zij de tabernakel als een plaats voor God om onder hen te wonen. Toen Salomo de tempel wijdde als Gods verblijfplaats, was God zeer behaagd en 2 Chronicles 7:1 zegt dat de heerlijkheid van de HEER de tempel vervulde. De tempel werd beschouwd als het Huis des Heren–Jezus zelf verwees er herhaaldelijk naar als het huis van God en was er zeer hartstochtelijk over dat het heilig moest worden gehouden.

Tegenwoordig herbergt noch de tabernakel noch de tempel de tegenwoordigheid van God, maar veeleer is Zijn goddelijke hartstocht geconcentreerd op de kerk van Jezus Christus. Hier zijn de mensen die Hem werkelijk liefhebben en bereid zijn hun leven voor Hem neer te leggen. Hier zijn de mensen die bereid zijn hun rechten als individuen op te geven en zich over te geven aan een groter doel. Hier heeft menig heilige Zijn eigen levensbloed gegeven voor het Evangelie. En hier is waar onze Heiland op een dag zal terugkeren zoals Hij beloofd heeft, en Zijn bruid, de kerk, zal vervoeren naar haar eeuwige verblijf. “And I John saw the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a great voice out of heaven saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be His people, and God Himself shall be with them, and be their God” (Revelation 21:2-3).

Hoe zouden wij, als Gods volk, Zijn schoonheid in de kerk moeten weerspiegelen? Door samen te wonen in eenheid en harmonie met liefde voor alle mensen, vooral het huis van God. De kerk zou een plaats moeten zijn waar de wereld een glimp kan krijgen van wat er in de hemel plaatsvindt. Het zou een plaats moeten zijn waar Christus altijd wordt verhoogd als de overwinnende overwinnaar van zonde, dood en hel.

Jammer genoeg zijn veel mensen de weg kwijtgeraakt door de fouten van de kerk en hebben zij zich afgewend van het ware apostolische geloof. Ondanks onze teleurstellingen, laten we “lift up the hands which hang down and the feeble knees” (Hebrews 12:12) en laten we vooruitgaan. We zullen nooit een hogere roeping hebben, en nooit een edeler strijd om te voeren.

Ten slotte, hoe zouden wij Zijn schoonheid in ons leven moeten weerspiegelen? Door ons te verblijden in Hem. “Delight thyself also in the LORD; and He shall give thee the desires of thine heart” (Psalm 37:4). De grootste vervulling in het leven komt voort uit het genoegen vinden in het brengen van vreugde in het hart van God door ons te verheugen in wat Hij verheugt en lief te hebben wat Hij liefheeft. Laten we nooit het wonder verliezen van de schoonheid van onze Zaligheid!

Our spiritual forefathers had much to say on the many issues facing the American Mennonite church in their time, and we can still learn from the collected writings of these church leaders and brethren. We will look first at the hermeneutics of the early American Mennonite church, endeavoring to draw examples from which we, as 21st-century Christians, can learn.

First, the correct interpretation of Scripture was a matter of great importance to these earlier Christians. They had only recently emigrated away from a largely hostile area, where they had been constantly tested to the point of death on matters of faith and now faced a different set of challenges when confronted with peace and religious freedom. We will look at how they navigated these challenges by studying several of their doctrines and practices.

The Doctrine of Nonresistance

One matter that was well interpreted and applied by many of the early Mennonite writers is the principle and doctrine of the nonresistant Christian. Although many of their Anabaptist descendants of today still hold, to varying degrees, this doctrine, it is oftentimes not done with the clarity and solemnity of their forefathers. The early American Mennonites understood nonresistance as a foundational aspect of the Christian life, as it should be, and taught extensively on the practical application and appearance of nonresistance in the life of a believer. Their primary motivation for living peaceably and without malice toward one’s fellow man was the given example of Jesus. Christ typified the acceptable response to violence and ill-will: gentleness, meekness, as befitted one who is called a Lamb.

The Emphasis of Biblical Foundations

There was also a firm focus amongst early Mennonite writers against building doctrine on the writings of men. This emphasis comes through strongly in their works, as they quote Scripture extensively. They made their point by bringing in an example of Christ or by way of an applicable Scripture verse, rather than building on the sandy soil of a man’s opinions. One of the areas in which they did so was the matter of salvation.

Importance of Practical Salvation

We can learn much from the early Mennonites about the practical working out of salvation. First, salvation is portrayed as both an inward and an outward change. The inward is affected first through the working of the Holy Spirit in the willful sinner’s life. It is an important distinction that the sinner is willful. This position was contrary to most of the greater established churches of the time. If a sinner must be willful, then it implies that all men can willfully accept salvation, an idea that is fundamental in nature, if not always verbalized, to the church of today.

In the early Mennonites’ time, predestination as taught by Calvinism seems to have necessitated this emphasis on man’s ability to choose freely, which is still true today. There is also another flavoring of the “unwillingly saved” interpretation, and that comes from the aftereffects of the charismatic movement and the effect it has had on Mennonite and Amish circles. This “unwilling salvation” is not a matter of predestination, but rather is described as almost a coercive calling by the Spirit. It has been observed in several salvation testimonies where the testifiers recalled how they were completely comfortable in their lives of sin and debauchery when suddenly they would be struck down in the manner of Saul and could not help themselves but follow after God and give their lives to Him. There are numerous pitfalls with this dramatic understanding of conversion, namely that it absolves responsibility from the one converted for his decision to convert. This leads to a lack of counting the cost of Christianity, which is a death of oneself, a death of pride, and a death of favor with man. If the believer hops headfirst into Christianity, not reckoning that he must give up all these self-pleasing traits, how will he be able to grow spiritually if he cannot let go of his former vices? While this form of conversion may be genuine at the beginning, it does not often progress beyond the milk of the Word to the meat of which a mature Christian must partake. This maturing of a Christian is emphasized in writings ranging from those of Menno Simons up to Abraham Goshalk. It is also important for the sake of the church that the believer be firmly committed and engaged in the steady growth of his faith.

The Seriousness of a Pure Church

The idea of church to the early American Mennonite seems to have been a more serious thought, less individualistic than our current state. It is the pitiable state of nominal Christianity that the church has become a social organization with room for all sin and depravity.

It behooves us to consider closely the character of the church that Christ established and to note as well the character of the true churches, unspotted by apostasy and laxness. This character is, like Christ himself, simple and yet incredibly full of meaning and spiritual vitality.

The first aspect of the church to recognize is its pure state as the bride of Christ. Here again, we should consider the character of Christ. Did He ever give Himself space for sin? Do we find Him occasionally indulging in a brief enjoyment of a “guilty pleasure”? The understanding reader will agree that Christ was pure in His entirety, and so how else should the bride be with which He is to be intimately and eternally joined? To aid our minds in answering such a question, let us consider the earthly symbol of this heavenly union: that of a man and a woman joined together for life. This earthly union is recognized even by non-Christians as something set aside purely for the two individuals involved, a relationship and a sharing of each other that is not and never to be partaken of by anyone outside of the intimate union. This paints clearly for our earth-bound minds the mind of Christ, insomuch as that marriage is a symbol of Christ and His bride. The bride and Christ are for each other and give themselves to nothing and no one other.

Now that we can see the purity of the church, let us examine its practical working out amongst fallen man. If it is to be pure, then how are we to be a part of it? Here enters the need for a clear understanding of regeneration, a doctrine held in high regard by these Mennonite forefathers. They taught that the Spirit affects the spiritual washing and cleansing that will be made apparent in a changed state of thought and action in the believer. This change is still at variance with our fallen nature, but through continued surrender and a deep humility, the Spirit will fill the believer until the nature of sin becomes the dominated instead of the dominant. It is important to realize, however, that this victory over sin is brought into effect by the believer yielding his will and allowing the Spirit complete control.

Thus, a pure church is a surrendered, Spirit-filled group of believers who recognize in true humility that their power is not in any way linked to their own merit. The absence of pride, achieved only by the constant aid of the Spirit, gives further room for purification of the willing believer. In this way, we can see the Christian life in shoe leather.

The Teachings of Practical Christianity

The practicality of the early American Mennonite’s faith was continually on display. In his book, “Pride and Humility,” John M. Brenneman maintains that the outward appearance of a person is directly related to his inward heart, a view which extends as well to the actions of the individual. It is necessary to build on the beliefs of willful salvation, regeneration, and a pure church previously examined to frame the mindset of a Mennonite’s interactions in daily living.

To these serious-minded Christians, there was no difference in importance between the religious belief expressed on Sundays and the mundane actions of the rest of the week. This is evidenced by their general abstinence from political matters and other elements of a worldly nature that would infringe upon the beliefs they held. This put them in direct opposition to many of the churches of their day, where thrived two schools of thought: either that one’s earthly duties in a political manner were carried out completely separate from one’s faith, or that the accomplishment of these civic duties were incorporated in the will of God and so permissible for the Christian to engage in freely.

To the early American Mennonite, these types of stances betrayed the very meaning of his Christianity: he was a new person, alive only in the power of Christ that flowed through him. This influenced and directed every aspect of his life, from his business dealings, which were carried out in a way so as not to take advantage of any party involved, to his dress and manner of deportment, which was to be based on humility and plainness, to his method of conversing with his fellow man, which was to show a genuine concern for the spiritual well-being and eternal destiny.

Conclusion

The sum of all these colonial Mennonite beliefs was the doctrine of how to grow into a mature, humble, repentant, but spiritually powerful servant of God. He denied the allures of the world around him in favor of an eternal reward promised upon the purity of his faith and willing renunciation of the sin in which he had formerly lived. This example, lived out by believers like us, should inspire us to further press into the Kingdom of God, working out our faith in humility and repentance.

Unsere geistlichen Vorväter haben zu den vielen Fragen, mit denen die amerikanische mennonitische Kirche zu ihrer Zeit konfrontiert war, viel zu sagen gehabt, und wir können noch immer aus den gesammelten Schriften dieser Kirchenleiter und Brüder lernen. Zuerst wollen wir uns der Hermeneutik der frühen amerikanischen Mennonitenkirche zuwenden und versuchen, Beispiele herauszuarbeiten, aus denen wir als Christen des 21. Jahrhunderts lernen können.

Zunächst war die richtige Auslegung der Schrift für diese früheren Christen von großer Bedeutung. Sie waren erst vor Kurzem aus einer weitgehend feindlichen Gegend ausgewandert, wo ihr Glaube bis an den Tod auf die Probe gestellt worden war, und nun sahen sie sich in einer anderen Situation mit Frieden und Religionsfreiheit konfrontiert. Wir werden betrachten, wie sie diese Herausforderungen bewältigten, indem wir mehrere ihrer Lehren und Praktiken studieren.

The Doctrine of Nonresistance

Eine Frage, die von vielen der frühen mennonitischen Schriftsteller gut ausgelegt und angewandt wurde, ist das Prinzip und die Lehre des nichtwiderständigen Christen. Obwohl viele ihrer anabaptistischen Nachkommen heute dieses Dogma noch in unterschiedlichem Maße festhalten, geschieht dies oft nicht mit der Klarheit und Erhabenheit ihrer Vorväter. Die frühen amerikanischen Mennoniten verstanden Nichtwiderstand als einen grundlegenden Aspekt des christlichen Lebens, wie es sein sollte, und lehrten ausführlich über die praktische Anwendung und Erscheinung des Nichtwiderstands im Leben eines Gläubigen. Ihre vorrangige Motivation, friedlich und ohne Bosheit gegenüber dem Mitmenschen zu leben, war das gegebene Beispiel Jesu. Christus typisierte die annehmbare Antwort auf Gewalt und Übelwollen: Sanftmut, Demut, wie es einem geziemt, der ein Lamm genannt wird.

The Emphasis of Biblical Foundations

Unter den frühen mennonitischen Schriftstellern gab es außerdem einen festen Fokus darauf, die Lehre nicht auf den Schriften von Menschen aufzubauen. Dieser Akzent kommt in ihren Werken stark zum Ausdruck, da sie ausgiebig die Schrift zitieren. Sie machten ihren Punkt, indem sie ein Beispiel aus Christus anführten oder einen anwendbaren Schriftvers anführten, statt auf dem sandigen Boden menschlicher Meinungen zu bauen. Eines der Gebiete, in denen sie dies taten, war die Frage des Heils.

Importance of Practical Salvation

Wir können viel von den frühen Mennoniten über das praktische Auswirken des Heils lernen. Zunächst wird das Heil sowohl als innerliche als auch als äußerliche Veränderung dargestellt. Das Innerliche wird zuerst durch das Wirken des Heiligen Geistes im Leben des willentlichen Sünders bewirkt. Es ist eine wichtige Unterscheidung, dass der Sünder willentlich ist. Diese Position stand im Gegensatz zu den meisten der damals etablierten großen Kirchen. Wenn ein Sünder willentlich sein muss, dann impliziert das, dass alle Menschen willentlich das Heil annehmen können, eine Idee, die grundsätzlich der Kirche von heute zugrunde liegt, wenn auch nicht immer verbalisiert.

Zur Zeit der frühen Mennoniten schien die von der calvinistischen Lehre vertretene Prädestination diese Betonung auf die Fähigkeit des Menschen, frei zu wählen, zu erfordern, was auch heute noch zutrifft. Es gibt auch eine andere Färbung der Interpretation des „widerwillig Gerettetwerdens“, die aus den Nachwirkungen der charismatischen Bewegung und ihrem Einfluss auf mennonitische und amische Kreise herrührt. Dieses „widerwillige Heil“ ist keine Frage der Prädestination, sondern wird eher als nahezu zwingende Berufung durch den Geist beschrieben. Es wurde in mehreren Bekehrungszeugnissen beobachtet, wobei die Zeugenden schilderten, wie sie völlig zufrieden in ihrem Leben voller Sünde und Ausschweifung gewesen seien, als sie plötzlich wie Saulus niedergestreckt wurden und nicht anders konnten, als Gott nachzufolgen und ihr Leben Ihm zu geben. Mit diesem dramatischen Verständnis von Bekehrung sind zahlreiche Fallstricke verbunden, nämlich dass es dem Bekehrten die Verantwortung für seine Entscheidung zur Bekehrung enthebt. Das führt zu einem Nicht-Abwägen der Kosten des Christentums, welches ein Sterben des Selbst, ein Sterben des Stolzes und ein Verlust der Gunst der Menschen ist. Wenn der Gläubige kopfüber in das Christentum einsteigt, ohne zu berücksichtigen, dass er all diese selbstgefälligen Eigenschaften aufgeben muss, wie soll er geistlich wachsen können, wenn er seine früheren Laster nicht loslassen kann? Während diese Form der Bekehrung am Anfang echt sein mag, entwickelt sie sich oft nicht über die Milch des Wortes hinaus zu dem Fleisch, von dem ein reifer Christ kosten muss. Dieses Reifen eines Christen wird in Schriften von Menno Simons bis Abraham Goshalk betont. Ebenfalls wichtig für das Wohl der Kirche ist, dass der Gläubige fest verpflichtet ist und sich am stetigen Wachstum seines Glaubens beteiligt.

The Seriousness of a Pure Church

Die Idee von Kirche schien den frühen amerikanischen Mennoniten eine ernstere Angelegenheit zu sein, weniger individualistisch als in unserem gegenwärtigen Zustand. Es ist der beklagenswerte Zustand des nominalen Christentums, dass die Kirche zu einer sozialen Organisation geworden ist, die Platz für alle Sünde und Verderbtheit lässt.

Es gebührt uns, den Charakter der von Christus gestifteten Kirche genau zu bedenken und auch den Charakter der wahren Kirchen zu beachten, unbefleckt von Abfall und Laxheit. Dieser Charakter ist, wie Christus selbst, schlicht und doch unglaublich voller Sinn und geistlicher Lebenskraft.

Der erste Aspekt der Kirche, den es zu erkennen gilt, ist ihr reiner Zustand als Braut Christi. Auch hier sollten wir den Charakter Christi bedenken. Hat Er sich jemals Raum für Sünde gelassen? Finden wir Ihn gelegentlich einem kurzen Genuss eines „heimlichen Vergnügens“ frönend? Der verständige Leser wird zustimmen, dass Christus in seiner Gesamtheit rein war, und wie sollte die Braut also anders sein, mit der Er innig und ewig verbunden sein soll? Um unseren irdischen Gedanken bei der Beantwortung einer solchen Frage zu helfen, betrachten wir das irdische Symbol dieser himmlischen Verbindung: jenes eines Mannes und einer Frau, die lebenslang verbunden sind. Diese irdische Verbindung wird auch von Nichtchristen als etwas angesehen, das allein den beiden Beteiligten vorbehalten ist, eine Beziehung und ein Miteinander, das nicht und niemals von jemandem außerhalb dieser innigen Verbindung geteilt werden darf. Das zeichnet für unsere erdgebundenen Gedanken deutlich den Sinn Christi, insofern als die Ehe ein Symbol für Christus und seine Braut ist. Die Braut und Christus sind füreinander und geben sich niemand anderem hin.

Nun, da wir die Reinheit der Kirche sehen können, lassen Sie uns ihr praktisches Wirken unter gefallenen Menschen untersuchen. Wenn sie rein sein soll, wie sollen wir dann Teil von ihr sein? Hier tritt die Notwendigkeit eines klaren Verständnisses der Wiedergeburt ein, einer Lehre, die von diesen mennonitischen Vorvätern hoch geachtet wurde. Sie lehrten, dass der Geist die geistliche Waschung und Reinigung bewirkt, die sich in einem veränderten Zustand von Denken und Handeln des Gläubigen zeigen wird. Diese Veränderung steht weiterhin im Widerstreit mit unserer gefallenen Natur, aber durch fortgesetzte Hingabe und tiefe Demut wird der Geist den Gläubigen erfüllen, sodass die Natur der Sünde beherrscht statt herrschend zu sein. Es ist jedoch wichtig zu erkennen, dass dieser Sieg über die Sünde durch das Nachgeben des Willens des Gläubigen und die vollständige Kontrolle durch den Geist in Wirksamkeit gesetzt wird.

So ist eine reine Kirche eine hingegebene, vom Geist erfüllte Gemeinschaft von Gläubigen, die in wahrer Demut anerkennen, dass ihre Kraft in keiner Weise mit ihrem eigenen Verdienst verknüpft ist. Das Fehlen von Stolz, das nur durch die ständige Hilfe des Geistes erreicht wird, schafft weiteren Raum für die Reinigung des willigen Gläubigen. Auf diese Weise können wir das christliche Leben in der praktischen Anwendung sehen.

The Teachings of Practical Christianity

Die Praktikabilität des Glaubens der frühen amerikanischen Mennoniten war fortwährend sichtbar. In seinem Buch „Pride and Humility“ behauptet John M. Brenneman, dass das äußere Erscheinungsbild einer Person in direktem Zusammenhang mit ihrem inneren Herzen steht, eine Ansicht, die sich auch auf das Handeln des Einzelnen erstreckt. Es ist notwendig, auf den zuvor untersuchten Überzeugungen von willentlichem Heil, Wiedergeburt und einer reinen Kirche aufzubauen, um die Denkweise eines Mennoniten in seinen Interaktionen im täglichen Leben zu rahmen.

Für diese ernstgesinnten Christen bestand kein Unterschied in der Bedeutung zwischen dem religiösen Glauben, der sonntags zum Ausdruck kommt, und den alltäglichen Handlungen der restlichen Woche. Dies zeigt sich in ihrem allgemeinen Verzicht auf politische Angelegenheiten und andere weltliche Elemente, die ihren Überzeugungen zuwiderlaufen würden. Dadurch standen sie in direktem Gegensatz zu vielen Kirchen ihrer Zeit, in denen zwei Denkschulen herrschten: entweder, dass die irdischen Pflichten in politischer Hinsicht völlig getrennt vom Glauben erfüllt würden, oder dass die Erfüllung dieser bürgerlichen Pflichten in den Willen Gottes einbezogen sei und daher dem Christen frei erlaubt sei.

Für den frühen amerikanischen Mennoniten verrieten solche Haltungen den wahren Sinn seines Christseins: Er war eine neue Person, lebendig allein in der Kraft Christi, die durch ihn strömte. Das beeinflusste und leitete jeden Aspekt seines Lebens, von seinen Geschäftshandlungen, die so ausgeführt wurden, dass keine Partei benachteiligt wurde, bis zu seiner Kleidung und seinem Auftreten, die auf Demut und Schlichtheit beruhen sollten, und bis zu seiner Art, mit seinem Nächsten zu sprechen, die echtes Interesse an dessen geistlichem Wohl und ewigem Schicksal zeigen sollte.

Conclusion

Die Summe all dieser mennonitischen kolonialen Überzeugungen war die Lehre darüber, wie man zu einem reifen, demütigen, reuigen, aber geistlich mächtigen Knecht Gottes heranwächst. Er verleugnete die Verlockungen der ihn umgebenden Welt zugunsten einer ewigen Belohnung, die auf der Reinheit seines Glaubens und der willigen Verzichtleistung der Sünde beruht, in der er früher gelebt hatte. Dieses Beispiel, gelebt von Gläubigen wie wir, sollte uns dazu anspornen, weiter ins Reich Gottes vorzudringen und unseren Glauben in Demut und Buße zu leben.
