“Get out of my shop! I don’t need people like you around me! And never come back!” My lips quivered as I looked into the dark, angry eyes of the yelling man. I blinked back the unbidden tears, realizing that once more, I had to leave this man that I loved. All night I could sense that we were coming to this, and I had tried so hard not to let it happen. With one last attempt, I feebly yelled above the tension, “Ken, we don’t want to ...” but once more, I was rudely cut off. With slumped shoulders and downcast eyes, I turned to escape the confines of his dingy, pawn shop, his ever-crescendoing voice drowning the last hope of respite.

The lingering smell of smoke and the echo of his angry voice joined the troubled thoughts of my emotionally overwrought mind, as I slowly walked up the street. “What do you think, Josh?” I asked my faithful, quiet friend.

“I don’t know, " he responded, and we fell back into silent anguish at the outcome of our supposed Bible study, grasping for an explanation for the terrible response. What could we have done differently? Why could he not accept the truth? What lay behind those flashing eyes, and what memories are stored beneath his ever-crowning beanie?

Ken was born on a country farm in the rolling hills of Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, a splendid place for a curious and adventurous little boy to live.

When Ken was four years old, his parents separated. He had heard them fighting a lot, but he didn’t know that it was possible for Mom and Dad to separate. It crushed his heart and confused his innocent soul. He did not know how to handle the stress and change that was tossed on his peaceful life.

The terror and confusion of his mom hurriedly packing their belongings, loading him and his siblings in the car, and driving away are still riveted in his mind. It made no sense! Why couldn’t they just go home? In his musty bedroom at their little, dingy apartment, he lay staring at the moldy ceiling, wondering endlessly what had gone so wrong.

Ken soon adjusted to his new home in the city of Pottsville with only cars, people, and sidewalks instead of cows, frogs, and mud. But fate did not leave the small security his new lifestyle provided him. His mom was not able to properly care for him and his siblings, and so the children were placed in different foster homes. That was even worse than leaving Dad! The clothes he wore were the only things familiar to him. Instead of understanding and loving him, each new family brought more yelling, hatred, and beating. Terror, tears, loneliness, and pain accompanied him.

Ken thought the second foster home that he was placed in would be a safe, loving home. The dad was tall and strong and appeared to be gentle. The mom was overweight, but her friendly smile resolved his fears. But the first night, when he reached for the food, he accidentally dumped a cup of water. She screamed at him and told him that he was worthless, and she wished they had never gotten him. The dad continued eating as if he didn't hear or care. Why didn’t the strong man stop her?

That evening, Ken crawled into his big, strange bed, already crying in loneliness, when he heard the mom yell. He quickly jumped out of bed and, with trembling legs, slipped behind the door to hide. She charged up the stairs bellowing angrily, and Ken was sure that he was in trouble. To his relief, she continued down the hall. He was still too scared to leave his hiding place for fear of receiving a beating. He wiped his tears as he began to sing under his breath a song he had heard in Sunday school, “Jesus loves the little children, all the children of the world.” He stopped to think, and his crying quit. “Then why am I here? " he wondered. “Have I done something wrong? God must not love little children. That song is not true! If God loved me I would not be here!" With that conclusion, he burst into tears and lost hope in God. He woke the next morning, still hidden behind the door.

Darkness had long fallen, and my family was all peacefully sleeping in our old farmhouse. I cried myself to sleep, crying for Ken's soul, crying because I didn’t know what to do, crying because my friend, the man I longed to see at peace with God, hated me.

Ken continued to fire questions. “How can God be good and allow so much bad? How could God let children suffer?” I listened on as he continued saying the same things that I heard so many times before, giving me no chance to talk.

Again, it was time to leave, and I was so glad to do so. He kept talking as we backed out the door. Once more, my friend and I walked up the street —tired, frustrated, and wishing never to come back.

Ken was 13 years old, and his life was no better than it had been when he was first put into the foster system. His life was in turmoil. He was continually yelled at and belittled at home. Ken was tired of crying. No one cared, and there was no one with whom he could share his problem. That’s when he came up with his clever plan. His school friend was a hippie, and his parents traveled a lot. They were called Gypsies. He heard that they were headed to California. So, Ken told them about his terrible life and asked if they would give him a ride. They were glad to help.

That exciting morning, he just did his usual thing. He left for school and instead went to California. He didn’t mind leaving all his stuff behind—he really didn’t have much anyway. His foster parents didn’t even care that he left.

In California, Ken lived on the beach and worked for fishermen, and whoever else needed help. He always had enough to eat and something to do. He had his fellow beach bums, but he was still alone inside. His heart was still empty. He longed for love.

Ken lived on the beach for a year and a half and then hitchhiked to Arizona. There he found a home in a homeless shelter and got a job. He did well and soon was on his own, but his search for love took him down the wrong roads. Ken really wanted to be married to a loving wife and have a family, but the girl he married did not marry him because of love. She was hurt, and Ken’s own hurt soul was attracted to her. They got married and all was well for a few years until he found out that his wife was seeing other men. His heart was broken, and his world was thrown into turmoil. Ken wanted desperately to provide security for the children that were born to them, and so he tried his best to stay together. He did not want to put his children through the life that he experienced. But after eight rough years, they got a divorce.

Ken moved on and tried to recover from the devastation of the divorce. His search for love brought him only more sadness and pain. Since Ken was hurt and unhappy, he found satisfaction in making others happy. He spent all his money on them, and when he had nothing more to offer, they left.

Now Ken is sitting in his pawn shop, alone, hurt, sad, and hiding. He found through his sad life that no one cared. Every time that he opened himself to love, he was always hurt. Deep down inside, he truly felt that God did not care. He lost hope in God, people, and last of all, he lost hope in love itself. That is why we were still visiting the dingy, smoke-stained shop after six years of very little apparent success. God kept bringing us back. He put in us a persistent love and relentless burden for this wounded soul. That is why we spent many hours hearing the same criticisms over and over. The same problems, the same confusion.

Nearly every month, he would fluctuate between hope and despair, love and hate, new life in God, and sadness and sin. We never knew what the next visit would bring. We could be swelling with hope and filled with blessing, or torn with angry words and sickened with dread. But we kept going back, and slowly he emerged from the pit of despair, and slowly allowed himself to be wrapped in the wonderful love of God and the glorious message of His redeeming grace. It was amazing to see the change in his life and to hear his ever-growing confidence in the love of Christ.

Today Ken loves the Lord. He is learning to walk with God. He has seen the love of God. He has found hope in God. He has experienced the unconditional love of God. He is still growing, and we are excited to see what God has for him.

I’m so glad that God brought Ken into my life. God had a plan for Ken and I. God wanted to show Ken that He loved him and that He would be there for him even when Josh turned his back on Him. God also wanted me to carry a burden in my youth. He knew how easily I would be distracted with money and fun. He knew that I needed a burden to carry, a soul to care for. He wanted me to be able to see beneath the shell of a hard soul and see a hurting child within. He wanted to give me a burden too big for me to carry so that I would learn to lean on Him. And most of all, He wanted to equip me to serve Him in broader ways.

Fellow Christians, open your lives to the work of God. Find an opportunity to love a hurting soul. Search out someone who needs a friend and love them, and wait and see what God has in store for you. Love until it hurts so badly that you don’t know what to do, and then turn to Jesus, who is there to help you through. God may be waiting for you to make the first step before He will use you. Your life is before you. You can choose to live a comfortable, happy life, or you can open yourself up to be hurt and find that after years pass, your life is overflowing with meaning and purpose. Jesus opened Himself to the pain and anguish of this world, and only through that do we have hope. He is asking us to follow His example, to open ourselves to pain so that others can have hope. And as He was glorified, so will we be glorified, in some measure, someday, and we will never regret the pain that we faced.

”Ut ur min butik! Jag behöver inte människor som du omkring mig! Och kom aldrig tillbaka!” Mina läppar darrade medan jag tittade in i den mörka, arga blicken hos den man som skrek. Jag blinkade bort de ovälkomna tårarna och insåg att jag ännu en gång måste lämna denna man som jag älskade. Hela natten hade jag känt att vi skulle komma till detta, och jag hade försökt så hårt att hindra det från att hända. Med ett sista försök ropade jag svagt över spänningen: ”Ken, vi vill inte ...” men återigen blev jag rudt avbruten. Med sjunkna axlar och nedslagna ögon vände jag mig för att fly från hans sunkiga pantbank, hans ständigt stigande röst dränkte den sista hoppet om vila.

Den kvarvarande lukten av rök och ekot av hans arga röst förenade sig med de bekymrade tankarna i mitt känslomässigt överansträngda sinne när jag långsamt promenerade uppför gatan. ”Vad tror du, Josh?” frågade jag min trogna, tysta vän.

”Jag vet inte,” svarade han, och vi föll tillbaka i tyst förtvivlan över utgången av vår påstådda bibelstudie, greppande efter en förklaring till den fruktansvärda reaktionen. Vad kunde vi ha gjort annorlunda? Varför kunde han inte ta emot sanningen? Vad låg bakom de blixtrande ögonen, och vilka minnen fanns nedlagrade under hans ständigt sittande mössa?

Ken föddes på en bondgård i de böljande kullarna i Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, en förträfflig plats för en nyfiken och äventyrlig liten pojke att växa upp på.

När Ken var fyra år gamla separerade hans föräldrar. Han hade hört dem bråka mycket, men han visste inte att det var möjligt för mamma och pappa att skiljas. Det krossade hans hjärta och förvirrade hans oskyldiga själ. Han visste inte hur han skulle hantera den stress och förändring som kastades in i hans lugna liv.

Skräcken och förvirringen när hans mamma hastigt packade deras tillhörigheter, lastade honom och hans syskon i bilen och körde iväg sitter fortfarande fast i hans minne. Det var meningslöst! Varför kunde de inte bara åka hem? I sitt instängda sovrum i deras lilla, sunkiga lägenhet låg han och stirrade på den mögliga taket och undrade utan slut vad som gått så fel.

Ken anpassade sig snart till sitt nya hem i staden Pottsville med bara bilar, människor och trottoarer istället för kor, grodor och lera. Men ödet övergav inte den lilla trygghet hans nya livsstil gav honom. Hans mamma kunde inte ta hand om honom och hans syskon på rätt sätt, och så placerades barnen i olika fosterhem. Det var ännu värre än att lämna pappa! Kläderna han bar var de enda saker som kändes bekanta. Istället för förståelse och kärlek förde varje ny familj mer skrik, hat och slag. Skräck, tårar, ensamhet och smärta följde honom.

Ken trodde att det andra fosterhemmet där han placerades skulle vara ett tryggt, kärleksfullt hem. Pappan var lång och stark och verkade mild. Mamman var överviktig, men hennes vänliga leende lät hans rädslor försvinna. Men första natten, när han sträckte sig efter maten, råkade han spilla en kopp vatten. Hon skrek åt honom och sa att han var värdelös och att hon önskade att de aldrig hade fått honom. Pappan fortsatte äta som om han inte hörde eller brydde sig. Varför stoppade inte den starke mannen henne?

Den kvällen kröp Ken upp i sin stora, främmande säng, redan gråtande av ensamhet, när han hörde mamman skrika. Han hoppade snabbt ur sängen och med skakiga ben smög han bakom dörren för att gömma sig. Hon stormade uppför trappan och vrålade ilsket, och Ken var säker på att han skulle få problem. Till hans lättnad fortsatte hon nerför korridoren. Han var fortfarande för rädd för att lämna sitt gömställe av rädsla för att få ett stryk. Han torkade sina tårar och började nynna en sång han hört i söndagsskolan, ”Jesus loves the little children, all the children of the world.” Han stannade upp för att tänka, och hans gråt upphörde. ”Varför är jag då här?” undrade han. ”Har jag gjort något fel? Gud måste inte älska små barn. Den sången är inte sann! Om Gud älskade mig skulle jag inte vara här!” Med den slutsatsen brast han i gråt och förlorade hoppet om Gud. Han vaknade nästa morgon fortfarande gömd bakom dörren.

Mörkret hade länge fallit, och min familj sov fridfullt i vårt gamla bondhus. Jag grät mig till sömns, gråtande för Kens själ, gråtande för att jag inte visste vad jag skulle göra, gråtande för att min vän, mannen jag längtade att se stå i frid med Gud, hatade mig.

Ken fortsatte ställa frågor. ”Hur kan Gud vara god och tillåta så mycket ont? Hur kan Gud låta barn lida?” Jag lyssnade medan han fortsatte säga samma saker som jag hört så många gånger förr, utan att ge mig en chans att tala.

Återigen var det dags att gå, och jag var så lättad över det. Han fortsatte tala medan vi backade ut genom dörren. Återigen gick min vän och jag uppför gatan — trötta, frustrerade och önskande att aldrig behöva komma tillbaka.

Ken var 13 år gammal, och hans liv var inte bättre än det varit när han först placerades i fostervården. Hans liv var i kaos. Han blev ständigt skriket åt och förminskad hemma. Ken var trött på att gråta. Ingen brydde sig, och det fanns ingen att dela problemet med. Då kom han på sin listiga plan. Hans skolkamrat var en hippie, och hans föräldrar reste mycket. De kallades zigenare. Han hörde att de var på väg till Kalifornien. Så Ken berättade om sitt hemska liv och frågade om de kunde ge honom skjuts. De var glada att hjälpa.

Den upphetsande morgonen gjorde han helt enkelt som vanligt. Han gick till skolan men åkte i stället till Kalifornien. Han brydde sig inte om att lämna alla sina saker — han hade ju inte mycket ändå. Hans fostrföräldrar brydde sig inte ens om att han försvann.

I Kalifornien bodde Ken på stranden och arbetade för fiskare och den som än behövde hjälp. Han hade alltid tillräckligt att äta och något att göra. Han hade sina medstrandvänner, men han var fortfarande ensam inuti. Hans hjärta var fortfarande tomt. Han längtade efter kärlek.

Ken bodde på stranden i ett och ett halvt år och lifthoppade sedan till Arizona. Där fann han ett hem i ett härbärge för hemlösa och fick ett jobb. Han gjorde det bra och stod snart på egna ben, men hans sökande efter kärlek förde honom på fel vägar. Ken ville verkligen gifta sig med en kärleksfull fru och skaffa familj, men den kvinna han gifte sig med gjorde det inte av kärlek. Hon var sårad, och Kens egen sargade själ drogs till henne. De gifte sig och allt var bra i några år tills han upptäckte att hans fru träffade andra män. Hans hjärta krossades och hans värld kastades i tumult. Ken ville förtvivlat ge trygghet åt de barn som fötts av dem, och han försökte sitt bästa för att hålla ihop. Han ville inte utsätta sina barn för det liv han själv upplevt. Men efter åtta tuffa år blev det skilsmässa.

Ken gick vidare och försökte återhämta sig från skilsmässans förödelse. Hans jakt efter kärlek gav honom bara mer sorg och smärta. Eftersom Ken var sårad och olycklig fann han tillfredsställelse i att göra andra lyckliga. Han lade alla sina pengar på dem, och när han inte hade mer att erbjuda lämnade de honom.

Nu sitter Ken i sin pantbank, ensam, sårad, ledsen och gömd. Han hade genom sitt sorgliga liv funnit att ingen brydde sig. Varje gång han öppnade sig för kärlek blev han alltid sårad. Djupt inom sig kände han verkligen att Gud inte brydde sig. Han förlorade hoppet om Gud, människor och sist av allt, hoppet om kärleken själv. Det är därför vi fortfarande besökte den sunkiga, rökskadade butiken efter sex år av mycket lite synlig framgång. Gud fortsatte att föra oss tillbaka. Han planterade i oss en uthållig kärlek och en obeveklig börda för denna sargade själ. Det är därför vi ägnade många timmar åt att höra samma kritik om och om igen. Samma problem, samma förvirring.

Nästan varje månad svängde han mellan hopp och förtvivlan, kärlek och hat, nytt liv i Gud och sorg och synd. Vi visste aldrig vad nästa besök skulle föra med sig. Vi kunde vara fyllda av hopp och välsignelse, eller sletna av arga ord och sjukliga av bävan. Men vi fortsatte att gå tillbaka, och långsamt reste han sig ur förtvivandets grop och tillät sakta sig själv att svepas in i Guds underbara kärlek och det härliga budskapet om Hans förlösande nåd. Det var fantastiskt att se förändringen i hans liv och höra hans växande förtroende för Kristi kärlek.

Idag älskar Ken Herren. Han lär sig att vandra med Gud. Han har sett Guds kärlek. Han har funnit hopp i Gud. Han har upplevt Guds ovillkorliga kärlek. Han växer fortfarande, och vi är glada att se vad Gud har för honom.

Jag är så glad att Gud förde Ken in i mitt liv. Gud hade en plan för Ken och mig. Gud ville visa Ken att Han älskade honom och att Han skulle finnas där för honom även när Josh vände ryggen mot Honom. Gud ville också att jag skulle bära en börda i min ungdom. Han visste hur lätt jag kunde bli distraherad av pengar och nöjen. Han visste att jag behövde en börda att bära, en själ att vårda. Han ville att jag skulle kunna se bortom skalet av en hård själ och se ett sårat barn därinne. Han ville ge mig en börda som var för stor för mig att bära så att jag skulle lära mig att luta mig mot Honom. Och mest av allt ville Han utrusta mig för att tjäna Honom på bredare sätt.

Kära kristna, öppna era liv för Guds verk. Hitta en möjlighet att älska en sargad själ. Sök upp någon som behöver en vän och älska dem, och vänta och se vad Gud har i beredskap för er. Älska tills det gör så ont att ni inte vet vad ni ska göra, och vänd er sedan till Jesus, som är där för att hjälpa er igenom. Gud väntar kanske på att ni tar första steget innan Han kan använda er. Ditt liv ligger framför dig. Du kan välja att leva ett bekvämt, lyckligt liv, eller så kan du öppna dig för att bli sårad och finna att efter år av väntan flödar ditt liv över av mening och syfte. Jesus öppnade sig för denna världens smärta och ångest, och endast genom det har vi hopp. Han ber oss följa Hans exempel, att öppna oss för smärta så att andra kan få hopp. Och som Han blev förhärligad, så ska också vi bli förhärligade, i någon mån, en dag, och vi kommer aldrig ångra den smärta vi mötte.

It's incredible to me to see how God uses His people throughout history to bring glory to His name. He uses the weak things to confound the wise; the base things to bring to nothing the wisdom of earthly wise men. God uses physical weakness, hardship, loss, grief, toil, and pain to increase our spiritual treasures and build His Kingdom here on the earth!

This hymn became precious to my family and me several years ago as we awaited the birth of our fourth genetically challenged baby. We knew she couldn't stay with us very long. She passed away at just three days old. After researching this hymn, I was amazed to find out that the man whose story had inspired this hymn had lost eight out of his nine children.

The story of this man is a notable one. His 61 years on earth were marked by grief and loss, persecution and imprisonment. Yet, his dedication to Christ was outstanding, and his fire for God and zeal for preaching the gospel never waned until his last day.

Samuel Rutherford, son of a prosperous farmer, was born in the year 1600. His life began in the small village of Nisbet, Scotland. As we glimpse into his life, we notice the hand of God at work in Samuel’s early years. At only three years old, he was playing with his friends when he fell into the town well. His sister and friends ran to get help. When they returned, they found a very wet Samuel sitting on the grass beside the well. They asked him how he got out, and his reply was, "A bonny white man came and drew me out of the well." His family believed that God sent an angel to rescue him that day.

From what we know about Samuel Rutherford, he had two brothers and one sister. He was sent to school when he was young, and he became a very diligent scholar. He learned Latin and Greek so well that he eventually became a professor. He married Eupham Hamilton around 1624, soon after he began teaching at Edinburgh University. At this time, Samuel was yet unconverted and cared only for pursuing his academic goals.

In 1626, at the age of 26, Samuel came to a clear and saving faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. He said, "O but Christ hath a saving eye. When He first looked on me I was saved. It cost Him but a look to make hell quit to me." From that moment he was filled with a passion to preach and to speak about his Saviour. This change of life caused such a stir in the university that Rutherford ended up resigning his professorship.

In 1627, Samuel took his wife and two young children to Galloway, Scotland, where he began pastoring the small church of Anwoth. As he commenced his calling there he said, "I have received the commission from the royal and princely Master, my Lord Jesus, to preach Christ to the people." His passion was for the conversion of the people, and it is said that he seemed to be always praying, always preaching, always visiting the sick, always teaching and instructing, always writing or studying. The zeal with which he preached and his concern for the welfare of his congregation had a great effect on them. Not only them, but folks came from the surrounding towns and villages to hear his preaching. A friend once reported, "Many times I thought he would have flown out of the pulpit when he came to speak of Jesus Christ."

Samuel was not estranged from grief and sorrow. In 1631, only four short years after he began his work as a pastor, his wife passed away. His two children also became ill and left this world. In 1636, after nine years of preaching, he was banished to Aberdeen, where he was forbidden to preach the gospel. This was a very difficult time for him as he greatly missed his wife and children as well as his congregation, the Church at Anwoth. This time in his life is indeed one reason he is so well remembered, for he began writing letters back to his church people and friends. Out of the 365 letters he wrote, 220 of them were written during these 22 months of banishment.

The government eventually changed hands, which gave more liberty to the non-conformist Covenanters. Thereupon Rutherford quickly returned to his beloved flock at Anwoth. About a year later, in the fall of 1639, he again reluctantly left Anwoth but this time to fulfill an appointment to become Professor of Divinity at St Mary's College in St. Andrews. This change was difficult for him, as he again greatly missed his congregation. He writes, "My removal from my flock is so heavy to me, that it maketh my life a burden to me, I had never such a longing for death. The Lord help and hold up this sad clay."

After five months in his new position and having been alone for nearly ten years, the 40-year-old Samuel married Jean McMath. Together they had seven children. Sadly, six of them died in infancy and early childhood. Only a daughter named Agnes survived to adulthood.

Rutherford continued to be an influential leader in the non-conformist movement in Scotland for the next 20 years until 1660. With the death of Cromwell, the rule of the commonwealth came to an end, and Charles II was restored to power. Once again, the wrath of the monarchy fell on Samuel. He was summoned to appear before the judge and charged with high treason against the government for preaching the truth. He was put in prison to await execution. However, before the king could put him to death, Samuel became quite sick. He said, "I have a summons already from a superior Judge, and I behoove to answer my first summons and when your day arrives I shall be where few Kings and great folks come."

Late in the afternoon of the last day of his life in answer to the question, "What think ye now of Christ?" answered thusly, "Oh, that all my brethren in the land may know what a Master I have served, and what peace I have this day! I shall sleep in Christ, and when I awake, I shall be satisfied with His likeness. This night shall close the door, and put my anchor within the veil, and I shall go away in a sleep by five of the clock in the morning. Glory! glory to my Creator and my Redeemer forever! I Shall live and adore Him. Oh, for arms to embrace Him! Oh, for a well-tuned harp! Glory! glory dwelleth in Immanuel's land!" These words were heard by his wife, daughter and friends, and he was indeed with his Lord by five in the morning.

Nearly two centuries later, Annie Ross Cousin, a Scottish poet and hymn writer and the wife of a minister, was inspired by the life and writings of Samuel Rutherford. She summarized his life in a biographical hymn,"The Sands of Time are Sinking". This hymn was first published in 1857 in the Christian Treasury. Out of the nineteen original verses, only four are used in our hymn books. (in bold copy)

The sands of time are sinking,
The dawn of heaven breaks,
The summer morn I’ve sighed for,
The fair, sweet morn awakes:
Dark, dark hath been the midnight,
But dayspring is at hand,
And glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

2. Oh! well it is forever,
Oh! well forevermore
My nest hung in no forest
Of all this death-doomed shore!
Yea, let the vain world vanish,
As from the ship the stand,
While glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

3. There the Red Rose of Sharon
Unfolds its heart-most bloom.
And fills the air of Heaven
With ravishing perfume;
Oh, to behold its blossom,
While by its fragrance fann’d
Where glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

4. The King there in His beauty,
Without a veil is seen:
It were a well-spent journey
Though seven deaths lay between:
The Lamb with His fair army,
Doth on Mount Zion stand;
And glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

5. Oh! Christ He is the fountain,
The deep sweet well of Love!
The streams on earth I’ve tasted,
More deep I’ll drink above;
There, to an ocean fullness,
His mercy doth expand,
And glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

6. E’en Anwoth was not heaven—
E’en preaching was not Christ;
And in my sea-beat prison
My Lord and I held tryst:
And aye my murkiest storm-cloud
Was by a rainbow spann’d,
Caught from the glory dwelling
In Immanuel’s land.

7. But that He built a heaven
Of His surpassing love,
A little New Jerus’lem,
Like to the one above,—
“Lord, take me o’er the water,”
Had been my loud demand,
“Take me to love’s own country,
Unto Immanuel’s land.”

8. But flowers need night’s cool darkness,
The moonlight and the dew;
So Christ, from one who loved it,
His shining oft withdrew;
And then, for cause of absence,
My troubled soul I scann’d—
But glory, shadeless, shineth
In Immanuel’s land.

9. The little birds of Anwoth,
used to count them blest,—
Now, beside happier alters,
go to built my nest:
O’er these there broods no silence,
No graves around them stand,
For glory, deathless, dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

10. Fair Anwoth by the Solway,
To me thou still art dear!
E’en from the verge of Heaven
I drop for thee a tear.
Oh! if one soul from Anwoth
Meet me at God’s right hand,
My Heaven will be two Heavens,
In Immanuel’s land!

11. I’ve wrestled on towards Heaven,
‘Ganst storm, and wind, and tide;—
Now, like a weary traveler,
That leaneth on his guide,
Amid the shades of evening,
While sinks life’s ling’ring sand,
I hail the glory dawning
From Immanuel’s land.

12. Deep waters cross’d life’s pathway,
The hedge of thorns was sharp;
Now these lie all behind me,—
Oh, for a well-tuned harp!
Oh, to join Hallelujah
With yon triumphant band,
Who sing where glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land!

13. With mercy and with judgment
My web of time He wove,
And aye the dews of sorrow
Were lustered with His love!
I’ll bless the hand that guided,
I’ll bless the heart that plann’d,
When throned where glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

14. Soon shall the cup of glory
Wash down earth’s bitterest woes,
Soon shall the desert brier
Break into Eden’s rose:
The curse shall change to blessing–
The name on earth that’s bann’d,
Be graven on the white stone
In Immanuel’s land.

15. Oh! I am my Beloved’s,
And my Beloved’s mine!
He brings a poor vile sinner
Into His “house of wine:”
I stand upon His merit,
I know no other stand,
Not e’en where glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

16. I shall sleep sound in Jesus,
Fill’d with His likeness rise,
To live and to adore Him,
To see Him with these eyes:
‘Tween me and resurrection
But Paradise doth stand;
Then—then for glory dwelling
In Immanuel’s land!

17. The bride eyes not her garment,
But her dear Bridegroom’s face;
I will not gaze at glory,
But on my King of Grace—
Not at the crown He giveth,
But on His pierced hand:
The Lamb is all the glory
Of Immanuel’s land.

18. I have borne scorn and hatred,
I have borne wrong and shame,
Earth’s proud ones have reproach’d me,
For Christ’s thrice blessed name:
Where God His seal set fairest
They’ve stamp’d their foulest brand;
But judgment shines like noonday
In Immanuel’s land.

19. They’ve summoned me before them,
But there I may not come,—
My Lord says, “Come up hither,”
My Lord says, “Welcome home!
My King now at His white throne,
My presence doth command,
Where glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

The fine complementary tune for this text was composed in the early 1800s by a French musician, Chretien D`Urhan. It is well fitted to the words of the hymn—its solemn tempo matches the solemnity of the words. The rising melodic line of the last phrase perfectly matches the anticipated joy expressed by the refrain—"And glory, glory dwelleth in Immanuel's land."

As we conclude this hymn history, let us continue to marvel at the providence of God in the lives of those who have gone before us. May we follow Christ with all our hearts and be vessels ready for the Master's use! One last quote by Samuel Rutherford to take with us. "They lose nothing who gain Christ."

Me maravilla ver cómo Dios usa a Su pueblo a lo largo de la historia para traer gloria a Su nombre. Él usa lo débil para confundir a los sabios; las cosas humildes para dejar sin efecto la sabiduría de los sabios terrenales. ¡Dios usa la debilidad física, las dificultades, la pérdida, el dolor, el trabajo y el sufrimiento para aumentar nuestros tesoros espirituales y edificar Su Reino aquí en la tierra!

Este himno llegó a ser precioso para mi familia y para mí hace varios años mientras aguardábamos el nacimiento de nuestro cuarto bebé con dificultades genéticas. Sabíamos que no podría quedarse con nosotros por mucho tiempo. Falleció con apenas tres días de nacido. Tras investigar sobre este himno, me sorprendió descubrir que el hombre cuya historia inspiró este himno había perdido ocho de sus nueve hijos.

La historia de este hombre es notable. Sus 61 años en la tierra estuvieron marcados por el dolor y la pérdida, la persecución y el encarcelamiento. Sin embargo, su dedicación a Cristo fue sobresaliente, y su celo por Dios y por predicar el evangelio no menguaron hasta su último día.

Samuel Rutherford, hijo de un próspero agricultor, nació en el año 1600. Su vida comenzó en la pequeña aldea de Nisbet, Escocia. Al asomarnos a su vida, notamos la mano de Dios obrando en los primeros años de Samuel. Con apenas tres años, jugaba con sus amigos cuando cayó al pozo del pueblo. Su hermana y amigos corrieron a pedir ayuda. Cuando regresaron, encontraron a un muy mojado Samuel sentado en la hierba junto al pozo. Le preguntaron cómo había salido, y él respondió: "Un hombre blanco y hermoso vino y me sacó del pozo." Su familia creyó que Dios envió un ángel para rescatarlo aquel día.

Por lo que sabemos de Samuel Rutherford, tuvo dos hermanos y una hermana. Fue enviado a la escuela de pequeño, y se volvió un estudiante muy aplicado. Aprendió latín y griego tan bien que finalmente llegó a ser profesor. Se casó con Eupham Hamilton alrededor de 1624, poco después de que comenzó a enseñar en la Universidad de Edimburgo. En ese tiempo, Samuel aún no había sido convertido y sólo se preocupaba por perseguir sus metas académicas.

En 1626, a la edad de 26 años, Samuel llegó a una fe clara y salvadora en el Señor Jesucristo. Dijo: "¡Oh, pero Cristo tiene un ojo que salva. Cuando Él me miró por primera vez fui salvo. No le costó más que una mirada para hacer que el infierno me dejara en paz!" Desde ese momento estuvo lleno de pasión por predicar y hablar de su Salvador. Este cambio de vida causó tal revuelo en la universidad que Rutherford terminó renunciando a su cátedra.

En 1627, Samuel llevó a su esposa y a dos hijos pequeños a Galloway, Escocia, donde comenzó a pastorear la pequeña iglesia de Anwoth. Al comenzar su ministerio allí dijo: "He recibido la comisión del Maestro real y principesco, mi Señor Jesús, para predicar a Cristo al pueblo." Su pasión era la conversión de la gente, y se dice que parecía estar siempre orando, siempre predicando, siempre visitando a los enfermos, siempre enseñando e instruyendo, siempre escribiendo o estudiando. El celo con que predicaba y su preocupación por el bienestar de su congregación tuvieron un gran efecto en ellos. No sólo en ellos; gente de los pueblos y aldeas circundantes venía a escuchar su predicación. Un amigo contó una vez: "Muchas veces pensé que habría volado fuera del púlpito cuando venía a hablar de Jesucristo."

Samuel no estuvo ajeno al dolor y al duelo. En 1631, sólo cuatro cortos años después de comenzar su trabajo como pastor, su esposa falleció. Sus dos hijos también enfermaban y dejaron este mundo. En 1636, tras nueve años de predicación, fue desterrado a Aberdeen, donde se le prohibió predicar el evangelio. Fue un tiempo muy difícil para él, pues extrañaba profundamente a su esposa e hijos, así como a su congregación, la Iglesia de Anwoth. Este período de su vida es, en verdad, una razón por la que es tan recordado, porque comenzó a escribir cartas de vuelta a su gente de iglesia y a sus amigos. De las 365 cartas que escribió, 220 de ellas fueron escritas durante estos 22 meses de destierro.

El gobierno eventualmente cambió de manos, lo que dio más libertad a los disidentes covenanters. Entonces Rutherford regresó rápidamente a su amada grey en Anwoth. Un año después, en el otoño de 1639, de nuevo dejó a regañadientes Anwoth, pero esta vez para cumplir un nombramiento como Profesor de Divinidad en el St Mary's College en St. Andrews. Este cambio fue difícil para él, pues de nuevo extrañaba profundamente a su congregación. Escribe: "Mi separación de mi grey me pesa tanto, que hace mi vida una carga; nunca tuve tal anhelo de la muerte. El Señor ayude y sostenga esta triste carne."

Tras cinco meses en su nueva posición y habiendo estado solo casi diez años, el Samuel de 40 años se casó con Jean McMath. Juntos tuvieron siete hijos. Lamentablemente, seis de ellos murieron en la infancia o en la niñez temprana. Sólo una hija llamada Agnes sobrevivió hasta la edad adulta.

Rutherford continuó siendo un líder influyente en el movimiento disidente en Escocia durante los siguientes 20 años, hasta 1660. Con la muerte de Cromwell, el gobierno del commonwealth llegó a su fin y Carlos II fue restaurado en el poder. Una vez más, la ira de la monarquía cayó sobre Samuel. Fue citado a comparecer ante el juez y acusado de alta traición contra el gobierno por predicar la verdad. Fue encarcelado a la espera de ejecución. Sin embargo, antes de que el rey pudiera darle la muerte, Samuel cayó gravemente enfermo. Dijo: "Ya tengo un citatorio de un Juez superior, y debo responder a mi primer citatorio y cuando llegue vuestro día estaré donde pocos reyes y personas grandes vienen."

Tarde en la tarde del último día de su vida, en respuesta a la pregunta: "¿Qué pensáis ahora de Cristo?" respondió así: "¡Oh, que todos mis hermanos en la tierra sepan qué Maestro he servido, y qué paz tengo este día! Dormiré en Cristo, y cuando despierte, estaré satisfecho con Su semejanza. Esta noche se cerrará la puerta, y pondrá mi ancla dentro del velo, e iré lejos en un sueño a las cinco de la mañana. ¡Gloria! ¡gloria a mi Creador y a mi Redentor por siempre! Viviré y le adoraré. ¡Oh, por brazos para abrazarle! ¡Oh, por un arpa bien afinada! ¡Gloria! ¡la gloria mora en la tierra de Emanuel!" Estas palabras fueron oídas por su esposa, su hija y amigos, y de hecho estuvo con su Señor a las cinco de la mañana.

Casi dos siglos después, Annie Ross Cousin, poetisa y escritora de himnos escocesa y esposa de un ministro, fue inspirada por la vida y los escritos de Samuel Rutherford. Ella resumió su vida en un himno biográfico, "The Sands of Time are Sinking". Este himno fue publicado por primera vez en 1857 en el Christian Treasury. De las diecinueve estrofas originales, sólo cuatro se usan en nuestros himnarios. (en copia en negrita)

The glory of the spring, how sweet!
The newborn life, how glad!
What joy the happy earth to greet
In new, bright raiment clad!

Divine Redeemer, Thee I bless;
I greet Thy going forth;
I love Thee in the loveliness
Of Thy renewed earth.

But O these wonders of Thy grace,
These nobler works of Thine,
These marvels sweeter far to trace,
These new births more divine:

This new-born glow of faith so strong,
This bloom of love so fair,
This new-born ecstasy of song,
And fragrancy of prayer!

Creator Spirit, work in me
These wonders sweet of Thine;
Divine Redeemer, graciously
Renew this heart of mine.

Still, let new life and strength upspring,
Still, let new joy be given;
And grant the glad new song to ring
Through the new earth and Heaven.

Our spiritual forefathers had much to say on the many issues facing the American Mennonite church in their time, and we can still learn from the collected writings of these church leaders and brethren. We will look first at the hermeneutics of the early American Mennonite church, endeavoring to draw examples from which we, as 21st-century Christians, can learn.

First, the correct interpretation of Scripture was a matter of great importance to these earlier Christians. They had only recently emigrated away from a largely hostile area, where they had been constantly tested to the point of death on matters of faith and now faced a different set of challenges when confronted with peace and religious freedom. We will look at how they navigated these challenges by studying several of their doctrines and practices.

The Doctrine of Nonresistance

One matter that was well interpreted and applied by many of the early Mennonite writers is the principle and doctrine of the nonresistant Christian. Although many of their Anabaptist descendants of today still hold, to varying degrees, this doctrine, it is oftentimes not done with the clarity and solemnity of their forefathers. The early American Mennonites understood nonresistance as a foundational aspect of the Christian life, as it should be, and taught extensively on the practical application and appearance of nonresistance in the life of a believer. Their primary motivation for living peaceably and without malice toward one’s fellow man was the given example of Jesus. Christ typified the acceptable response to violence and ill-will: gentleness, meekness, as befitted one who is called a Lamb.

The Emphasis of Biblical Foundations

There was also a firm focus amongst early Mennonite writers against building doctrine on the writings of men. This emphasis comes through strongly in their works, as they quote Scripture extensively. They made their point by bringing in an example of Christ or by way of an applicable Scripture verse, rather than building on the sandy soil of a man’s opinions. One of the areas in which they did so was the matter of salvation.

Importance of Practical Salvation

We can learn much from the early Mennonites about the practical working out of salvation. First, salvation is portrayed as both an inward and an outward change. The inward is affected first through the working of the Holy Spirit in the willful sinner’s life. It is an important distinction that the sinner is willful. This position was contrary to most of the greater established churches of the time. If a sinner must be willful, then it implies that all men can willfully accept salvation, an idea that is fundamental in nature, if not always verbalized, to the church of today.

In the early Mennonites’ time, predestination as taught by Calvinism seems to have necessitated this emphasis on man’s ability to choose freely, which is still true today. There is also another flavoring of the “unwillingly saved” interpretation, and that comes from the aftereffects of the charismatic movement and the effect it has had on Mennonite and Amish circles. This “unwilling salvation” is not a matter of predestination, but rather is described as almost a coercive calling by the Spirit. It has been observed in several salvation testimonies where the testifiers recalled how they were completely comfortable in their lives of sin and debauchery when suddenly they would be struck down in the manner of Saul and could not help themselves but follow after God and give their lives to Him. There are numerous pitfalls with this dramatic understanding of conversion, namely that it absolves responsibility from the one converted for his decision to convert. This leads to a lack of counting the cost of Christianity, which is a death of oneself, a death of pride, and a death of favor with man. If the believer hops headfirst into Christianity, not reckoning that he must give up all these self-pleasing traits, how will he be able to grow spiritually if he cannot let go of his former vices? While this form of conversion may be genuine at the beginning, it does not often progress beyond the milk of the Word to the meat of which a mature Christian must partake. This maturing of a Christian is emphasized in writings ranging from those of Menno Simons up to Abraham Goshalk. It is also important for the sake of the church that the believer be firmly committed and engaged in the steady growth of his faith.

The Seriousness of a Pure Church

The idea of church to the early American Mennonite seems to have been a more serious thought, less individualistic than our current state. It is the pitiable state of nominal Christianity that the church has become a social organization with room for all sin and depravity.

It behooves us to consider closely the character of the church that Christ established and to note as well the character of the true churches, unspotted by apostasy and laxness. This character is, like Christ himself, simple and yet incredibly full of meaning and spiritual vitality.

The first aspect of the church to recognize is its pure state as the bride of Christ. Here again, we should consider the character of Christ. Did He ever give Himself space for sin? Do we find Him occasionally indulging in a brief enjoyment of a “guilty pleasure”? The understanding reader will agree that Christ was pure in His entirety, and so how else should the bride be with which He is to be intimately and eternally joined? To aid our minds in answering such a question, let us consider the earthly symbol of this heavenly union: that of a man and a woman joined together for life. This earthly union is recognized even by non-Christians as something set aside purely for the two individuals involved, a relationship and a sharing of each other that is not and never to be partaken of by anyone outside of the intimate union. This paints clearly for our earth-bound minds the mind of Christ, insomuch as that marriage is a symbol of Christ and His bride. The bride and Christ are for each other and give themselves to nothing and no one other.

Now that we can see the purity of the church, let us examine its practical working out amongst fallen man. If it is to be pure, then how are we to be a part of it? Here enters the need for a clear understanding of regeneration, a doctrine held in high regard by these Mennonite forefathers. They taught that the Spirit affects the spiritual washing and cleansing that will be made apparent in a changed state of thought and action in the believer. This change is still at variance with our fallen nature, but through continued surrender and a deep humility, the Spirit will fill the believer until the nature of sin becomes the dominated instead of the dominant. It is important to realize, however, that this victory over sin is brought into effect by the believer yielding his will and allowing the Spirit complete control.

Thus, a pure church is a surrendered, Spirit-filled group of believers who recognize in true humility that their power is not in any way linked to their own merit. The absence of pride, achieved only by the constant aid of the Spirit, gives further room for purification of the willing believer. In this way, we can see the Christian life in shoe leather.

The Teachings of Practical Christianity

The practicality of the early American Mennonite’s faith was continually on display. In his book, “Pride and Humility,” John M. Brenneman maintains that the outward appearance of a person is directly related to his inward heart, a view which extends as well to the actions of the individual. It is necessary to build on the beliefs of willful salvation, regeneration, and a pure church previously examined to frame the mindset of a Mennonite’s interactions in daily living.

To these serious-minded Christians, there was no difference in importance between the religious belief expressed on Sundays and the mundane actions of the rest of the week. This is evidenced by their general abstinence from political matters and other elements of a worldly nature that would infringe upon the beliefs they held. This put them in direct opposition to many of the churches of their day, where thrived two schools of thought: either that one’s earthly duties in a political manner were carried out completely separate from one’s faith, or that the accomplishment of these civic duties were incorporated in the will of God and so permissible for the Christian to engage in freely.

To the early American Mennonite, these types of stances betrayed the very meaning of his Christianity: he was a new person, alive only in the power of Christ that flowed through him. This influenced and directed every aspect of his life, from his business dealings, which were carried out in a way so as not to take advantage of any party involved, to his dress and manner of deportment, which was to be based on humility and plainness, to his method of conversing with his fellow man, which was to show a genuine concern for the spiritual well-being and eternal destiny.

Conclusion

The sum of all these colonial Mennonite beliefs was the doctrine of how to grow into a mature, humble, repentant, but spiritually powerful servant of God. He denied the allures of the world around him in favor of an eternal reward promised upon the purity of his faith and willing renunciation of the sin in which he had formerly lived. This example, lived out by believers like us, should inspire us to further press into the Kingdom of God, working out our faith in humility and repentance.

Наши духовные предшественники много говорили о многочисленных вопросах, с которыми сталкивалась американская меннонитская церковь в их время, и мы до сих пор можем многому научиться у собранных сочинений этих церковных лидеров и братьев. Сначала мы рассмотрим герменевтику ранней американской меннонитской церкви, стараясь извлечь примеры, которым мы, как христиане XXI века, можем следовать.

Во-первых, правильное толкование Писания было предметом большого значения для этих ранних христиан. Они совсем недавно эмигрировали из преимущественно враждебной среды, где их постоянно испытывали до смерти по вопросам веры, и теперь столкнулись с иным набором трудностей, встречая мир и религиозную свободу. Мы посмотрим, как они ориентировались в этих испытаниях, изучив несколько их доктрин и практик.

Доктрина ненасилия

Одним из вопросов, который многие из ранних меннонитских писателей правильно истолковали и применяли, был принцип и доктрина ненасильственного христианина. Хотя многие их анабаптистские потомки и сегодня в той или иной степени придерживаются этой доктрины, часто это делается без той ясности и торжественности, которые были у их предков. Ранние американские меннониты понимали ненасилие как основополагающий аспект христианской жизни, как и должно быть, и широко учили практическому применению и проявлению ненасилия в жизни верующего. Их главным стимулом жить мирно и без злобы к ближнему был данный пример Иисуса. Христос олицетворял приемлемый ответ на насилие и враждебность: кротость, смирение, как подобает Тому, кто наречён Агнцем.

Акцент на библейских основаниях

Среди ранних меннонитских писателей также присутствовал твёрдый акцент против построения доктрины на сочинениях людей. Этот акцент сильно проявляется в их трудах: они обильно цитировали Писание. Они подкрепляли свою мысль приведением примера Христа или применимого стихотворения из Писания, а не строили на песчаной почве человеческих мнений. Одной из областей, где они так поступали, было дело спасения.

Важность практического спасения

Мы можем многому научиться у ранних меннонитов о практической реализации спасения. Во-первых, спасение изображается как внутреннее и внешнее изменение. Внутреннее воздействие происходит прежде всего через действие Святого Духа в жизни намеренного грешника. Важно отметить, что грешник здесь описывается как намеренный. Эта позиция противостояла большинству тогдашних крупных установленных церквей. Если грешник должен быть намеренным, то это подразумевает, что все люди могут благонамеренно принять спасение, идея, которая по своей сути фундаментальна, если не всегда и проговорена, для современной церкви.

Во времена ранних меннонитов, доктрина предопределения, как её преподавал кальвинизм, казалось бы, требовала этого акцента на способности человека свободно выбирать, что остаётся верным и сегодня. Существует также другое оттенок интерпретации «нежеланного спасения», и он происходит от последействий харизматического движения и влияния, которое оно оказало на меннонитские и амишские круги. Это «нежеланное спасение» не связано с предопределением, но описывается как почти принудительное призвание Духом. Оно наблюдалось во многих свидетельствах о спасении, где свидетельствующие вспоминали, что были полностью довольны своей жизнью греха и распущенности, когда вдруг на них снизошло подобно Саулу, и они не могли не последовать за Богом и отдать Ему свою жизнь. В этом драматическом понимании обращения есть многочисленные подводные камни, а именно то, что оно снимает ответственность с обратившегося за его решение обратиться. Это приводит к отсутствию подсчёта цены христианства, которой является смерть для себя, смерть гордости и утрата благосклонности человека. Если верующий бросается в христианство, не считая, что он должен отказаться от всех этих самоудовлетворяющих черт, как он сможет духовно расти, если не умеет отпустить прежние пороки? Хотя такая форма обращения может быть подлинной в начале, она редко продвигается дальше молока Слова к той плоти, которой должен вкушать зрелый христианин. Это взросление христианина подчёркивается в трудах от Менно Саймонса до Авраама Гошалка. Также важно для блага церкви, чтобы верующий твёрдо приверженно и последовательно участвовал в устойчивом росте своей веры.

Серьёзность чистой церкви

Понятие церкви для ранних американских меннонитов, по-видимому, было более серьёзным, менее индивидуалистичным, чем в нашем нынешнем состоянии. Жалкое положение номинального христианства таково, что церковь превратилась в общественную организацию с местом для всех грехов и развращения.

Нам следует всерьёз задуматься о характере церкви, установленной Христом, и также отметить характер истинных церквей, незапятнанных отпадением и вялостью. Этот характер, подобно самому Христу, прост и вместе с тем невероятно наполнен смыслом и духовной жизнеспособностью.

Первый аспект церкви, который следует признать, — её чистое состояние как невесты Христа. Здесь снова мы должны рассмотреть характер Христа. Давал ли Он когда-нибудь Себе пространство для греха? Употреблялся ли Он когда-либо в кратком наслаждении «виноватым удовольствием»? Вдумчивый читатель согласится, что Христос был чист во всей полноте Своей, и как иначе должна быть невеста, с которой Он будет тесно и вечно соединён? Чтобы помочь нашим земным мыслям ответить на такой вопрос, давайте рассмотрим земный символ этого небесного союза: союз мужчины и женщины, соединённых на всю жизнь. Этот земной союз признан даже нехристианами как нечто, предназначенное исключительно для двух вовлечённых лиц, отношения и взаимное деление, которое не должно и никогда не должно быть доступно никому за пределами интимного союза. Это ясно для наших земных умов отображает ум Христов, насколько брак символизирует Христа и Его невесту. Невеста и Христос друг для друга и не отдают себя ничему и никому другому.

Теперь, когда мы видим чистоту церкви, давайте рассмотрим её практическую реализацию среди падшего человека. Если она должна быть чистой, то как нам быть её частью? Тут вступает потребность в ясном понимании возрождения, доктрины, которой эти меннонитские предки придавали большое значение. Они учили, что Дух производит духовное омовение и очищение, которое станет явным в изменённом состоянии мыслей и поступков верующего. Это изменение всё ещё противоречит нашей падшей природе, но через продолженную покорность и глубокое смирение Дух наполнит верующего до тех пор, пока природа греха не станет подчинённой, а не господствующей. Важно понять, однако, что эта победа над грехом вводится в действие через то, что верующий уступает свою волю и позволяет Духу полный контроль.

Таким образом, чистая церковь — это покорная, наполненная Духом группа верующих, которые в истинном смирении признают, что их сила никоим образом не связана с их собственными заслугами. Отсутствие гордости, достигаемое только постоянной помощью Духа, даёт дальнейшее пространство для очищения благорасположенного верующего. Так мы можем видеть христианскую жизнь в практическом, будничном выражении.

Учения о практическом христианстве

Практичность веры ранних американских меннонитов постоянно проявлялась. В своей книге «Гордыня и смирение» Джон М. Бреннеман утверждает, что внешний вид человека прямо связан с его внутренним сердцем, взгляд, который также распространён и на действия индивидуума. Необходимо опереться на убеждения о намеренном спасении, возрождении и чистой церкви, рассмотренные ранее, чтобы сформировать образ мышления меннонитского подхода к взаимодействию в повседневной жизни.

Для этих серьёзно настроенных христиан не было разницы в важности между религиозным верованием, выражаемым по воскресеньям, и обыденными действиями в остальные дни недели. Это подтверждается их общим воздержанием от политических дел и других элементов мирского характера, которые могли бы посягать на их убеждения. Это ставило их в прямое противостояние со многими церквями их эпохи, где преобладали две школы мысли: либо что земные обязанности в политической сфере выполняются совершенно отдельно от веры, либо что исполнение этих гражданских обязанностей включено в волю Божью и потому допустимо для христианина заниматься ими свободно.

Для раннего американского меннонита такие позиции предавали сам смысл его христианства: он был новым человеком, живым только в силе Христа, которая течёт через него. Это влияло на каждый аспект его жизни, от деловых отношений, которые велись так, чтобы не извлекать выгоду за счёт какой-либо стороны, до его одежды и манеры поведения, основанных на смирении и простоте, до его образа общения с ближним, в котором проявлялась искренняя забота о духовном благополучии и вечной участи.

Заключение

Сумма всех этих колониальных меннонитских убеждений — доктрина о том, как вырасти в зрелого, смиренного, кающегося, но духовно сильного слугу Божьего. Он отвергал прелести окружающего мира в пользу вечной награды, обещанной на основании чистоты его веры и добровольного отречения от прежнего греховного образа жизни. Этот пример, воплощённый верующими, подобными нам, должен вдохновлять нас ещё глубже вступать в Царство Божие, проявляя нашу веру в смирении и покаянии.

“Adrianna, what’s the temperature outside?” asked Asher. He and Adrianna were sitting at the table doing school with their siblings Emily and Kianna.

“Probably about 50.” Adrianna glanced lazily at the thermometer. “Hey, it’s 65 degrees! Mom, may we eat lunch outside?”

Mom looked up from the sink. “If you do a good job with your school until then, you may,” she told them. “And if you get your school done before lunch, you may play outside for a while this afternoon.”

Asher let out a whoop and started writing fast. The girls grinned at each other and picked up their pencils.

Everyone worked diligently until lunchtime. Then Adrianna made sandwiches while Asher put cookies in bags, Emily collected bags of chips, and Kianna ran down to the basement to grab a few apples. They each packed their lunch in a shopping bag and went out to their picnic spot, a big, flat rock in a clearing in the woods.

They ate quickly, then Adrianna suggested, “Let’s go kayak on the pond!”

“I guess we could,” said Asher slowly. “But didn’t Mom say that Emily and Kianna are too small to handle the kayaks?”

“Oh, yes, I guess she did. Well, they can play on the swings or something,” she shrugged

“I think we should play something everyone can help with,” said Asher. He turned to Emily and Kianna. “What do you want to do?”

“Let’s make a playhouse!” suggested Kianna.

“Yes, let’s!” Emily agreed. “You could hunt for us,” she told Asher.

“And Adrianna could be the mom!” said Kianna.

Adrianna stood with a scowl on her face. Playhouse indeed! She was way too old for that! “I’m going kayaking,” she announced. “You can just have your playhouse.” She picked up her shopping bag and put her sandwich and cookie bags into it. She threw her apple core to the dogs and started for the house.

“Adrianna, can you please take ours too?” begged Emily. “You're going to the house anyway.”

“You can take care of your own stuff,” Adrianna called back, crossly. She dropped her shopping bag on the counter, hoping to slip out of the house before Mom saw her.

She heard her mom’s voice. “Wait, Adrianna, what’s wrong? Your face looks like a thunderstorm!”

Adrianna sighed. She hadn’t been fast enough. “I wanted to go kayaking, but Asher doesn’t want to,” she grumbled.

“Well,” said Mom slowly, “I think Asher is remembering that the other girls can't handle kayaks yet. What are they doing?”

“They’re building a playhouse. I'm way too old for that!” Adrianna burst out.

Mom smiled, “What makes you think that?”

“I'm sure none of the girls my age do stuff like that with their little siblings.”

“Are you sure you're not being selfish?” Mom asked. “Sometimes, we need to give up what we want so that others can be happy.”

Adrianna shrugged and went out to the shed to get a kayak. She lifted her blue kayak off the rack and hauled it down to the pond. She snapped the paddle together, hopped into the seat, and pushed the kayak onto the smooth surface of the water. She sighed with pleasure. This was way better than building a playhouse in the woods! She took a few loops around the pond before her paddle began to slow. Somehow it wasn’t as fun this time. She heard Asher and the girls laughing and shouting as they played. Maybe Mom was right, she thought. Maybe I would be happier if I gave up what I want so that we can all play together. Slowly she paddled to the edge of the pond. She stepped out of the kayak, pulled it out of the water, and flipped it over to dry. Resolutely, she walked out of the pasture to find Asher and the girls.

“Hey! Here comes Adrianna!” called Emily happily as Adrianna walked up.

Adrianna grinned, “It looks like you have your house about set up,” she said encouragingly. “What do you need to finish it?”

“We still need a stove, and something for a countertop,” said Kianna.

“I can help you find something,” Adrianna told them. Together they hunted in the woods and the shed for boards and logs to finish the house. When suppertime came and they went in for supper, Adrianna was very happy. Mom was right, she thought. It is more fun to give up my way and do what everyone else wants to.

«Αντριάνα, τι θερμοκρασία έχει έξω;» ρώτησε ο Άσερ. Εκείνος και η Αντριάνα κάθονταν στο τραπέζι και διάβαζαν μαζί με τις αδελφές τους Έμιλι και Κιάνα.

«Πιθανότατα γύρω στους 10.» Η Αντριάνα κοίταξε νωχελικά το θερμόμετρο. «Ωω, είναι 18 βαθμοί! Μαμά, μπορούμε να φάμε έξω;»

Η μαμά σήκωσε το βλέμμα από το νεροχύτη. «Αν τελειώσετε το μάθημά σας καλά μέχρι τότε, μπορείτε», τους είπε. «Και αν τελειώσετε πριν το μεσημέρι, μπορείτε να παίξετε έξω για λίγο το απόγευμα.»

Ο Άσερ φώναξε από χαρά και άρχισε να γράφει γρήγορα. Τα κορίτσια χαμογέλασαν η μία στην άλλη και πήραν τα μολύβια τους.

Όλοι δούλεψαν επιμελώς μέχρι το μεσημεριανό. Τότε η Αντριάνα έφτιαξε σάντουιτς ενώ ο Άσερ έβαζε μπισκότα σε σακουλάκια, η Έμιλι μάζευε σακουλάκια με πατατάκια και η Κιάνα έτρεξε στο υπόγειο να πάρει μερικά μήλα. Ο καθένας πακετάρισε το φαγητό του σε μια σακούλα αγορών και πήγαν στο σημείο του πικνίκ, μια μεγάλη, επίπεδη πέτρα σε ένα ξέφωτο στο δάσος.

Έφαγαν γρήγορα, και τότε η Αντριάνα πρότεινε: «Ας κάνουμε κανό στη λίμνη!»

«Υποθέτω ότι μπορούμε», είπε ο Άσερ αργά. «Αλλά δεν είπε η μαμά ότι η Έμιλι και η Κιάνα είναι πολύ μικρές για να χειριστούν τα κανό;»

«Ω, ναι, νομίζω ότι το είπε. Λοιπόν, μπορούν να παίξουν στις κούνιες ή κάτι τέτοιο», είπε αδιάφορα.

«Νομίζω ότι πρέπει να κάνουμε κάτι που να μπορούν να βοηθήσουν όλοι», είπε ο Άσερ. Γύρισε στην Έμιλι και την Κιάνα. «Τι θέλετε να κάνετε;»

«Ας φτιάξουμε ένα σπιτάκι παιχνιδιού!» πρότεινε η Κιάνα.

«Ναι, ας το κάνουμε!» συμφώνησε η Έμιλι. «Εσύ μπορείς να ψάξεις για πράγματα για μας», είπε στον Άσερ.

«Και η Αντριάνα μπορεί να είναι η μαμά!» είπε η Κιάνα.

Η Αντριάνα στάθηκε με μούτρα. Σπιτάκι παιχνιδιού! Πραγματικά; Ήταν πολύ μεγάλη γι’ αυτό! «Πάω να κάνω κανό», ανακοίνωσε. «Μπορείτε να κρατήσετε το σπιτάκι σας.» Άρπαξε τη σακούλα της και έβαλε μέσα το σάντουιτς και τα μπισκότα. Έριξε το φλούδι του μήλου στους σκύλους και ξεκίνησε για το σπίτι.

«Αντριάνα, μπορείς σε παρακαλώ να πάρεις και τα δικά μας;» παρακάλεσε η Έμιλι. «Πάντως πας στο σπίτι.»

«Μπορείτε να φροντίσετε τα δικά σας», φώναξε η Αντριάνα, θυμωμένα. Έριξε τη σακούλα της πάνω στον πάγκο, ελπίζοντας να βγει απ’ το σπίτι πριν τη δει η μαμά.

Άκουσε τη φωνή της μαμάς. «Περίμενε, Αντριάνα, τι συμβαίνει; Το πρόσωπό σου μοιάζει με καταιγίδα!»

Η Αντριάνα αναστέναξε. Δεν είχε προλάβει αρκετά γρήγορα. «Ήθελα να κάνω κανό, αλλά ο Άσερ δεν θέλει», γκρίνιαξε.

«Λοιπόν», είπε η μαμά αργά, «νομίζω ότι ο Άσερ θυμάται πως τα άλλα κορίτσια δεν μπορούν να χειριστούν ακόμα τα κανό. Τι κάνουν;»

«Φτιάχνουν ένα σπιτάκι παιχνιδιού. Είμαι πολύ μεγάλη γι’ αυτό!» ξέσπασε η Αντριάνα.

Η μαμά χαμογέλασε, «Τι σε κάνει να το νομίζεις αυτό;»

«Είμαι σίγουρη ότι κανένα από τα κορίτσια της ηλικίας μου δεν κάνει τέτοια πράγματα με τα μικρά τους αδελφάκια.»

«Είσαι σίγουρη ότι δεν είσαι εγωίστρια;» ρώτησε η μαμά. «Μερικές φορές πρέπει να παραχωρούμε αυτό που θέλουμε για να είναι κι οι άλλοι χαρούμενοι.»

Η Αντριάνα σήκωσε τους ώμους και πήγε στο υπόστεγο να πάρει ένα κανό. Κατέβασε το μπλε κανό από τη σχάρα και το κουβάλησε μέχρι τη λίμνη. Σύνδεσε την κουπαστή, κάθισε στη θέση και πέταξε το κανό πάνω στην ήρεμη επιφάνεια του νερού. Αναστέναξε ευχάριστα. Αυτό ήταν πολύ καλύτερο από το να φτιάχνει ένα σπιτάκι στο δάσος! Έκανε μερικούς κύκλους στη λίμνη πριν το κουπί της αρχίσει να επιβραδύνει. Κάπως δεν ήταν τόσο διασκεδαστικό αυτή τη φορά. Άκουγε τον Άσερ και τα κορίτσια να γελούν και να φωνάζουν καθώς έπαιζαν. Ίσως η μαμά να είχε δίκιο, σκέφτηκε. Ίσως θα ήμουν πιο ευτυχισμένη αν παράχω αυτό που θέλω έτσι ώστε να παίξουμε όλοι μαζί. Αργά κουνούσε το κουπί προς την άκρη της λίμνης. Βγήκε από το κανό, το τράβηξε έξω από το νερό και το γύρισε ανάποδα για να στεγνώσει. Με αποφασιστικότητα, βγήκε από το λιβάδι για να βρει τον Άσερ και τα κορίτσια.

«Κοίτα! Έρχεται η Αντριάνα!» φώναξε η Έμιλι χαρούμενα καθώς η Αντριάνα πλησίαζε.

Η Αντριάνα χαμογέλασε, «Φαίνεται ότι σχεδόν έχετε το σπιτάκι έτοιμο», είπε ενθαρρυντικά. «Τι χρειάζεστε για να το τελειώσετε;»

«Μας χρειάζεται ακόμα μια κουζίνα και κάτι για πάγκο», είπε η Κιάνα.

«Μπορώ να σας βοηθήσω να βρείτε κάτι», τους είπε η Αντριάνα. Μαζί έψαξαν στο δάσος και στο υπόστεγο για σανίδες και κορμούς για να τελειώσουν το σπιτάκι. Όταν ήρθε η ώρα του δείπνου και μπήκαν μέσα για φαγητό, η Αντριάνα ήταν πολύ ευτυχισμένη. Η μαμά είχε δίκιο, σκέφτηκε. Είναι πιο διασκεδαστικό να παραχωρώ τον δικό μου τρόπο και να κάνω ό,τι θέλει όλη η ομάδα.

“Adrianna, berapa suhu di luar?” tanya Asher. Dia dan Adrianna sedang duduk di meja mengerjakan pelajaran bersama saudara-saudara mereka, Emily dan Kianna.

“Mungkin sekitar 50.” Adrianna melirik termometer dengan malas. “Hei, ini 65 derajat! Ibu, bolehkah kami makan siang di luar?”

Ibu menatap dari wastafel. “Jika kalian menyelesaikan sekolah dengan baik sampai saat itu, kalian boleh,” katanya kepada mereka. “Dan jika kalian selesai sebelum makan siang, kalian boleh bermain di luar sebentar sore ini.”

Asher bersorak dan mulai menulis dengan cepat. Para gadis saling tersenyum dan mengambil pensil mereka.

Semua orang bekerja tekun sampai waktu makan siang. Lalu Adrianna membuat sandwich sementara Asher memasukkan kue ke dalam kantong, Emily mengumpulkan kantong keripik, dan Kianna berlari ke ruang bawah tanah untuk mengambil beberapa apel. Mereka masing-masing mengemas bekal mereka dalam tas belanja dan pergi ke tempat piknik mereka, sebuah batu besar dan datar di sebuah lapangan di dalam hutan.

Mereka makan dengan cepat, lalu Adrianna menyarankan, “Ayo kayak di kolam!”

“Kurasa kita bisa,” kata Asher pelan. “Tapi bukankah Ibu bilang Emily dan Kianna terlalu kecil untuk menangani kayak?”

“Oh, ya, sepertinya dia memang bilang begitu. Yah, mereka bisa bermain di ayunan atau sesuatu,” dia mengangkat bahu.

“Kupikir kita harus bermain sesuatu yang bisa dibantu semua orang,” kata Asher. Dia menoleh ke Emily dan Kianna. “Kalian mau apa?”

“Ayo buat rumah bermain!” usul Kianna.

“Iya, ayo!” setuju Emily. “Kamu bisa berburu untuk kami,” katanya kepada Asher.

“Dan Adrianna bisa jadi ibu!” kata Kianna.

Adrianna berdiri dengan raut wajah cemberut. Rumah bermain benar-benar! Dia terlalu tua untuk itu! “Aku mau kayak,” umumnya. “Kalian boleh punya rumah bermain kalian sendiri.” Dia mengambil tas belanjanya dan memasukkan sandwich dan kantong kuenya ke dalamnya. Dia melemparkan ampas apel ke anjing-anjing dan berjalan menuju rumah.

“Adrianna, bisa tolong bawa milik kami juga?” pinta Emily. “Lagipula kamu kan menuju rumah.”

“Kalian urus sendiri saja barang-barang kalian,” teriak Adrianna dengan kesal. Dia menjatuhkan tas belanjanya di meja dapur, berharap bisa keluar rumah sebelum Ibu melihatnya.

Dia mendengar suara ibunya. “Tunggu, Adrianna, ada apa? Mukamu seperti sedang badai!”

Adrianna menghela napas. Dia tidak cukup cepat. “Aku ingin kayak, tapi Asher tidak mau,” gumamnya.

“Nah,” kata Ibu perlahan, “kupikir Asher ingat bahwa gadis-gadis lain belum bisa menangani kayak. Apa yang mereka lakukan?”

“Mereka sedang membangun rumah bermain. Aku terlalu tua untuk itu!” seru Adrianna.

Ibu tersenyum, “Apa yang membuatmu berpikir begitu?”

“Aku yakin tidak ada gadis seusia aku melakukan hal seperti itu dengan adik-adik kecil mereka.”

“Kamu yakin tidak sedang bersikap egois?” tanya Ibu. “Terkadang, kita perlu mengorbankan apa yang kita inginkan agar orang lain bisa bahagia.”

Adrianna mengangkat bahu dan pergi ke gudang untuk mengambil kayak. Dia mengangkat kayak birunya dari rak dan membawanya turun ke kolam. Dia mengitari kolam beberapa putaran sebelum dayungnya mulai melambat. Entah kenapa kali ini tidak semenyenangkan biasanya. Dia mendengar Asher dan para gadis tertawa dan berteriak saat mereka bermain. Mungkin Ibu benar, pikirnya. Mungkin aku akan lebih bahagia jika mengorbankan keinginanku agar kita semua bisa bermain bersama. Perlahan dia mendayung ke tepi kolam. Dia turun dari kayak, menariknya keluar dari air, dan membaliknya untuk mengeringkan. Dengan tekad, dia berjalan keluar dari padang mencari Asher dan para gadis.

“Hei! Adrianna datang!” seru Emily dengan gembira saat Adrianna berjalan mendekat.

Adrianna tersenyum, “Sepertinya rumahmu sudah hampir jadi,” katanya dengan dorongan. “Apa yang kalian butuhkan untuk menyelesaikannya?”

“Kita masih butuh kompor, dan sesuatu untuk meja dapur,” kata Kianna.

“Aku bisa bantu carikan sesuatu,” kata Adrianna kepada mereka. Bersama-sama mereka mencari di hutan dan gudang papan serta kayu untuk menyelesaikan rumah itu. Ketika tiba waktu makan malam dan mereka masuk untuk makan, Adrianna sangat bahagia. Ibu benar, pikirnya. Lebih menyenangkan mengorbankan caraku dan melakukan apa yang diinginkan semua orang.
