The winter of 1882 unfolded in the small southern town of Tuscumbia, Alabama. A happy, normal two-year-old girl fell desperately ill with a strange fever. The fever came and went, came and went, and came again. The family doctor feared the child would die of the strain, but the child was strong and one day the fever finally left for good. The following day the mother waved a hand past her daughter's face, but the child did not blink. Subsequent efforts wrought no results and a new day dawned upon the family with a blind daughter.

As the child gained strength enough to resume play, the great dinner bell released its peal to all around, but Helen did not respond. Other noises produced similar results and the Keller family came to the stark realization that life would never be the same again. Most of us may never face the grim circumstances that Helen Keller's family did, but each of us will certainly endure hardships tailored specifically by our God.

The human mind is an amazing and intricate creation. Though many have sought to understand it, its operational ability remains incomprehensible to mankind. It is no small wonder that a portion of the keenest insight into the health of the mind is revealed in God's Word. “For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.” (2 Timothy 1:7)

Fear is the ominous adversary to a sound mind. It towers over the soul and taunts the saint with its menacing derision. Fear can take a sunny meadow and turn it into a lonely wilderness. It can render a grand wedding celebration as dark as a cave, and turn a banquet fit for a king into a nauseating affair. It is the most powerful and devastating tool in the devil's employment. Despite many bold claims, none are exempt from its wielding. “A dreadful sound is in his ears: in prosperity the destroyer shall come upon him. He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness, and he is waited for of the sword.” (Job 15:21, 22) It is fear that stands to attack and quench all the prosperity of the soul. If we are to resist it in these days, we he must rise with all diligence in defiant warfare.

We do not need to look very far to behold the disarmament and weakening of man's mind. Medication for the mind ranks among the leading prescriptions consumed in America today. This is no pointed accusation at any individuals who may find themselves in need of medical assistance to control their mind. But it takes no scholar to look at obesity and consider the diet, to see rebellious teens and connect it to the infrastructure of the home, or to see men's hearts (minds) failing them and believe that fear is at the root. While some may totally master their diet, few can claim to be accomplished parents. Fewer yet are those who are not, at times, accosted by fear. Though pride and sense may keep the outward man in check, and remaining perfectly calm, the inward man, at least subconsciously, must deal with the strain. Americans love to claim the motto, "No fear!" but our medication consumption tells a different story. Paul claimed no exemption, for he was “troubled on every side; without were fightings, within were fears.” (2 Corinthians 7:5)

What do we fear? Loss, pain, and humility. No one likes to lose something that we have fought to obtain. No one enjoys pain. No one loves to be humiliated. Still, we do not need to read far in the Scriptures to realize that these are often the avenues that God uses to further urge His servants down the path into His likeness. There is no insurance on earth that can secure the vibrancy of youth, the love of a family, or the respect of friends. The things that supply us with earth's greatest vanguard are all vulnerable to the risks of loss. Therefore, we fear. Though we lie in bed until the dawn of the morning, we can in no wise increase our stature nor alleviate the loss that God has laid upon our lives. This anxiety only furthers our grief and adds fuel to our fears.

“Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6 7) Herein is the keeping of our hearts and minds: prayer, peace, and thanksgiving.

Like a skillful artisan we must carefully weave these two scriptures together on the loom of life for there seems to be a direct correlation between the fruitful - power, love and sound mind, to the “rootful”- prayer, peace, and thankfulness. There will be no conquering of our fears without these things, and every society that is anemic to these ingredients will certainly be handicapped.

Prayer Begets Power

In our weakened condition we cannot apprehend prayer as we ought. It is then we must rely on those who can or perhaps the Spirit, which maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. Communing with the Omnipotent Head of the universe is a tremendously bold task. Many will administer prayer as merely a formal task, seeking to be perfectly reverent in it. This is not communing as with a friend, nor is it bold. It is more apt to fall under the description of fear. The remedial therapy for fear is in pouring out all our anxiety, bitterness, and complaint onto our God. The saints of yesteryear had been known to vehemently pour out their accusations and the bitterness of their soul unto God.

“Then Job answered and said, Even to day is my complaint bitter: my stroke is heavier than my groaning. Oh that I knew where I might find him! That I might come even to his seat! I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments. I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would say unto me. Will he plead against me with his great power? No; but he would put strength in me.” (Job 23:1-6)

  • David —“I poured out my complaint before him; I shewed before him my trouble.” (Psalm 142:2)
  • Hannah —“For out of the abundance of my complaint and grief have I spoken hitherto.” (1 Samuel 1:16)
  • Jeremiah —“He hath filled me with bitterness, he hath made me drunken with wormwood.”
    (Lamentations 3:15)
  • Naomi —“Call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me.” (Ruth 1:20)
  • Hezekiah —“He will cut me off with pining sickness: from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me.” (Isaiah 38:12)
  • Jesus — “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46)

All these spewed forth bold accusations and complaints against God in fervent prayer and none of them offended Him. On the contrary, God had not given them the spirit of fear but of power, and they serve as our examples. It was faithless Ahab who was told to ask of God a sign in the heavens or earth. In his pious reply he refused to "tempt" God. This lack of boldness and abundance of fear is more tempting to God than the abundance of bitterness in our complaint for “there is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.” (1 John 4:18)

Peace Begets Love

We are all at rest with the things we love. "Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them.” (Psalm 119:165) A sparkling young child who is at peace with his father worships the man and strives to imitate him. Through the lad's tender eyes, his father's character is unflawed. His skill is unmatched. Even the brand of vehicle he drives is the best, and he emulates his every action. Even though every father knows the limitations of his son's expectations, we all bask in the seasonal loyalty. It is knowledge and fear that undermines this loyal love. An abusive father will destroy such childhood esteem and fear will be its replacement. It was through base fear that the evil servant buried his talent and did not trade with it. In his eyes his master was austere and to be feared. But God has not given us the spirit of fear but of love.

“We love him, because he first loved us. If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” (1 John 4:19, 20) The soul who is affected by this love cannot but imitate it. He is at great peace with his Father’s love and the eyes through which he views his Father's character can only enlist replication. However dire the circumstances we may find ourselves in, this spirit of love and peace will carry us through whatever opposition we may meet with on life's pathway. Jacob made nothing of the hard service he was to endure for Rachel; the spirit of love to God will set us above the fear of man, and all the hurt that a man can do us.

Thankfulness Begets a Sound Mind

We do not need to study happy souls long to find buried within the bedrock of each one, a foundation of gratitude. The spirit of a sound mind, or quietness of mind, is a peaceable enjoyment of life. We are oftentimes discouraged in our way when the features of our environment do not measure not up to our own fancy and imagination. A mere sober, solid, thinking mind would obviate and defuse such fruitless notions, yet we are all tempted to entertain formidable ingratitude. It takes no brainpower to expose things we disdain, for Satan is certain to magnify and outline every unsatisfactory detail we encounter. We each may think ourselves into a deep cave, but we must thank ourselves out.

Fear of losing our health, wealth, reputation, and happiness is the biggest hindrance to securing it. To focus on our pain is to invite more. To be constantly analyzing our life to see if we are being fulfilled is a sure avenue to ingratitude. The world is constantly asking, "Are we having fun yet?" The answer is, "No". To these souls, life will never be adequate, and they must wander forth seeking the bigger fulfillment that the last one did not secure. It is the fear that we are not receiving our fair allotment in life that breeds discontentment. It is discontentment that produces more fear, and the downward spiral progresses. Such was the consternation of the soul who asked Christ to speak to his brother to divide the inheritance with him. This may be logical thinking, but it is not conducive to a sound and peaceable mind. This offended soul has no root in himself and will forever be wronged in some fashion and spend his days in search of a savior to come and fix the other party. “... neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid. Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.” (Isaiah 8:12, 13)

There is no earthly level of attainment or perfect environment that will promote a sound mind. It can only be secured through prayer, peace, and thankfulness. This may take some reprogramming of our minds to reach into the subconscious recesses, but we must soberly gird up the loins of our minds and exercise them if we ever hope to obtain “the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ;” (1 Peter 1:13)

“And the peace of God,
which passeth all understanding,
shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.
Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true,
whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just,
whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely,
whatsoever things are of good report;
if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise,
think on these things.

— Philippians 4:7, 8

1882 की सर्दियों में अलबामा के छोटे दक्षिणी कस्बे तुसकुम्बिया में एक घटना घटी। एक खुश, सामान्य दो साल की लड़की एक अजीब बुखार से बुरी तरह बीमार पड़ गई। बुखार आता गया, जाता आया, गया और फिर वापस आ गया। परिवार का डॉक्टर डर गया कि बच्ची इस कष्ट से मर जाएगी, पर बच्ची मजबूत थी और एक दिन बुखार हमेशा‑के‑लिए चला गया। अगले दिन माँ ने अपनी बेटी के चेहरे के पास हाथ लहराया, पर बच्ची ने पलक भी नहीं झपकाई। बाद की कोशिशों का कोई परिणाम नहीं हुआ और एक नया दिन उस परिवार पर एक अंधी बेटी के साथ आ गया।

जब बच्ची खेलने की हिम्मत फिर से जुटा गई, तो बड़ा डिनर घंटा चारों ओर अपनी ध्वनि निकालने लगा, पर हेलेन ने प्रतिक्रिया नहीं दी। अन्य आवाज़ों के भी समान परिणाम हुए और केलर परिवार को कठोर एहसास हुआ कि जीवन अब फिर कभी वैसा नहीं रहेगा। हम में से अधिकांश शायद हेलेन के परिवार जैसी भयानक परिस्थितियों का सामना कभी न करें, पर हम में से हर कोई निश्चित रूप से उन कठिनाइयों से होकर गुजरेगा जो हमारे परमेश्वर ने विशेष रूप से हमारे लिए तैयार की हैं।

मानव मन एक अद्भुत और जटिल रचना है। कई लोगों ने इसे समझने की कोशिश की, पर इसकी कार्य क्षमता मानव के लिए अकल्पनीय बनी रहती है। इसमें कोई आश्चर्य नहीं कि मन के स्वास्थ्य के बारे में सबसे तीखे अंतर्दृष्टि में से एक परमेश्वर के वचन में प्रकट होती है। “For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.” (2 Timothy 1:7)

भय एक शांत मन का भयावह विरोधी है। यह आत्मा के ऊपर पहाड़ की तरह खड़ा होता है और संत को अपनी कटु उपहास से चिढ़ाता है। भय किसी उज्जवल मैदान को अकेलेपन के वीरान स्थान में बदल सकता है। यह एक भव्य विवाह समारोह को गुफा जितना अंधेरा कर सकता है, और राजा के लिए योग्य भोज को उल्टी सी बातें करने वाला बना सकता है। यह शैतान की नौकरशाही में सबसे शक्तिशाली और विनाशकारी उपकरण है। कई निडर दावों के बावजूद, कोई भी इससे छूट नहीं पा सकता। “A dreadful sound is in his ears: in prosperity the destroyer shall come upon him. He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness, and he is waited for of the sword.” (Job 15:21, 22) यह भय ही है जो आत्मा की सारी समृद्धि पर हमला करने और उसे बुझाने के लिए खड़ा रहता है। यदि हम आज के दिनों में इसका विरोध करना चाहते हैं, तो हमें सभी परिश्रम के साथ विद्रोही युद्ध में उठना होगा।

मनुष्य के मन की अचेतनता और कमजोरी देखने के लिए हमें बहुत दूर नहीं देखना पड़ता। मन के लिए दवाइयां आज अमेरिका में सबसे अधिक लिखी जाने वाली दवाओं में हैं। यह किसी ऐसे व्यक्ति पर तिरस्कृत आरोप नहीं है जिन्हें अपने मन को नियंत्रित करने के लिए चिकित्सा सहायता की आवश्यकता पड़ सकती है। पर मोटापा देखकर उसके आहार के बारे में सोचना, विद्रोही किशोरों को देखकर उसे घर की संरचना से जोड़ना, या पुरुषों के हृदय (मन) का फेल होना देखकर यह मान लेना कि भय जड़ है — इसके लिए किसी विद्वान की आवश्यकता नहीं। जबकि कुछ लोग अपने आहार पर पूरी तरह नियंत्रण कर सकते हैं, बहुत कम दावा कर सकते हैं कि वे सिद्ध माता‑पिता हैं। और उससे भी कम ऐसे हैं जिन्हें कभी‑कभी भय सताता ही न हो। हालांकि अभिमान और समझ बाह्य व्यक्ति को नियंत्रण में रख सकते हैं और वह पूरी तरह शांत दिखता है, भीतर का व्यक्ति, कम से कम अवचेतन रूप से, उस तनाव से जूझता है। अमेरिकियों को अपना आदर्श वाक्य कहना पसंद है, “कोई डर नहीं!” पर हमारी दवा की खपत एक अलग कहानी बताती है। पॉल ने भी कोई छूट का दावा नहीं किया, क्योंकि वह "troubled on every side; without were fightings, within were fears." (2 Corinthians 7:5)

हम किस से डरते हैं? हानि, दर्द, और अपमान से। कोई भी उस चीज़ को खोना पसंद नहीं करता जिसके लिए उसने लड़ाई लड़ी हो। कोई भी दर्द का आनंद नहीं लेता। कोई भी अपमानित होना पसंद नहीं करता। फिर भी, हमें स्पष्ट रूप से पवित्र शास्त्रों को थोड़ी सी ही पढ़ना होगा यह समझने के लिए कि ये अक्सर वे मार्ग होते हैं जिनके द्वारा परमेश्वर अपने सेवकों को और अधिक उनकी आत्मरूपता की ओर प्रेरित करते हैं। पृथ्वी पर कोई बीमा युवा‑उत्साह, पारिवारिक प्रेम, या मित्रों के सम्मान की जीवंतता को सुरक्षित नहीं कर सकता। जो चीजें हमें पृथ्वी की सबसे बड़ी अग्रिम सुरक्षा देती हैं वे सभी हानि के जोखिम के प्रति असुरक्षित हैं। इसलिए हम भयभीत होते हैं। भले हम सुबह तक बिस्तर पर पड़े रहें, हम किसी भी प्रकार अपनी महत्ता नहीं बढ़ा सकते और न ही उस हानि को कम कर सकते जो परमेश्वर ने हमारे जीवन पर रखा है। यह चिंता केवल हमारे शोक को बढ़ाती है और हमारे भय को और ईंधन देती है।

“Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6 7) यहीं हमारे हृदयों और मनों की रक्षा है: प्रार्थना, शांति, और कृतज्ञता।

किसी कुशल कारीगर की तरह हमें इन दो शास्त्रों को जीवन के ताने‑बाने पर सावधानीपूर्वक बुनना चाहिए क्योंकि ऐसा प्रतीत होता है कि फलदायी — शक्ति, प्रेम और शांत मन — और "मूलभूत" — प्रार्थना, शांति, और कृतज्ञता — के बीच सीधा सम्बन्ध है। इन चीज़ों के बिना हमारे भय पर विजय नहीं मिलेगी, और हर समाज जो इन तत्वों के प्रति रक्तहीन होगा वह निश्चित रूप से हतांग रहेगा।

प्रार्थना से शक्ति उत्पन्न होती है

हमारी कमजोर स्थिति में हम वैसे प्रार्थना का ग्रहण नहीं कर पाते जैसा हमें करना चाहिए। तब हमें उन लोगों पर भरोसा करना चाहिए जो कर सकते हैं या शायद आत्मा पर, जो हमारे लिए अनकहे कराहों के साथ दलीलें करता है। जगत के सर्वशक्तिमान प्रधान से संवाद करना एक अत्यंत साहसिक कार्य है। कई लोग प्रार्थना को केवल औपचारिक कर्तव्य के रूप में करते हैं, उसमें पूर्ण भक्ति दिखाने की कोशिश करते हैं। यह मित्र के साथ संवाद जैसा नहीं है, न ही यह साहसपूर्ण है। यह अधिक उपहास करते हुए भय के वर्णन के दायरे में आता है। भय के लिए औषधि हमारी सारी चिंता, कटुता, और शिकायतें अपने परमेश्वर पर ढोर डालने में हैं। पिछले युगों के संतों को परमेश्वर के पास प्रबलता से अपनी आरोप‑प्रवचन और आत्मा की कटुता ढेर करने के लिए जाना जाता था।

“Then Job answered and said, Even to day is my complaint bitter: my stroke is heavier than my groaning. Oh that I knew where I might find him! That I might come even to his seat! I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments. I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would say unto me. Will he plead against me with his great power? No; but he would put strength in me.” (Job 23:1-6)

  • David —“I poured out my complaint before him; I shewed before him my trouble.” (Psalm 142:2)
  • Hannah —“For out of the abundance of my complaint and grief have I spoken hitherto.” (1 Samuel 1:16)
  • Jeremiah —“He hath filled me with bitterness, he hath made me drunken with wormwood.”
    (Lamentations 3:15)
  • Naomi —“Call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me.” (Ruth 1:20)
  • Hezekiah —“He will cut me off with pining sickness: from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me.” (Isaiah 38:12)
  • Jesus — “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46)

ये सभी परमेश्वर के विरुद्ध साहसपूर्ण आरोप‑प्रवचन और शिकायतों को प्रबल प्रार्थना में उंडेलते थे और इन में से किसी ने भी उसे आहत नहीं किया। इसके विपरीत, परमेश्वर ने उन्हें भय की आत्मा नहीं दी बल्कि शक्ति की, और वे हमारे उदाहरण के रूप में सेवा करते हैं। अविश्वासी अहाब को वह कहा गया था कि वह स्वर्ग या पृथ्वी में परमेश्वर से एक चिह्न माँगे। अपने धर्मात्मा उत्तर में उसने परमेश्वर को "लुभाने" से इंकार कर दिया। साहस की इस कमी और भय की अधिकता परमेश्वर के लिए हमारे कड़वे आरोपों की अधिकता से अधिक परीक्षात्मक होती है, क्योंकि “there is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.” (1 John 4:18)

शांति से प्रेम उत्पन्न होता है

हम सब उन चीज़ों के साथ शांत रहते हैं जिन्हें हम प्रेम करते हैं। "Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them.” (Psalm 119:165) एक चमकीला छोटा बच्चा जो अपने पिता के साथ शांत है, उस आदमी की उपासना करता है और उसकी नकल करने का प्रयत्न करता है। बच्चे की नाज़ुक आँखों से, उसके पिता का चरित्र दोषरहित दिखाई देता है। उसकी कला बेमिसाल है। यहां तक कि वह जिस वाहन का ब्रांड चलाता है वह सर्वश्रेष्ठ है, और वह उसके हर कृत्य की नकल करता है। यद्यपि हर पिता अपने बेटे की अपेक्षाओं की सीमाएँ जानता है, हम सब मौसमी निष्ठा में नहाते हैं। यह ज्ञान और भय है जो इस निष्ठावान प्रेम को कमज़ोर करता है। एक अपमानजनक पिता ऐसे बचपन के समान्य आदर को नष्ट कर देगा और भय उसका स्थान ले लेगा। इसी नीच भय के द्वारा दुराचारी सेवक ने अपनी प्रतिभा जमीन में दबा दी और उससे व्यापार नहीं किया। उसकी आँखों में उसका स्वामी कठोर और भयानक था। पर परमेश्वर ने हमें भय की आत्मा नहीं दी बल्कि प्रेम की दी है।

“We love him, because he first loved us. If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” (1 John 4:19, 20) जिस आत्मा पर यह प्रेम प्रभाव डालता है वह इसे नकल करने के सिवा कुछ नहीं कर सकता। वह अपने पिता के प्रेम के साथ महान शांति में है और जिन आँखों से वह अपने पिता के चरित्र को देखता है वे केवल अनुकरण को प्रेरित कर सकती हैं। चाहे हम जिस भी भयावह परिस्थिति में मिलें, प्रेम और शांति की यह आत्मा हमें जीवन के मार्ग में किसी भी विरोध का सामना करते हुए पार करा देगी। याकूब ने राचेल के लिए जो कठोर सेवा उसे सहनी थी उसे कुछ भी माना नहीं; परमेश्वर के प्रति प्रेम की आत्मा हमें मनुष्य के भय से ऊपर उठा देगी, और मनुष्य हमें जो भी चोट दे सकता है उससे भी।

कृतज्ञता से शांत मन उत्पन्न होता है

हमें खुश आत्माओं का अध्ययन लंबे समय तक करने की आवश्यकता नहीं है ताकि प्रत्येक के भीतर चट्टान की नींव में दबी कृतज्ञता की बुनियाद मिल सके। शांत मन की आत्मा, अथवा मन की शांति, जीवन का शांतिपूर्ण आनन्द है। जब हमारे पर्यावरण की विशेषताएँ हमारी अपनी कल्पना और रुचि के अनुरूप नहीं होतीं तो हम अक्सर अपने मार्ग में हतोत्साहित हो जाते हैं। एक सामान्य, ठोस, सोचने वाला मन ऐसे निष्फल विचारों को टाल और निष्क्रिय कर दे सकता है, पर हम सभी को प्रबल अभाग्यता के विचारों के प्रलोभन में लाया जाता है। हमारी नाखुशी दिखाने के लिए किसी बड़ी बुद्धि की आवश्यकता नहीं है, क्योंकि शैतान निश्चित रूप से हर असंतोषजनक विवरण को बड़ा करेगा और उसका रूपरेखांकन करेगा। हम में से हर कोई खुद को एक गहरी गुफा में सोच सकता है, पर हमें खुद को धन्यवाद करना होगा।

हमारी सेहत, धन, प्रतिष्ठा, और सुख को खोने का भय उसे सुरक्षित करने में सबसे बड़ा अवरोध है। हमारे दर्द पर ध्यान केंद्रित करना और अधिक दर्द आमंत्रित करना है। लगातार अपने जीवन का विश्लेषण करना यह देखने के लिए कि क्या हम संतुष्ट हैं, कृतघ्नता की निश्चित मार्ग है। दुनिया लगातार पूछती रहती है, "Are we having fun yet?" उत्तर है, "No". इन आत्माओं के लिए, जीवन कभी पर्याप्त नहीं होगा, और उन्हें उस बड़े आनन्द की खोज करते हुए भटकना होगा जिसे पिछला आनंद पूरा नहीं कर सका। यह भय कि हमें जीवन में हमारा उचित हिस्सा नहीं मिल रहा है असन्तोष को जन्म देता है। असन्तोष और अधिक भय पैदा करता है, और डाउनवार्ड स्पाइरल जारी रहती है। ऐसी ही वह व्यथित आत्मा थी जिसने मसीह से कहा कि वह अपने भाई से कहे कि वह विरासत बाँट दे। यह तार्किक सोच हो सकती है, पर यह शांत और शान्तिपूर्ण मन के अनुकूल नहीं है। इस आहत आत्मा का अपने भीतर कोई मूल नहीं है और वह सदा किसी न किसी रूप में अपमानित रहेगी और अपने दिनों को ऐसे उद्धारकर्ता की खोज में बिताएगी जो आकर दूसरी पार्टी को सुधार दे। “... neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid. Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.” (Isaiah 8:12, 13)

कोई भी सांसारिक स्तर की उपलब्धि या परिपूर्ण वातावरण ऐसा नहीं है जो शांत मन को बढ़ावा दे सके। इसे केवल प्रार्थना, शांति, और कृतज्ञता के माध्यम से ही सुरक्षित किया जा सकता है। यह हमारे मनों में कुछ पुन:प्रोग्रामिंग की आवश्यकता कर सकता है ताकि अवचेतन कोनों तक पहुँचा जा सके, पर हमें गंभीरता से अपने मनों की कमर कसनी चाहिए और उन्हें व्यायाम कराना चाहिए यदि हम कभी भी "the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ;" (1 Peter 1:13) को प्राप्त करने की आशा रखते हैं।

“And the peace of God,
which passeth all understanding,
shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.
Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true,
whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just,
whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely,
whatsoever things are of good report;
if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise,
think on these things.

— Philippians 4:7, 8

Asher let out a whoop and started writing fast. The girls grinned at each other and picked up their pencils.

Everyone worked diligently until lunchtime. Then Adrianna made sandwiches while Asher put cookies in bags, Emily collected bags of chips, and Kianna ran down to the basement to grab a few apples. They each packed their lunch in a shopping bag and went out to their picnic spot, a big, flat rock in a clearing in the woods.

They ate quickly, then Adrianna suggested, “Let’s go kayak on the pond!”

“I guess we could,” said Asher slowly. “But didn’t Mom say that Emily and Kianna are too small to handle the kayaks?”

“Oh, yes, I guess she did. Well, they can play on the swings or something,” she shrugged

“I think we should play something everyone can help with,” said Asher. He turned to Emily and Kianna. “What do you want to do?”

“Let’s make a playhouse!” suggested Kianna.

“Yes, let’s!” Emily agreed. “You could hunt for us,” she told Asher.

“And Adrianna could be the mom!” said Kianna.

Adrianna stood with a scowl on her face. Playhouse indeed! She was way too old for that! “I’m going kayaking,” she announced. “You can just have your playhouse.” She picked up her shopping bag and put her sandwich and cookie bags into it. She threw her apple core to the dogs and started for the house.

“Adrianna, can you please take ours too?” begged Emily. “You're going to the house anyway.”

“You can take care of your own stuff,” Adrianna called back, crossly. She dropped her shopping bag on the counter, hoping to slip out of the house before Mom saw her.

She heard her mom’s voice. “Wait, Adrianna, what’s wrong? Your face looks like a thunderstorm!”

Adrianna sighed. She hadn’t been fast enough. “I wanted to go kayaking, but Asher doesn’t want to,” she grumbled.

“Well,” said Mom slowly, “I think Asher is remembering that the other girls can't handle kayaks yet. What are they doing?”

“They’re building a playhouse. I'm way too old for that!” Adrianna burst out.

Mom smiled, “What makes you think that?”

“I'm sure none of the girls my age do stuff like that with their little siblings.”

“Are you sure you're not being selfish?” Mom asked. “Sometimes, we need to give up what we want so that others can be happy.”

Adrianna shrugged and went out to the shed to get a kayak. She lifted her blue kayak off the rack and hauled it down to the pond. She snapped the paddle together, hopped into the seat, and pushed the kayak onto the smooth surface of the water. She sighed with pleasure. This was way better than building a playhouse in the woods! She took a few loops around the pond before her paddle began to slow. Somehow it wasn’t as fun this time. She heard Asher and the girls laughing and shouting as they played. Maybe Mom was right, she thought. Maybe I would be happier if I gave up what I want so that we can all play together. Slowly she paddled to the edge of the pond. She stepped out of the kayak, pulled it out of the water, and flipped it over to dry. Resolutely, she walked out of the pasture to find Asher and the girls.

“Hey! Here comes Adrianna!” called Emily happily as Adrianna walked up.

Adrianna grinned, “It looks like you have your house about set up,” she said encouragingly. “What do you need to finish it?”

“We still need a stove, and something for a countertop,” said Kianna.

“I can help you find something,” Adrianna told them. Together they hunted in the woods and the shed for boards and logs to finish the house. When suppertime came and they went in for supper, Adrianna was very happy. Mom was right, she thought. It is more fun to give up my way and do what everyone else wants to.

“Adrianna, qual é a temperatura lá fora?” perguntou Asher. Ele e Adrianna estavam sentados à mesa estudando com as irmãs Emily e Kianna.

“Provavelmente uns 10.” Adrianna olhou preguiçosamente para o termômetro. “Ei, está 18 graus! Mãe, podemos almoçar lá fora?”

A mãe levantou os olhos da pia. “Se vocês fizerem um bom trabalho nos estudos até lá, podem,” disse ela. “E se terminarem os deveres antes do almoço, podem brincar lá fora um pouco esta tarde.”

Asher soltou um grito de alegria e começou a escrever rapidamente. As meninas sorriram uma para a outra e pegaram seus lápis.

Todos trabalharam diligentemente até a hora do almoço. Então Adrianna preparou sanduíches enquanto Asher colocava biscoitos em saquinhos, Emily recolhia pacotes de salgadinhos e Kianna descia ao porão para pegar algumas maçãs. Cada um arrumou seu almoço numa sacola de compras e foram para o local do piquenique, uma grande pedra plana numa clareira na mata.

Comeram depressa, então Adrianna sugeriu: “Vamos andar de caiaque no lago!”

“Acho que poderíamos,” disse Asher devagar. “Mas a mamãe não disse que a Emily e a Kianna ainda são pequenas demais para os caiaques?”

“Ah, é, acho que ela disse. Bem, elas podem brincar nos balanços ou algo assim,” ela deu de ombros.

“Acho que deveríamos brincar de algo em que todo mundo possa ajudar,” disse Asher. Ele se virou para Emily e Kianna. “O que vocês querem fazer?”

“Vamos construir uma casinha de brincar!” sugeriu Kianna.

“Sim, vamos!” concordou Emily. “Você poderia procurar as coisas para nós,” disse ela a Asher.

“E a Adrianna poderia ser a mamãe!” disse Kianna.

Adrianna ficou em pé com um cenho carrancudo. Casinha de brincar, é? Ela era muito velha para isso! “Vou andar de caiaque,” anunciou. “Vocês fiquem com a casinha.” Pegou sua sacola de compras e colocou nela o sanduíche e os saquinhos de biscoito. Jogou o caroço da maçã para os cachorros e se dirigiu para a casa.

“Adrianna, você pode pegar as nossas também, por favor?” implorou Emily. “Você vai para a casa de qualquer jeito.”

“Cuidem das suas próprias coisas,” Adrianna respondeu, irritada. Largou a sacola de compras no balcão, esperando escapar de casa antes que a mãe a visse.

Ouviu a voz da mãe. “Espere, Adrianna, o que aconteceu? Seu rosto parece uma tempestade!”

Adrianna suspirou. Ela não havia sido rápida o suficiente. “Eu queria ir andar de caiaque, mas o Asher não quer,” resmungou.

“Bem,” disse a mãe devagar, “acho que o Asher está lembrando que as outras meninas ainda não sabem lidar com os caiaques. O que elas estão fazendo?”

“Estão construindo uma casinha de brincar. Eu sou muito velha para isso!” explodiu Adrianna.

A mãe sorriu, “O que te faz pensar isso?”

“Tenho certeza de que nenhuma das garotas da minha idade faz essas coisas com as irmãs pequenas.”

“Você tem certeza de que não está sendo egoísta?” perguntou a mãe. “Às vezes precisamos abrir mão do que queremos para que os outros possam ser felizes.”

Adrianna deu de ombros e foi ao galpão buscar um caiaque. Tirou seu caiaque azul do suporte e o levou até o lago. Encaixou o remo, sentou-se e empurrou o caiaque para a superfície lisa da água. Suspirou de prazer. Isso era muito melhor do que construir uma casinha na mata! Deu algumas voltas no lago antes de o remo começar a perder velocidade. De alguma forma não estava tão divertido dessa vez. Ouviu Asher e as meninas rindo e gritando enquanto brincavam. Talvez a mãe estivesse certa, pensou ela. Talvez eu fique mais feliz se abrir mão do que quero para que possamos todos brincar juntos. Lentamente remou até a margem do lago. Saiu do caiaque, puxou-o para fora da água e o virou para secar. Resoluta, saiu da pastagem para procurar Asher e as meninas.

“Ei! Lá vem a Adrianna!” chamou Emily feliz quando Adrianna apareceu.

Adrianna sorriu, “Parece que a casinha já está quase pronta,” disse ela, encorajadora. “O que vocês ainda precisam para terminá-la?”

“Ainda precisamos de um fogão e de algo para bancada,” disse Kianna.

“Posso ajudar a encontrar alguma coisa,” disse Adrianna. Juntas procuraram na mata e no galpão tábuas e troncos para terminar a casa. Quando chegou a hora do jantar e foram para dentro, Adrianna estava muito feliz. A mãe estava certa, pensou. É mais divertido abrir mão do meu jeito e fazer o que todo mundo quer.

This hymn became precious to my family and me several years ago as we awaited the birth of our fourth genetically challenged baby. We knew she couldn't stay with us very long. She passed away at just three days old. After researching this hymn, I was amazed to find out that the man whose story had inspired this hymn had lost eight out of his nine children.

The story of this man is a notable one. His 61 years on earth were marked by grief and loss, persecution and imprisonment. Yet, his dedication to Christ was outstanding, and his fire for God and zeal for preaching the gospel never waned until his last day.

Samuel Rutherford, son of a prosperous farmer, was born in the year 1600. His life began in the small village of Nisbet, Scotland. As we glimpse into his life, we notice the hand of God at work in Samuel’s early years. At only three years old, he was playing with his friends when he fell into the town well. His sister and friends ran to get help. When they returned, they found a very wet Samuel sitting on the grass beside the well. They asked him how he got out, and his reply was, "A bonny white man came and drew me out of the well." His family believed that God sent an angel to rescue him that day.

From what we know about Samuel Rutherford, he had two brothers and one sister. He was sent to school when he was young, and he became a very diligent scholar. He learned Latin and Greek so well that he eventually became a professor. He married Eupham Hamilton around 1624, soon after he began teaching at Edinburgh University. At this time, Samuel was yet unconverted and cared only for pursuing his academic goals.

In 1626, at the age of 26, Samuel came to a clear and saving faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. He said, "O but Christ hath a saving eye. When He first looked on me I was saved. It cost Him but a look to make hell quit to me." From that moment he was filled with a passion to preach and to speak about his Saviour. This change of life caused such a stir in the university that Rutherford ended up resigning his professorship.

In 1627, Samuel took his wife and two young children to Galloway, Scotland, where he began pastoring the small church of Anwoth. As he commenced his calling there he said, "I have received the commission from the royal and princely Master, my Lord Jesus, to preach Christ to the people." His passion was for the conversion of the people, and it is said that he seemed to be always praying, always preaching, always visiting the sick, always teaching and instructing, always writing or studying. The zeal with which he preached and his concern for the welfare of his congregation had a great effect on them. Not only them, but folks came from the surrounding towns and villages to hear his preaching. A friend once reported, "Many times I thought he would have flown out of the pulpit when he came to speak of Jesus Christ."

Samuel was not estranged from grief and sorrow. In 1631, only four short years after he began his work as a pastor, his wife passed away. His two children also became ill and left this world. In 1636, after nine years of preaching, he was banished to Aberdeen, where he was forbidden to preach the gospel. This was a very difficult time for him as he greatly missed his wife and children as well as his congregation, the Church at Anwoth. This time in his life is indeed one reason he is so well remembered, for he began writing letters back to his church people and friends. Out of the 365 letters he wrote, 220 of them were written during these 22 months of banishment.

The government eventually changed hands, which gave more liberty to the non-conformist Covenanters. Thereupon Rutherford quickly returned to his beloved flock at Anwoth. About a year later, in the fall of 1639, he again reluctantly left Anwoth but this time to fulfill an appointment to become Professor of Divinity at St Mary's College in St. Andrews. This change was difficult for him, as he again greatly missed his congregation. He writes, "My removal from my flock is so heavy to me, that it maketh my life a burden to me, I had never such a longing for death. The Lord help and hold up this sad clay."

After five months in his new position and having been alone for nearly ten years, the 40-year-old Samuel married Jean McMath. Together they had seven children. Sadly, six of them died in infancy and early childhood. Only a daughter named Agnes survived to adulthood.

Rutherford continued to be an influential leader in the non-conformist movement in Scotland for the next 20 years until 1660. With the death of Cromwell, the rule of the commonwealth came to an end, and Charles II was restored to power. Once again, the wrath of the monarchy fell on Samuel. He was summoned to appear before the judge and charged with high treason against the government for preaching the truth. He was put in prison to await execution. However, before the king could put him to death, Samuel became quite sick. He said, "I have a summons already from a superior Judge, and I behoove to answer my first summons and when your day arrives I shall be where few Kings and great folks come."

Late in the afternoon of the last day of his life in answer to the question, "What think ye now of Christ?" answered thusly, "Oh, that all my brethren in the land may know what a Master I have served, and what peace I have this day! I shall sleep in Christ, and when I awake, I shall be satisfied with His likeness. This night shall close the door, and put my anchor within the veil, and I shall go away in a sleep by five of the clock in the morning. Glory! glory to my Creator and my Redeemer forever! I Shall live and adore Him. Oh, for arms to embrace Him! Oh, for a well-tuned harp! Glory! glory dwelleth in Immanuel's land!" These words were heard by his wife, daughter and friends, and he was indeed with his Lord by five in the morning.

Nearly two centuries later, Annie Ross Cousin, a Scottish poet and hymn writer and the wife of a minister, was inspired by the life and writings of Samuel Rutherford. She summarized his life in a biographical hymn,"The Sands of Time are Sinking". This hymn was first published in 1857 in the Christian Treasury. Out of the nineteen original verses, only four are used in our hymn books. (in bold copy)

The sands of time are sinking,
The dawn of heaven breaks,
The summer morn I’ve sighed for,
The fair, sweet morn awakes:
Dark, dark hath been the midnight,
But dayspring is at hand,
And glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

2. Oh! well it is forever,
Oh! well forevermore
My nest hung in no forest
Of all this death-doomed shore!
Yea, let the vain world vanish,
As from the ship the stand,
While glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

3. There the Red Rose of Sharon
Unfolds its heart-most bloom.
And fills the air of Heaven
With ravishing perfume;
Oh, to behold its blossom,
While by its fragrance fann’d
Where glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

4. The King there in His beauty,
Without a veil is seen:
It were a well-spent journey
Though seven deaths lay between:
The Lamb with His fair army,
Doth on Mount Zion stand;
And glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

5. Oh! Christ He is the fountain,
The deep sweet well of Love!
The streams on earth I’ve tasted,
More deep I’ll drink above;
There, to an ocean fullness,
His mercy doth expand,
And glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

6. E’en Anwoth was not heaven—
E’en preaching was not Christ;
And in my sea-beat prison
My Lord and I held tryst:
And aye my murkiest storm-cloud
Was by a rainbow spann’d,
Caught from the glory dwelling
In Immanuel’s land.

7. But that He built a heaven
Of His surpassing love,
A little New Jerus’lem,
Like to the one above,—
“Lord, take me o’er the water,”
Had been my loud demand,
“Take me to love’s own country,
Unto Immanuel’s land.”

8. But flowers need night’s cool darkness,
The moonlight and the dew;
So Christ, from one who loved it,
His shining oft withdrew;
And then, for cause of absence,
My troubled soul I scann’d—
But glory, shadeless, shineth
In Immanuel’s land.

9. The little birds of Anwoth,
used to count them blest,—
Now, beside happier alters,
go to built my nest:
O’er these there broods no silence,
No graves around them stand,
For glory, deathless, dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

10. Fair Anwoth by the Solway,
To me thou still art dear!
E’en from the verge of Heaven
I drop for thee a tear.
Oh! if one soul from Anwoth
Meet me at God’s right hand,
My Heaven will be two Heavens,
In Immanuel’s land!

11. I’ve wrestled on towards Heaven,
‘Ganst storm, and wind, and tide;—
Now, like a weary traveler,
That leaneth on his guide,
Amid the shades of evening,
While sinks life’s ling’ring sand,
I hail the glory dawning
From Immanuel’s land.

12. Deep waters cross’d life’s pathway,
The hedge of thorns was sharp;
Now these lie all behind me,—
Oh, for a well-tuned harp!
Oh, to join Hallelujah
With yon triumphant band,
Who sing where glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land!

13. With mercy and with judgment
My web of time He wove,
And aye the dews of sorrow
Were lustered with His love!
I’ll bless the hand that guided,
I’ll bless the heart that plann’d,
When throned where glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

14. Soon shall the cup of glory
Wash down earth’s bitterest woes,
Soon shall the desert brier
Break into Eden’s rose:
The curse shall change to blessing–
The name on earth that’s bann’d,
Be graven on the white stone
In Immanuel’s land.

15. Oh! I am my Beloved’s,
And my Beloved’s mine!
He brings a poor vile sinner
Into His “house of wine:”
I stand upon His merit,
I know no other stand,
Not e’en where glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

16. I shall sleep sound in Jesus,
Fill’d with His likeness rise,
To live and to adore Him,
To see Him with these eyes:
‘Tween me and resurrection
But Paradise doth stand;
Then—then for glory dwelling
In Immanuel’s land!

17. The bride eyes not her garment,
But her dear Bridegroom’s face;
I will not gaze at glory,
But on my King of Grace—
Not at the crown He giveth,
But on His pierced hand:
The Lamb is all the glory
Of Immanuel’s land.

18. I have borne scorn and hatred,
I have borne wrong and shame,
Earth’s proud ones have reproach’d me,
For Christ’s thrice blessed name:
Where God His seal set fairest
They’ve stamp’d their foulest brand;
But judgment shines like noonday
In Immanuel’s land.

19. They’ve summoned me before them,
But there I may not come,—
My Lord says, “Come up hither,”
My Lord says, “Welcome home!
My King now at His white throne,
My presence doth command,
Where glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

The fine complementary tune for this text was composed in the early 1800s by a French musician, Chretien D`Urhan. It is well fitted to the words of the hymn—its solemn tempo matches the solemnity of the words. The rising melodic line of the last phrase perfectly matches the anticipated joy expressed by the refrain—"And glory, glory dwelleth in Immanuel's land."

As we conclude this hymn history, let us continue to marvel at the providence of God in the lives of those who have gone before us. May we follow Christ with all our hearts and be vessels ready for the Master's use! One last quote by Samuel Rutherford to take with us. "They lose nothing who gain Christ."

Il m'est incroyable de voir comment Dieu utilise Son peuple à travers l'histoire pour glorifier Son nom. Il use des choses faibles pour confondre les sages ; des choses viles pour réduire à néant la sagesse des hommes de ce monde. Dieu se sert de la faiblesse physique, des épreuves, de la perte, du deuil, du travail et de la douleur pour accroître nos trésors spirituels et bâtir Son royaume ici sur la terre !

Ce cantique est devenu précieux pour ma famille et moi il y a plusieurs années, alors que nous attendions la naissance de notre quatrième enfant porteur d'une anomalie génétique. Nous savions qu'elle ne pourrait pas rester longtemps avec nous. Elle est décédée à seulement trois jours. En recherchant l'histoire de ce cantique, j'ai été étonné d'apprendre que l'homme dont l'histoire avait inspiré ce chant avait perdu huit de ses neuf enfants.

L'histoire de cet homme est remarquable. Ses 61 années sur terre furent marquées par le chagrin et la perte, la persécution et l'emprisonnement. Pourtant, son dévouement envers le Christ était remarquable, et son zèle pour Dieu et pour la prédication de l'Évangile ne faiblit jamais jusqu'à son dernier jour.

Samuel Rutherford, fils d'un fermier prospère, naquit en l'an 1600. Sa vie commença dans le petit village de Nisbet, en Écosse. En jetant un coup d'œil sur son existence, on remarque la main de Dieu à l'œuvre durant les premières années de Samuel. À seulement trois ans, il jouait avec ses amis lorsqu'il tomba dans le puits de la ville. Sa sœur et ses amis coururent chercher de l'aide. À leur retour, ils trouvèrent un Samuel très mouillé assis sur l'herbe près du puits. Ils lui demandèrent comment il était sorti, et il répondit : « Un bel homme blanc est venu et m'a tiré du puits. » Sa famille crut que Dieu avait envoyé un ange pour le secourir ce jour-là.

D'après ce que nous savons de Samuel Rutherford, il avait deux frères et une sœur. Il fut envoyé à l'école dès son jeune âge et devint un étudiant très assidu. Il apprit si bien le latin et le grec qu'il devint finalement professeur. Il épousa Eupham Hamilton vers 1624, peu après avoir commencé à enseigner à l'Université d'Édimbourg. À cette époque, Samuel n'était pas encore converti et ne se préoccupait que de poursuivre ses objectifs académiques.

En 1626, à l'âge de 26 ans, Samuel arriva à une foi claire et salvatrice en le Seigneur Jésus-Christ. Il déclara : « Ô mais Christ a un œil qui sauve. Quand Il me regarda pour la première fois j'étais sauvé. Il ne Lui coûta qu'un regard pour rendre l'enfer vain pour moi. » Dès ce moment, il fut rempli d'une passion pour prêcher et parler de son Sauveur. Ce changement de vie provoqua un tel remous à l'université que Rutherford finit par démissionner de sa chaire.

En 1627, Samuel emmena sa femme et leurs deux jeunes enfants à Galloway, en Écosse, où il commença à diriger la petite église d'Anwoth. En entreprenant son ministère, il déclara : « J'ai reçu la commission du Maître royal et princier, mon Seigneur Jésus, pour prêcher Christ au peuple. » Sa passion visait la conversion des gens, et l'on disait qu'il semblait toujours en prière, toujours en train de prêcher, toujours en visite aux malades, toujours enseignant et instruisant, toujours écrivant ou étudiant. Le zèle de sa prédication et son souci du bien-être de sa congrégation eurent un grand effet sur eux. Non seulement les habitants d'Anwoth, mais des gens des villes et villages voisins vinrent entendre sa prédication. Un ami rapporta un jour : « Bien des fois j'ai cru qu'il allait s'envoler de la chaire quand il venait parler de Jésus-Christ. »

Samuel n'était pas étranger au chagrin et à la souffrance. En 1631, seulement quatre courtes années après le début de son ministère pastoral, sa femme mourut. Ses deux enfants tombèrent aussi malades et quittèrent ce monde. En 1636, après neuf ans de prédication, il fut banni à Aberdeen, où il se vit interdire de prêcher l'Évangile. Ce fut une période très difficile pour lui, car sa femme, ses enfants et sa congrégation d'Anwoth lui manquaient énormément. Cette période de sa vie est d'ailleurs une des raisons pour lesquelles on se souvient si bien de lui, car il commença à écrire des lettres à son peuple et à ses amis. Sur les 365 lettres qu'il écrivit, 220 furent rédigées durant ces 22 mois d'exil.

Le gouvernement changea finalement de mains, ce qui donna plus de liberté aux presbytériens non-conformistes (les Covenanters). Rutherford retourna promptement auprès de son troupeau bien-aimé à Anwoth. Environ un an plus tard, à l'automne 1639, il quitta de nouveau à regret Anwoth mais cette fois pour accepter une nomination comme professeur de théologie au St Mary's College à St. Andrews. Ce changement fut difficile pour lui, car sa congrégation lui manquait de nouveau profondément. Il écrit : « Mon éloignement de mon troupeau m'est si pénible, que cela fait de ma vie un fardeau pour moi, je n'ai jamais eu un tel désir de la mort. Que le Seigneur aide et soutienne cette pauvre chair. »

Après cinq mois dans sa nouvelle charge et ayant été seul pendant près de dix ans, le Samuel de 40 ans épousa Jean McMath. Ensemble ils eurent sept enfants. Hélas, six d'entre eux moururent en bas âge et durant la petite enfance. Seule une fille nommée Agnes survécut jusqu'à l'âge adulte.

Rutherford continua d'être un dirigeant influent du mouvement non-conformiste en Écosse pendant les vingt années suivantes, jusqu'en 1660. Avec la mort de Cromwell, le régime du Commonwealth prit fin et Charles II retrouva le pouvoir. Une fois de plus, la colère de la monarchie se déchaîna contre Samuel. Il fut sommé de comparaître devant le juge et accusé de haute trahison contre le gouvernement pour avoir prêché la vérité. Il fut emprisonné en attendant l'exécution. Cependant, avant que le roi ne put le faire mettre à mort, Samuel tomba gravement malade. Il dit : « J'ai déjà une convocation d'un Juge supérieur, et je dois répondre à ma première convocation et quand votre jour arrivera je serai là où peu de rois et de grands viennent. »

Tard dans l'après-midi du dernier jour de sa vie, en réponse à la question « Que pensez-vous maintenant du Christ ? » il répondit ainsi : « Oh, que tous mes frères dans le pays sachent quel Maître j'ai servi, et quelle paix j'ai aujourd'hui ! Je dormirai en Christ, et quand je me réveillerai, je serai rassasié de Sa ressemblance. Cette nuit fermera la porte, et mettra mon ancre au-dedans du voile, et je m'en irai dormir à cinq heures du matin. Gloire ! gloire à mon Créateur et mon Rédempteur pour toujours ! Je vivrai et L'adorerai. Oh, pour des bras afin de L'embrasser ! Oh, pour une harpe bien accordée ! Gloire ! la gloire habite dans la terre d'Emmanuel ! » Ces paroles furent entendues par sa femme, sa fille et ses amis, et il fut effectivement auprès de son Seigneur à cinq heures du matin.

Près de deux siècles plus tard, Annie Ross Cousin, poétesse et auteure de cantiques écossaise et épouse d'un pasteur, fut inspirée par la vie et les écrits de Samuel Rutherford. Elle résuma sa vie dans un cantique biographique, « The Sands of Time are Sinking ». Ce cantique fut publié pour la première fois en 1857 dans le Christian Treasury. Sur les dix-neuf couplets originaux, seulement quatre sont utilisés dans nos recueils de cantiques. (en copie en gras)

Les sables du temps s'ENFONCENT,
L'aube du ciel se lève,
Le matin d'été que j'ai soupiré,
Le beau et doux matin s'éveille :
Sombre, sombre a été la minuit,
Mais l'aurore est proche,
Et la gloire—la gloire habite
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel.

2. Oh ! que c'est pour toujours heureux,
Oh ! que pour toujours encore
Mon nid ne fut pas accroché
Dans quelque forêt de ce rivage voué à la mort !
Oui, que le monde vain s'évanouisse,
Comme on jette du bord le fardiau,
Tandis que la gloire—la gloire habite
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel.

3. Là la Rose rouge de Saron
Déploie son plus intime fleur.
Et emplit l'air du Ciel
D'un parfum ravissant ;
Oh, contempler sa floraison,
Tandis qu'on en est caressé par le souffle,
Où la gloire—la gloire habite
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel.

4. Le Roi là, dans Sa beauté,
Sans voile est vu :
Ce serait un voyage bien employé
Même si sept morts se trouvaient entre :
L'Agneau avec sa belle armée
Se tient sur le mont Sion ;
Et la gloire—la gloire habite
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel.

5. Oh ! Christ Il est la fontaine,
La profonde et douce source d'Amour !
Les ruisseaux que j'ai goûtés sur terre,
Plus profondément j'en boirai au-dessus ;
Là, jusqu'à une plénitude océanique,
Sa miséricorde s'étend,
Et la gloire—la gloire habite
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel.

6. Même Anwoth n'était pas le ciel—
Même la prédication n'était pas Christ ;
Et dans ma prison battue par la mer
Mon Seigneur et moi fîmes rendez-vous :
Et toujours mon nuage de tempête le plus sombre
Fut orné d'un arc-en-ciel,
Pris de la gloire habitant
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel.

7. Mais qu'il ait bâti un ciel
De Son amour surpassant,
Un petit Nouveau Jérusalem,
Semblable à celui d'en haut,—
« Seigneur, fais-moi passer par-dessus les eaux, »
Tel eût été mon cri ardent,
« Conduis-moi vers le pays de l'amour,
Vers la terre d'Emmanuel. »

8. Mais les fleurs ont besoin de l'obscurité fraîche de la nuit,
De la lumière de la lune et de la rosée ;
Ainsi Christ, de celui qui l'aimait,
Retirait souvent Sa lumière ;
Et alors, à cause de Son absence,
J'examinai mon âme troublée—
Mais la gloire, sans ombre, resplendit
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel.

9. Les petits oiseaux d'Anwoth,
que l'on jugeait bénis,—
Maintenant, près d'autels plus heureux,
vont y bâtir mon nid :
Sur eux ne plane aucun silence,
Aucune tombe autour d'eux ne se dresse,
Car la gloire, immortelle, habite
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel.

10. Belle Anwoth au bord du Solway,
Tu m'es toujours chère !
Même du seuil du Ciel
Je verse pour toi une larme.
Oh ! si une âme d'Anwoth
Me rencontre à la droite de Dieu,
Mon Ciel sera deux Cieux,
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel !

11. J'ai lutté vers le Ciel,
Contre la tempête, le vent et la marée ;—
Maintenant, comme un voyageur las,
Qui s'appuie sur son guide,
Parmi les ombres du soir,
Tandis que s'enfuit le sable de la vie,
J'accueille l'éclat de la gloire naissante
De la terre d'Emmanuel.

12. Des eaux profondes ont croisé le chemin de la vie,
Le roncier fut aigu ;
Maintenant tout cela est derrière moi,—
Oh, pour une harpe bien accordée !
Oh, pour joindre le Hallelujah
Au sein de cette troupe triomphante,
Qui chantent où la gloire habite
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel !

13. Avec miséricorde et jugement
Il tissa ma toile de temps,
Et toujours les rosées du chagrin
Brillaient de Son amour !
Je bénirai la main qui guida,
Je bénirai le cœur qui conçut le plan,
Quand je serai couronné là où la gloire habite
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel.

14. Bientôt la coupe de gloire
Laver[a] les plus amères douleurs de la terre,
Bientôt l'épine du désert
Rompra en la rose d'Éden :
La malédiction se changera en bénédiction—
Le nom sur terre qui est maudit,
Sera gravé sur la pierre blanche
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel.

15. Oh ! je suis à mon Bien-Aimé,
Et mon Bien-Aimé est à moi !
Il amène un pauvre pécheur vil
Dans Sa « maison de vin » :
Je tiens sur Son mérite,
Je ne connais aucun autre appui,
Même là où la gloire habite
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel.

16. Je dormirai profondément en Jésus,
Rempli de Sa ressemblance je ressusciterai,
Pour vivre et L'adorer,
Pour Le voir de mes propres yeux :
Entre moi et la résurrection
Se tient seulement le Paradis ;
Alors—alors pour habiter la gloire
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel !

17. La fiancée ne regarde pas sa robe,
Mais le visage de son cher Époux ;
Je ne contemplerai pas la gloire,
Mais mon Roi de Grâce—
Pas la couronne qu'Il donne,
Mais Sa main percée :
L'Agneau est toute la gloire
De la terre d'Emmanuel.

18. J'ai supporté le mépris et la haine,
J'ai supporté l'injustice et la honte,
Les orgueilleux de la terre m'ont insulté,
Pour le nom trois fois béni du Christ :
Là où Dieu plaça Son sceau le plus beau
Ils ont apposé leur marque la plus infâme ;
Mais le jugement resplendit comme le zénith
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel.

19. Ils m'ont convoqué devant eux,
Mais là je ne puis venir,—
Mon Seigneur dit, « Montez ici, »
Mon Seigneur dit, « Bienvenue chez toi ! »
Mon Roi maintenant à Son trône blanc,
Ma présence y commande,
Où la gloire—la gloire habite
Dans la terre d'Emmanuel.

La belle mélodie complémentaire pour ce texte fut composée au début des années 1800 par un musicien français, Chretien D'Urhan. Elle convient bien aux paroles du cantique—son tempo solennel correspond à la solennité des paroles. La ligne mélodique ascendante de la dernière phrase correspond parfaitement à la joie anticipée exprimée par le refrain—« And glory, glory dwelleth in Immanuel's land. »

En concluant cette histoire du cantique, continuons d'admirer la providence de Dieu dans la vie de ceux qui nous ont précédés. Puissions-nous suivre Christ de tout notre cœur et être des vases prêts à l'usage du Maître ! Une dernière citation de Samuel Rutherford à emporter : « They lose nothing who gain Christ. »

Our spiritual forefathers had much to say on the many issues facing the American Mennonite church in their time, and we can still learn from the collected writings of these church leaders and brethren. We will look first at the hermeneutics of the early American Mennonite church, endeavoring to draw examples from which we, as 21st-century Christians, can learn.

First, the correct interpretation of Scripture was a matter of great importance to these earlier Christians. They had only recently emigrated away from a largely hostile area, where they had been constantly tested to the point of death on matters of faith and now faced a different set of challenges when confronted with peace and religious freedom. We will look at how they navigated these challenges by studying several of their doctrines and practices.

The Doctrine of Nonresistance

One matter that was well interpreted and applied by many of the early Mennonite writers is the principle and doctrine of the nonresistant Christian. Although many of their Anabaptist descendants of today still hold, to varying degrees, this doctrine, it is oftentimes not done with the clarity and solemnity of their forefathers. The early American Mennonites understood nonresistance as a foundational aspect of the Christian life, as it should be, and taught extensively on the practical application and appearance of nonresistance in the life of a believer. Their primary motivation for living peaceably and without malice toward one’s fellow man was the given example of Jesus. Christ typified the acceptable response to violence and ill-will: gentleness, meekness, as befitted one who is called a Lamb.

The Emphasis of Biblical Foundations

There was also a firm focus amongst early Mennonite writers against building doctrine on the writings of men. This emphasis comes through strongly in their works, as they quote Scripture extensively. They made their point by bringing in an example of Christ or by way of an applicable Scripture verse, rather than building on the sandy soil of a man’s opinions. One of the areas in which they did so was the matter of salvation.

Importance of Practical Salvation

We can learn much from the early Mennonites about the practical working out of salvation. First, salvation is portrayed as both an inward and an outward change. The inward is affected first through the working of the Holy Spirit in the willful sinner’s life. It is an important distinction that the sinner is willful. This position was contrary to most of the greater established churches of the time. If a sinner must be willful, then it implies that all men can willfully accept salvation, an idea that is fundamental in nature, if not always verbalized, to the church of today.

In the early Mennonites’ time, predestination as taught by Calvinism seems to have necessitated this emphasis on man’s ability to choose freely, which is still true today. There is also another flavoring of the “unwillingly saved” interpretation, and that comes from the aftereffects of the charismatic movement and the effect it has had on Mennonite and Amish circles. This “unwilling salvation” is not a matter of predestination, but rather is described as almost a coercive calling by the Spirit. It has been observed in several salvation testimonies where the testifiers recalled how they were completely comfortable in their lives of sin and debauchery when suddenly they would be struck down in the manner of Saul and could not help themselves but follow after God and give their lives to Him. There are numerous pitfalls with this dramatic understanding of conversion, namely that it absolves responsibility from the one converted for his decision to convert. This leads to a lack of counting the cost of Christianity, which is a death of oneself, a death of pride, and a death of favor with man. If the believer hops headfirst into Christianity, not reckoning that he must give up all these self-pleasing traits, how will he be able to grow spiritually if he cannot let go of his former vices? While this form of conversion may be genuine at the beginning, it does not often progress beyond the milk of the Word to the meat of which a mature Christian must partake. This maturing of a Christian is emphasized in writings ranging from those of Menno Simons up to Abraham Goshalk. It is also important for the sake of the church that the believer be firmly committed and engaged in the steady growth of his faith.

The Seriousness of a Pure Church

The idea of church to the early American Mennonite seems to have been a more serious thought, less individualistic than our current state. It is the pitiable state of nominal Christianity that the church has become a social organization with room for all sin and depravity.

It behooves us to consider closely the character of the church that Christ established and to note as well the character of the true churches, unspotted by apostasy and laxness. This character is, like Christ himself, simple and yet incredibly full of meaning and spiritual vitality.

The first aspect of the church to recognize is its pure state as the bride of Christ. Here again, we should consider the character of Christ. Did He ever give Himself space for sin? Do we find Him occasionally indulging in a brief enjoyment of a “guilty pleasure”? The understanding reader will agree that Christ was pure in His entirety, and so how else should the bride be with which He is to be intimately and eternally joined? To aid our minds in answering such a question, let us consider the earthly symbol of this heavenly union: that of a man and a woman joined together for life. This earthly union is recognized even by non-Christians as something set aside purely for the two individuals involved, a relationship and a sharing of each other that is not and never to be partaken of by anyone outside of the intimate union. This paints clearly for our earth-bound minds the mind of Christ, insomuch as that marriage is a symbol of Christ and His bride. The bride and Christ are for each other and give themselves to nothing and no one other.

Now that we can see the purity of the church, let us examine its practical working out amongst fallen man. If it is to be pure, then how are we to be a part of it? Here enters the need for a clear understanding of regeneration, a doctrine held in high regard by these Mennonite forefathers. They taught that the Spirit affects the spiritual washing and cleansing that will be made apparent in a changed state of thought and action in the believer. This change is still at variance with our fallen nature, but through continued surrender and a deep humility, the Spirit will fill the believer until the nature of sin becomes the dominated instead of the dominant. It is important to realize, however, that this victory over sin is brought into effect by the believer yielding his will and allowing the Spirit complete control.

Thus, a pure church is a surrendered, Spirit-filled group of believers who recognize in true humility that their power is not in any way linked to their own merit. The absence of pride, achieved only by the constant aid of the Spirit, gives further room for purification of the willing believer. In this way, we can see the Christian life in shoe leather.

The Teachings of Practical Christianity

The practicality of the early American Mennonite’s faith was continually on display. In his book, “Pride and Humility,” John M. Brenneman maintains that the outward appearance of a person is directly related to his inward heart, a view which extends as well to the actions of the individual. It is necessary to build on the beliefs of willful salvation, regeneration, and a pure church previously examined to frame the mindset of a Mennonite’s interactions in daily living.

To these serious-minded Christians, there was no difference in importance between the religious belief expressed on Sundays and the mundane actions of the rest of the week. This is evidenced by their general abstinence from political matters and other elements of a worldly nature that would infringe upon the beliefs they held. This put them in direct opposition to many of the churches of their day, where thrived two schools of thought: either that one’s earthly duties in a political manner were carried out completely separate from one’s faith, or that the accomplishment of these civic duties were incorporated in the will of God and so permissible for the Christian to engage in freely.

To the early American Mennonite, these types of stances betrayed the very meaning of his Christianity: he was a new person, alive only in the power of Christ that flowed through him. This influenced and directed every aspect of his life, from his business dealings, which were carried out in a way so as not to take advantage of any party involved, to his dress and manner of deportment, which was to be based on humility and plainness, to his method of conversing with his fellow man, which was to show a genuine concern for the spiritual well-being and eternal destiny.

Conclusion

The sum of all these colonial Mennonite beliefs was the doctrine of how to grow into a mature, humble, repentant, but spiritually powerful servant of God. He denied the allures of the world around him in favor of an eternal reward promised upon the purity of his faith and willing renunciation of the sin in which he had formerly lived. This example, lived out by believers like us, should inspire us to further press into the Kingdom of God, working out our faith in humility and repentance.

Våra andliga föregångare hade mycket att säga om de många frågor som den amerikanska mennonitiska kyrkan stod inför på deras tid, och vi kan fortfarande lära oss av dessa kyrkoledares och bröders samlade skrifter. Vi ska först titta på hermeneutiken hos den tidiga amerikanska mennonitiska kyrkan och försöka utvinna exempel som vi, som kristna på 2000-talet, kan lära oss av.

För det första var korrekt tolkning av Skriften en fråga av stor vikt för dessa tidiga kristna. De hade endast nyligen emigrerat bort från ett till stora delar fientligt område, där de ständigt blivit prövade till döds på trosfrågor och nu stod inför en annan uppsättning utmaningar när de möttes av fred och religionsfrihet. Vi ska se hur de navigerade dessa utmaningar genom att studera flera av deras doktriner och praktiker.

Läran om icke-motstånd

En fråga som många av de tidiga mennonitiska författarna tolkade och tillämpade väl var principen och läran om den icke-motståndande kristen. Även om många av deras anabaptistiska efterföljare idag i varierande grad fortfarande håller fast vid denna lära, sker det ofta inte med samma klarhet och högtidlighet som hos deras föregångare. De tidiga amerikanska mennoniterna förstod icke-motstånd som en grundläggande aspekt av det kristna livet, såsom det bör vara, och undervisade utförligt om den praktiska tillämpningen och uttrycket av icke-motstånd i en troendes liv. Deras främsta motivation för att leva fridfullt och utan illvilja mot sin nästa var den givna förebilden i Jesus. Kristus typifierade det acceptabla svaret på våld och illvilja: mildhet, ödmjukhet, såsom bebor en som kallas ett Lamm.

Bibelska grunder i fokus

Det fanns också ett starkt fokus bland de tidiga mennonitiska författarna mot att bygga doktrin på människors skrifter. Denna betoning framträder tydligt i deras verk, där de citerar Skriften omfattande. De gjorde sin poäng genom att hänvisa till ett exempel i Kristus eller genom ett tillämpligt skriftställe, snarare än att bygga på en människas lösa åsikter. Ett av de områden där de gjorde detta var frågor rörande frälsningen.

Betydelsen av praktisk frälsning

Vi kan lära oss mycket av de tidiga mennoniterna om hur frälsningen praktiskt verkställs. För det första framställs frälsningen som både en inre och en yttre förändring. Det inre påverkas först genom den Helige Andes verk i den viljefasta syndarens liv. Det är en viktig distinktion att syndaren är viljefast. Denna ståndpunkt stod i motsats till de flesta av tidens större etablerade kyrkor. Om en syndare måste vara viljefast, innebär det att alla människor kan viljemässigt acceptera frälsning, en tanke som är grundläggande till sin natur, även om den inte alltid uttalas, för den kyrka vi har idag.

På de tidiga mennoniternas tid synes predestination enligt kalvinismen ha gjort denna betoning på människans förmåga att fritt välja nödvändig, vilket fortfarande är sant idag. Det finns också en annan färgning av tolkningen ”motvilligt frälst”, och den kommer från efterverkningarna av den karismatiska rörelsen och dess effekt på mennonitiska och amish-kretsar. Denna ”motvilliga frälsning” är inte en fråga om predestination, utan beskrivs snarare som en nästan tvångsmässig kallelse av Anden. Det har observerats i flera vittnesbörd om frälsning där vittnena återkallade hur de var fullkomligt bekväma i sina liv i synd och utsvävning när de plötsligt slogs ned på samma sätt som Saul och inte kunde låta bli att följa efter Gud och ge sitt liv åt Honom. Det finns många fallgropar med denna dramatiska förståelse av omvändelsen, nämligen att den fritar den omvända från ansvar för sitt beslut att omvända. Detta leder till en brist på att räkna kostnaden för kristendomen, vilket är en död av sig själv, en död av stolthet och en död av människors gunst. Om den troende hoppar huvudet före in i kristendomen utan att inse att han måste avstå från alla dessa självnöjande drag, hur ska han då kunna växa andligt om han inte kan släppa sina tidigare laster? Medan denna form av omvändelse kan vara genuin i början, går den ofta inte vidare från Skriftens modersmjölk till den föda som en mogen kristen måste ta del av. Denna mognad av en kristen betonas i skrifter från Menno Simons ända fram till Abraham Goshalk. Det är också viktigt för kyrkans skull att den troende är fast förankrad och engagerad i en stadig tillväxt i sin tro.

Kyrkans renhet tas på största allvar

Föreställningen om kyrkan hos de tidiga amerikanska mennoniterna synes ha varit en allvarligare tanke, mindre individualistisk än vårt nuvarande tillstånd. Det är en bedrövlig tillvaro av nominell kristendom att kyrkan har blivit en social organisation med rum för all synd och fördervelse.

Det ankommer oss att noggrant överväga karaktären hos den kyrka som Kristus upprättade och att också lägga märke till karaktären hos de sanna kyrkorna, opåverkade av avfall och slapphet. Denna karaktär är, liksom Kristus själv, enkel och ändå oerhört full av innebörd och andlig vitalitet.

Den första aspekten av kyrkan att känna igen är dess rena tillstånd som Kristi brud. Återigen bör vi betrakta Kristi karaktär. Gav Han någonsin sig själv utrymme för synd? Hittar vi Honom ibland tillåta ett kort nöje i en ”skyldig glädje”? Den förstående läsaren håller med om att Kristus var hel i sin helhet, och hur annars bör bruden vara med vilken Han ska vara intimt och evigt förenad? För att hjälpa våra jordbundna sinnen att svara på en sådan fråga, låt oss betrakta det jordiska symbolet för denna himmelska förening: en man och en kvinna förenade för livet. Denna jordiska förening erkänns även av icke-kristna som något avsett uteslutande för de två individerna inblandade, ett förhållande och ett delande av varandra som inte är och aldrig ska delas av någon utanför den intima föreningen. Detta målar klart för våra jordiska sinnen Kristi sinne, i så mån att äktenskapet är en symbol för Kristus och Hans brud. Bruden och Kristus är för varandra och ger sig själva åt inget annat och ingen annan.

Nu när vi kan se kyrkans renhet, låt oss granska dess praktiska verkning bland fallna människor. Om den ska vara ren, hur ska vi då vara en del av den? Här träder behovet av en klar förståelse av födelsen på nytt in, en lära högt aktad av dessa mennonitiska föregångare. De undervisade att Anden påverkar den andliga tvagningen och reningen som blir uppenbar i en förvandlad tanke- och handlingsordning hos den troende. Denna förändring står fortfarande i motsats till vår fallna natur, men genom fortsatt överlåtelse och djup ödmjukhet kommer Anden att fylla den troende tills syndens natur blir den dominerade istället för den dominerande. Det är viktigt att inse dock att denna seger över synden förverkligas genom att den troende överlämnar sin vilja och tillåter Anden full kontroll.

Således är en ren kyrka en överlämnad, Andefylld skara troende som i sann ödmjukhet inser att deras kraft på inget sätt är knuten till deras egen förtjänst. Frånvaron av stolthet, uppnådd endast genom Andens ständiga hjälp, ger vidare utrymme för rening av den viljefulla troende. På detta sätt kan vi se det kristna livet i vardagens konkreta handling.

Lärorna om praktisk kristendom

De tidiga amerikanska mennoniternas tro var ständigt praktiskt synlig. I sin bok, "Stolthet och ödmjukhet," hävdar John M. Brenneman att en persons yttre uppenbarelse är direkt relaterad till hans inre hjärta, en syn som även sträcker sig till individens handlingar. Det är nödvändigt att bygga på de tidigare undersökta övertygelserna om viljemässig frälsning, återfödelse och en ren kyrka för att rama in en mennonits sinnelag i vardagliga möten.

För dessa allvarstänkta kristna fanns ingen skillnad i betydelse mellan den religiösa övertygelsen som uttrycktes på söndagar och de världsliga handlingarna under resten av veckan. Detta bevisas av deras allmänna avhållsamhet från politiska frågor och andra världsliga element som skulle inkräkta på deras hållningar. Detta ställde dem i direkt motsättning till många av sin tids kyrkor, där två skolor frodades: antingen att ens jordiska plikter i politiskt hänseende utfördes helt åtskilt från ens tro, eller att fullgörandet av dessa medborgerliga plikter inlemmades i Guds vilja och därför var tillåtna för kristna att fritt engagera sig i.

För den tidiga amerikanska mennoniten förrådde dessa ståndpunkter själva innebörden av hans kristendom: han var en ny människa, levande endast i den kraft av Kristus som flöt genom honom. Detta påverkade och styrde varje aspekt av hans liv, från hans affärsmetoder, som utfördes så att ingen part skulle utnyttjas, till hans klädsel och uppförande, som skulle grundas i ödmjukhet och enkelhet, till hans sätt att samtala med sina medmänniskor, som skulle visa en genuin omsorg för deras andliga välbefinnande och eviga öde.

Slutsats

Summan av alla dessa koloniala mennonitiska övertygelser var läran om hur man växer till en mogen, ödmjuk, omvänd men andligt kraftfull Guds tjänare. Han förnekade världens lockelser till förmån för ett evigt löfte som gavs på grund av renheten i hans tro och viljemässig förnekelse av den synd i vilken han tidigare levt. Detta exempel, levt ut av troende som vi, bör inspirera oss att ännu mer tränga in i Guds rike och utverka vår tro i ödmjukhet och omvändelse.

Spring is my favorite time of the year. Everything is new. Hyacinths are trying their noble best to poke their buds through the cold constraint of the winter-bound earth. Migrating waterfowl bring new sounds as they honk and quack their way to their final nesting places. This year the spring peepers in our area were “winter peepers” as they feebly squeaked their greetings to the arriving spring in mid-February. Tree buds are swelling, waiting to burst forth in full glory.

Oh, the magnificence of God’s nature joining forces to proclaim the glory of new life. Surely it must have been during this exuberant time of the year when the Psalmist wrote, “Let the floods clap their hands: let the hills be joyful together before the LORD; for he cometh to judge the earth: with righteousness shall he judge the world, and the people with equity” (Psalms 98:8-9). This display of new life springing from the earth is a beautiful representation of new life found in Christ Jesus. The wonders of the newness of life springing from the deadness of sin cannot be fully displayed by even the best show of God’s creation. It can only be experienced within the soul.

As I write this, I am flying 35,000 feet over the sub-Saharan desert land of Chad and Niger. The stark contrast between the landscape described in the previous paragraphs and the parched desert land hurrying by six miles below me is nearly beyond my comprehension. The dry earth begs for rain as livestock scrounge for anything green to fulfill their appetite. The vast dryness loudly proclaims a reminder of the millions of parched souls who have never heard of the “well of water springing up into everlasting life” (John 4:14). Millions who never experienced Christ the fountain as described in the Hymn History article in this issue:

Oh! Christ He is the foutain,
The deep sweet well of Love!
The streams on earth I’ve tasted,
More deep I’ll drink above:
There, to an ocean fullness,
His mercy doth expand,
And glory—glory dwelleth
In Immanuel’s land.

At times a yearning stirs in my heart to live the relaxed, relational lifestyle experienced in these impoverished tribal communities. Family and friends are more important than calendars and commitments. As we read in the Sister to Sister article, commitments and busyness can bring us to the overload point when we feel we cannot handle anything more. Read more to learn how to take practical steps to avoid that breaking point.

Most people in this area are Muslims. As I write this, Muslims are in the middle of Ramadan, a month-long season of fasting. They fast from food and water every day from dawn to dusk, even though daytime temperatures exceed 110 degrees. Their rigorous fasting, along with stopping their work to pray many times a day, is driven by a fervent desire to seek forgiveness of sins and obtain enough merit to enter heaven. If they only knew that true grace and mercy comes from God through the salvation of his Son, Jesus Christ. Our works can never bring us into right standing with God. The writer of the article “How to Increase Your Faith” clearly points this out “Faith is one of the basic ingredients in getting right with God. We come into the Christian life (and receive the forgiveness of sins) through faith. . . We abandon all hope for saving ourselves by our own abilities, and instead, we put complete trust in Jesus Christ for our eternal safety.”

As we plant our gardens and watch the trees burst forth in bloom, let us be reminded of the words of the prophet Isaiah, “For as the earth bringeth forth her bud, and as the garden causeth the things that are sown in it to spring forth; so the Lord GOD will cause righteousness and praise to spring forth before all the nations” (Isaiah 61:11).

Blessings to all,

Edward Martin
